Peter Schiff Is Not Optimistic...

Authored by Peter Schiff via X,

The most likely legislation Congress can pass that Trump will sign will preserve all the tax cuts Trump brags about but include all the extra spending that Democrats want. It may also contain a complete repeal of the national debt ceiling and price controls on credit card interest rates. The result will be massive increases in already massive federal budget deficits.

If the economy also slips into recession due to a big slowdown in AI capex, budget deficits currently running at around $3 trillion annually could rise to nearly $5 trillion. That will send the national debt soaring to $50 trillion by the end of Trump's term. To accommodate those massive deficits, the Fed will open up the monetary spigots like never before, launching the mother of all QE programs. The U.S. dollar will tank, and consumer prices will go through the roof.

This will also put substantial upward pressure on long-term bond yields and mortgage rates, crushing the economy and housing market. To avoid a worse financial crisis than in 2008, the Fed will choose higher inflation instead and buy Treasuries and MBS in record amounts. Since the Fed won't buy corporate or municipal bonds, expect those yields to soar, wreaking havoc on state and local governments and the stock market.

Since credit card interest rates will likely be capped, expect most consumers to be completely cut off from credit. If price controls extend to consumer goods, expect shortages, long lines, black markets, widespread power outages, and civil unrest.

Since the war can't really end unless we surrender by caving in to Iran's demands, it will likely continue. Since the Strategic Petroleum Reserve will run dry if we don't stop the drain, oil prices will rise sharply, perhaps to $150-$200 per barrel. Even if Trump manages to end the war by promoting a defeat as a great victory, oil prices will rise anyway.

The 2028 election will be a blame game, with each party accusing the other of being responsible for the worst economy ever and the highest inflation in U.S. history. Voters have a track record of blaming presidents and their parties for the affordability crises, so not only will the Democrats win the White House, but they will also increase their majorities in both houses of Congress, likely reaching a filibuster-proof 60 seats in the Senate. Their policies will risk turning record-high inflation into hyperinflation.

The only thing you can do now is protect yourself, as there is nothing you can do to protect the country. In fact, by not going broke like the vast majority of Americans will, you will be better positioned to help rebuild what both Democrats and Republicans will have destroyed.

Load up on gold and silver now while you can still afford to buy them.

items.title: Asia's Bailout Brigade: Taiwan Curbs Shorts, Readies $15BN Fund As Seoul Waives Margin Calls To Stop The AI Rout
items.content_text:
Asia's Bailout Brigade: Taiwan Curbs Shorts, Readies $15BN Fund As Seoul Waives Margin Calls To Stop The AI Rout

It took just a few hours long for the AI unwind to go from a Wall Street problem to an Asian government problem.

After the post-midterm "sell everything" day in which the Nasdaq suffered its worst day since Covid and the SOX plunged 12%, Asia opened on Friday into a liquidation: Taiwan's Taiex plunged as much as 9% and entered a bear market, Korea's Kospi crashed as much as 8.8%, tripping a 20-minute market-wide halt and briefly breaking below 5,000, and the Nikkei joined the bear market club with a 6% drop. By the time Europe woke up, both Taipei and Seoul had pulled the emergency brake.

In Taiwan, according to Bloomberg, the Financial Supervisory Commission will impose curbs on short selling from Nov. 9, while the Finance Ministry said it is prepared to deploy its NT$500 billion ($15 billion) stock stabilization fund. In Korea, Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il promised "proactive" measures to stop the market "from reacting excessively relative to the fundamentals of our economy," and backed it up by suspending the margin-loan collateral rule that forces brokers to dump leveraged retail positions.

We saw it coming. At 9:06pm ET on Thursday, hours before the official announcements, we tweeted that Taipei was heading straight to bailouts:

Which is about as surprising as the sun rising in the east: these are the same two governments, using the same playbook, that have tried this before. The question is whether it works any better this time, when the thing being sold is the AI trade itself.

Taipei Dusts Off The April 2025 Crisis Kit

The Taiwanese package is, almost to the decimal point, a rerun. The FSC will cut the cap on intraday short-sale orders of borrowed securities to 3% of a stock's average daily volume over the prior 30 days, down from 30%, and raise the minimum margin requirement for short sales to 130% from 90% (Goldman's Asia prime desk flagged the regulator's notice to clients within minutes, helpfully offering to "help with long sell borrow over the weekend"). Those are exactly the numbers Taipei rolled out in April 2025, when Trump's Liberation Day tariffs crushed the Taiex into a bear market.

The Finance Ministry, for its part, did not mince words: it pointed to continued foreign selling as evidence of "a significant deterioration in market confidence." Which, in fairness, is the most honest thing any official said on Friday.

The damage was historic. The Taiex closed down 4.5% after the intraday plunge, but still posted its biggest weekly loss since 2001, while TSMC, which had been down nearly 10% at the open, closed 4.7% lower. According to Goldman's Asia desk (available to pro subs in the bank's Regional Wrap, futures and TSMC touched limit down, the OTC index had already erased its YTD gain, and the client chatter "focused mostly on retail capitulation and a potential short-selling ban." The desk itself "was very busy selling and shorting intraday, probably the highest activity level in the past three months."

Translation: everyone saw the short ban coming and got their shorts on before the door closed. Market efficiency at its finest.

Foreigners Sell, Locals Catch Knives

Taipei's real problem is the size of the foreign exit. In his latest flow and positioning observations (available to pro subs), Goldman's Harrison Flagler lays out the numbers, and they are brutal:

FINI outflow on Thursday of USD$3.1bn extended the selling streak to a 6th consecutive sessions totaling USD$19.2bn in outflows (and that is part of a larger trend of selling 19 of twenty sessions since 10/6 totaling USD$48bn outflows). In contrast, local funds continued to net buy for an 18th consecutive session, buying USD$11bn over that period. As a result, this extended the divergence of foreign vs local funds activity YTD, with FINI having net sold USD$86.7bn in the TWSE (incl. USD$68.9bn in TSMC), vs local funds having bought USD$33.5bn in the TWSE (incl. USD$10.6bn in TSMC).

Here is what that divergence looks like (chart source: Goldman, Bloomberg):

Bloomberg's tally is a bit more conservative at "only" $45 billion-plus of foreign net selling this quarter, but either way the math is not kind to the stabilization fund. NT$500 billion is about $15 billion, or roughly one-third of what foreigners have pulled out since Oct. 6, and one-sixth of this year's exodus. Put differently, Taiwan just brought a knife to a gunfight:

The defense extends to the currency, too. Bloomberg reported that USD/TWD briefly hit 33.04, its highest since April 2025, before the Taiwan dollar reversed to close 0.3% stronger at 32.768 per dollar as exporters, state-owned banks and life insurers sold dollars, the usual proxies when Taiwan's central bank would rather not leave fingerprints. Regular readers will recall that Asia's central banks were already dumping dollars to fight the tape back on Oct. 15, the day the AI unwind first went global and Taiwan suffered a record ~$9.3 billion foreign outflow. That record didn't last long either.

Meanwhile, the local buyers propping up the market are increasingly leveraged ones. Goldman notes that the retail margin balance dropped 3.4% on Thursday to its lowest since Aug. 31, but "as a percent of market cap, the margin balance remains near the recent highs" (chart source: Goldman, Bloomberg):

In other words, the forced-selling fuel hasn't burned off yet, which may explain why Taipei is going after the shorts instead.

Seoul Suspends Margin Calls (Again)

If Taiwan's day was historic, Korea's was merely the latest in a year of historic days. The Kospi tumbled as much as 8.8% at the open, triggering a circuit breaker, in a year that had already produced eight of the Kospi's 14 circuit-breaker halts since the Dot-Com era by late July. It closed down 6% at 5,059.7, as SK Hynix sank 10.4% and Samsung 6.4%. We put the round trip in perspective overnight:

Seoul's response came within hours:

Specifically, starting Nov. 9, brokers will be exempt for three months from the requirement to maintain a 140% collateral ratio on margin loans, so they don't have to liquidate retail accounts as prices fall. It is the first such reprieve since July 2022 (and before that, March 2020), and officials said more steps are ready if volatility widens.

The catch? The waiver is optional, and the brokers are the ones left holding the bad debt. According to the Seoul Economic Daily, same-day responses were limited to lowering collateral ratios by 10 to 20 points for clients who apply and deferring forced sales by one day, and critics point out that the 2020 version was followed by large-scale forced selling a week later. One unnamed securities official estimated that a 10-point cut buffers roughly another 7% decline. Which, given that the Kospi just fell 8.8% in a morning, is not a lot of buffer.

Goldman's Seoul desk, for its part, argues the leverage has already been flushed. In the bank's Korea market wrap, Emily Jee writes that "a cleaner setup in margin balance may have helped prevent an amplified post-circuit breaker sell-off, with margin loan balance relative to market cap currently sitting at 0.6%" (chart source: Goldman GIR, John Kwon):

Indeed, margin loans have fallen to about 28.6 trillion won, down 26% from the June 24 peak. The problem is that the dip buyers are running low on ammo too: investor deposits have collapsed 36.6% from their June peak to 88.5 trillion won, even as retail investors scooped up a net 4.5 trillion won over the past six sessions while foreigners dumped 12 trillion won.

The foreign selling, meanwhile, shows no sign of stopping. Per Goldman, foreigners sold another $2.0 billion on Friday, their sixth straight session of net selling, and the streak in the Kospi has now stretched to 12 consecutive weeks and $44.1 billion. Locals and retail continue to catch what they can. Back in September, we warned that only record buybacks were preventing a Kospi crash; a month later the only buyer had left the building. Now the government is the buyer of last resort, at least in spirit.

And in one case, in person: Park Yong-jin, vice chairman of Korea's presidential Committee on Regulatory Rationalization, announced on Facebook that he had bought 128 shares of the KODEX 200 ETF on Friday morning, about 10 million won, or roughly $6,800, because "I believe in the underlying strength of our economy." Against $44 billion of foreign selling, we estimate he only needs about 6.5 million more friends.

"Orderly"... Says The Desk

The irony is that the trading desks on the ground did not see panic. Goldman's Sean Navin (whose Friday wrap was aptly titled "Master of Puppets") wrote that while flows were 10-15% above the 20-day average, "the flow has been orderly, and we have not seen any significant signs of panic." The bank's Seoul team agreed, describing "limited signs of aggressive selling or capitulation" and a pad activity level of just 4 out of 10.

Navin also flagged the one thing worth watching: "keep an eye on the retail investor in the region." While foreigners have been dumping, retail in Taiwan and Korea "continue to be more constructive"... which is a polite way of saying they are the ones holding the bag if this turns into something worse.

The rest of Asia is improvising too. Japan's PM Takaichi said she is watching developments carefully while her chief cabinet secretary declined to comment at all; in China, Goldman calculates that inflows into the 14 ETFs favored by the "national team" have surpassed 400 billion yuan since mid-October, far more than during the April 2025 intervention. India, the one market that needs no help, is having its best week since 2021 as funds rotate out of AI. And in rates, Goldman's EM Asia desk notes Korean 5Y and 10Y swaps ripped about 15bps this week, with "KOSPI the dominant driver."

1998... Or 2022?

So will it work? Goldman's Rich Privorotsky, who admitted "what I got wrong" on AI just yesterday, frames the global question in his note "Liquidation. 1998 or 2000.":

Is this a 1998 style liquidity crisis and buying opportunity, or March 2000 and the beginning of a structural technology unwind? I lean toward 1998. Russia's default/LTCM were the external shocks but US growth remained intact. Once liquidity returned and the Fed eased, markets recovered rapidly... The uncomfortable parallel with 2000 is the sheer scale of spending and uncertainty around returns.

For Taipei and Seoul, history offers two templates. The optimistic one is April 2025, when the identical Taiwanese package was followed by a rebound... but only after the Taiex plunged a record 9.7% the very next morning, the day after the fund was authorized, and only because Trump paused tariffs hours later. The less optimistic one is 2022, when Bloomberg chronicled how plunging markets defied government intervention in Taiwan and Korea for months, as short-sale curbs, stabilization funds and FX intervention ran headlong into a Fed that kept hiking.

Our money is on something closer to the second. In 2025, the shock was a policy that could be (and was) reversed with a Truth Social post. This time, the shock is a new Congress and new governors gunning for data centers, and the trade being unwound is the one these two economies spent the past two years leveraging up on. Curbing short sellers and waiving margin calls probably slows the selling at the margin. What neither does is create a buyer for $87 billion of chip stocks, and the shorts were never the main problem anyway: Goldman's prime book shows long sales outnumbered short sales roughly 5 to 1 across Asia in October, and you don't need to borrow anything to sell what you already own.

Then again, nothing says "orderly market" like two governments rewriting the trading rules over a weekend.

Much more in the full Goldman "Flow and positioning observations" and the "GS Korea Final" notes, both available to pro subs.

items.title: FBI Arrests Meghan Markle's Father At Florida Care Home In Child Porn Case
items.content_text:
FBI Arrests Meghan Markle's Father At Florida Care Home In Child Porn Case

Philippine investigators say they've counted about 7,500 images and a video - and now call the son who turned him in a "person of interest."

Thomas Markle Sr., the estranged father of Meghan Markle, was arrested by federal agents in Florida on Friday morning on charges related to child sexual abuse material, two people familiar with the matter told the Associated Press, whose sources said he was taken into custody outside Tampa.

The Daily Mail, which first reported the arrest, said the 82-year-old was picked up at the Maravida Senior Living community in Lakeland. TMZ confirmed that FBI agents arrested him at the facility, and three sources confirmed the arrest to CBS News. Photos published by the Daily Mail and the Sun show him handcuffed in a wheelchair.

A Justice Department official confirmed the FBI arrest to Reuters but gave no reason for it, and it was not immediately clear whether Markle had been formally charged with any specific crime. FBI representatives could not immediately be reached, Reuters said. Markle has denied the allegations, telling the Daily Mail they were "sick lies." He also told the paper he had paid for sex in the Philippines, but said he had never been intimate with anyone underage.

As we reported last month, the case began when his son, Thomas Markle Jr., told the Sun he had found "hundreds, if not thousands" of child sexual abuse images in boxes his father left behind in Cebu, and that he had reported it to the FBI tip line on July 10 without hearing back. "I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years - but that stops now," Markle Jr. told the paper.

Philippine Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said Thursday that investigators have recovered about 7,500 photographs and one video showing underage boys and girls of Asian, Latina and European descent from devices linked to Markle Sr., GMA News reports. Some of the children appeared to be Filipino, he said, and the material included videos of children aged 10 to 11 engaged in sexual acts with adult men.

"It is the most deplorable display of impunity towards sexual activity that I have ever seen," Remulla said. A day earlier, Philippine police told AFP that three memory cards and a cellphone turned over by Markle Jr. contained child sexual abuse material.

Remulla also named Markle Jr., 60, a person of interest in the case after witnesses told investigators that underage girls were being brought to his house. "We are determining if the son is involved," Remulla said, adding that he is not yet being treated as a suspect. Ring lights were reportedly seen in the house; Markle Jr. told authorities he was making TikTok videos, and investigators found no underage girls in his TikTok account. Authorities expect to determine within a week whether he had any involvement. He remains in Cebu.

The Daily Mail reported last week that it had found images of children in a storage unit rented in Markle Sr.'s name in Rosarito, Mexico, about three miles from his former home, and referred it to the FBI. Mexican authorities then raided the unit, seizing computers, thumb drives, VHS tapes and other materials, per TMZ.

Last Friday, Markle was moved into a specialist memory care facility in Florida, ITV reported, raising concerns that legal barriers to questioning suspects with cognitive issues could keep the FBI from ever interviewing him.

Meghan said last month she was "deeply distressed" by the allegations, and disclosed that a 2018 letter to London's Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father." "I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them," she said.

The Met confirmed it passed that letter to her in 2019 but did not share its details with other law enforcement agencies, and said it was reviewing how it handled the matter, including whether it should be referred to the police watchdog.

Democrats Spent Year Demanding Data Center Moratoriums. They Own The Narrative. Will They Own The Fallout?

Thursday's selloff in hyperscaler and neocloud stocks deepened as investors reassessed the mounting risks that the Democratic sweep in the US midterms poses to the AI infrastructure boom. By midday in New York, the Nasdaq was down more than 5%, while Morgan Stanley's neocloud index had plunged 12%, reflecting concerns that Democratic-led moratoriums could delay projects, disrupt spending plans, and even undermine the US economy. We've extensively detailed where state-level restrictions could put the buildout most at risk (read here and here).

Earlier today, the doom headlines started pouring in. The Wall Street Journal reported that OpenAI leaders were discussing whether to reset expectations for next year's data center buildout after the blowout election results signaled dire straits for the AI boom.

WSJ said AI insider concerns surfaced Tuesday night at San Francisco's Opera House, where Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang hosted executives for "The Marriage of Figaro." Attendees discussed how midterm election results and mounting local opposition could put immense pressure on the planned expansion of computing capacity.

We've repeatedly warned about the implications of what follows a Democratic sweep. More specifically, Goldman highlighted the exposure of the US data center buildout to the blue wave, as Democrats won governorships in Texas, Ohio, Nevada, Georgia and Michigan, while gaining a trifecta in Pennsylvania and likely Arizona.

"The states where Democrats are likely to further restrict data centers account for roughly 45% of planned US data center capacity, with Texas alone accounting for roughly 25%," Goldman said.

This chart shows the states Democrats won and how much of the planned buildout could be at risk.

Economists view the data center buildout and grid expansion as among the largest economic drivers under the Trump administration's reindustrialization strategy for the US economy, accounting for an estimated 25% of total growth this year alone. Disrupting the construction boom could have severe consequences beyond plunging tech and chip stocks. It could translate into local economic turmoil if Democrats implement restrictions state by state, particularly in newly blue Texas.

With all this turmoil unfolding, we want to examine who owns the data center moratorium narrative. To no one's surprise, a key pillar of the Democratic Party's midterm campaign has been to stop President Trump's reindustrialization at all costs, even if that means crashing stocks and the economy.

The largest and most high-profile anti-data-center push came from the known socialists in Congress. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Bernie Sanders pushed for a nationwide moratorium from late 2025 into the 2026 midterm race. Representative Frank Pallone later endorsed a federal pause, adding to the ranks of Democrats seeking to derail the economic revival.

AoC and Bernie kicked off the "data center moratorium" narrative in late 2025. Dems ran with it. 

The headlines speak for themselves:

At the state level, particularly in Texas, Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged to continue pausing approvals until lawmakers adopt new protections. Ohio's Amy Acton has advocated a conditional moratorium, while Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms has called for a statewide pause to assess the industry's effects on communities.

Other Democratic governors have already acted. New York Governor Kathy Hochul imposed a permitting pause on new hyperscale facilities in July. Oregon Governor Tina Kotek expanded restrictions on projects. 

More headlines showing who owns the data center moratorium narrative:

Republicans have also backed restrictions but to a lesser degree. Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers supported a one-year statewide moratorium, while Democrat Abdul El-Sayed advocated local and state pauses. In Ohio, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy urged a temporary halt to approvals. 

So the moratorium narrative came from socialist Democrats, then some Republicans jumped on the bandwagon as they saw this topic was near and dear to voters. 

Beyond Democrats trying to crash the Trump economy, because that really is the end goal, they've also said since the election that they want revenge for Trump nuking all things DEI in what will be years of endless lawfare. Amplifying the anti-data center rhetoric was a far-left China-linked NGO sympathetic to Democrats, and oddly enough. 

All in all, Democrats own the narrative. Instead of being pro-growth and growing the US economy out of a debt trap, the party that has embraced far-left socialist DSA is willing to crash not just stocks but the economy over their hatred of Trump. 

... and what comes next will be an information war over who gets the blame for the deflating bubble.

items.title: If You Lie To Voters About Not Starting A New War, The Voters Make You Pay
items.content_text:
If You Lie To Voters About Not Starting A New War, The Voters Make You Pay

Authored by Larry C. Johnson via Sonar21,

American voters have a long memory for one particular kind of broken promise. Tell them you will keep their sons out of a foreign war, then march them into one, and they will eventually send you a bill. In 1920 the Democrats paid it. On Tuesday, the Republicans did.

On election night 2024, Donald Trump told a cheering crowd, "I'm not going to start a war, I'm going to stop wars." Fifteen months later came Operation Epic Fury. Eight months after that, CBS News projects that Democrats will take both the House and the Senate. JD Vance, never one to bury the lede, summed it up on X: "The reason we lost is the war."

Woodrow Wilson would have understood. He ran in 1916 on a slogan that a century of history teachers have never let anyone forget.

He kept us out of war, briefly

"He kept us out of war" carried Wilson to a narrow second term in November 1916. The voters took it as a pledge. It lasted about a month into his second term. On April 2, 1917, Wilson went before Congress and asked for a declaration of war against Germany. Congress obliged four days later.

What followed was not what the brochure promised. The draft came. So did the Espionage Act of 1917 and the Sedition Act of 1918, which made criticizing the war a good way to land in prison. More than 100,000 Americans died in uniform. At home, prices soared.

The voters started sending invoices early. In October 1918, Wilson publicly asked them to return a Democratic Congress as a vote of confidence. They returned a Republican one instead, in both chambers. Then came the hangover: the Senate's rejection of Wilson's League of Nations, his stroke in the fall of 1919, a wave of strikes, the Red Scare and a sharp postwar slump.

In 1920 the Democrats nominated James Cox, with a young Franklin Roosevelt as his running mate. The Republicans nominated Warren Harding, a man of no particular distinction who promised a "return to normalcy." Harding took about 60 percent of the popular vote and 404 electoral votes to Cox's 127. It was the most lopsided popular-vote margin of its era. Voters were not endorsing Harding so much as firing Wilson's war.

No more wars, he said

Trump did not have a slogan as tidy as Wilson's. He had something better: a promise repeated so often that it became the soundtrack of the 2024 campaign. At the Republican convention he boasted, "I don't have wars." At a Pennsylvania rally that August he said, "we will have no more wars." On election night it was "I'm not going to start a war, I'm going to stop wars." At his inauguration he said success would be measured partly by the wars America never gets into.

Then, on February 28, 2026, the United States and Israel went to war with Iran. Hormuz closed. Brent crude was still around $110 this week, about 50 percent above where it sat before the war. Every voter who filled a tank this year got a reminder.

By June, Trump had found a new position on his old promise. "I didn't guarantee no war," he told NBC. CNN's fact-checkers helpfully listed the times he had done precisely that. Voters were not persuaded either. In a Fox News poll in September, more than 60 percent called the war the wrong decision and 71 percent said the administration lacked a clear strategy for ending it. Trump's approval going into Election Day averaged about 38 percent.

Tuesday was the bill. CBS projects Democrats will hold somewhere between 251 and 268 House seats and at least 54 in the Senate. James Talarico beat Ken Paxton in Texas. Sherrod Brown is back in Ohio. Troy Jackson took Susan Collins's seat in Maine. Vance blamed the war. Trump, asked about it, said it was "largely true" that the war cost Republicans seats. Then he blamed the gas prices instead, as though they had arrived from another planet. As for the war itself, Trump's explanation was "You have no choice."

Not 1894, but not nothing

Before the Democrats start carving Tuesday into marble, some perspective. This was not the worst beating a ruling party has ever taken. It was not even close.

  • In 1894, after the Panic of 1893, Grover Cleveland's Democrats lost about 125 House seats.
  • In 1932, with the country sinking into the Depression, Herbert Hoover's Republicans lost roughly 100 House seats and 13 Senate seats.
  • Ulysses Grant's Republicans lost 96 House seats in 1874, after the Panic of 1873. Benjamin Harrison's lost 93 in 1890.

This year Republicans look set to lose something over 40 House seats. On the all-time list, that lands somewhere in the high teens, next to Trump's own 2018 loss and Lyndon Johnson's Vietnam-era beating in 1966. The Senate tells the same story. A loss of eight or nine seats hurts, but it falls well short of 1932 and 1958, when the ruling party lost a dozen or more. It was a rout, not an extinction event.

Look at what sits at the top of those lists. The real catastrophes were economic. Panics and depressions did what no single policy blunder ever has. Voters will forgive a great deal, but not an empty wallet.

That is what makes 2026 worth studying. Trump did not need a depression to lose Congress. He needed one broken promise, and the war made that promise expensive. The war shut Hormuz. Hormuz pushed up oil. Oil pushed up gasoline, and gasoline put the war into every family's monthly budget. Wilson's Democrats learned the same lesson in 1918, when they lost both chambers, including seven Senate seats, with the war still on. Tuesday's result is smaller than the great economic wipeouts. It is still the clearest demonstration in a generation of what happens when a president promises peace, delivers war, and hands the voters the bill.

Where the parallel bends

History rhymes, but it does not plagiarize, so here are the differences.

  • A promise, not an oath. Neither man swore to stay out of war. The oath of office binds a president to the Constitution. What both broke was a campaign promise, which voters treated as a contract anyway.
  • Wilson's slogan was written for him. "He kept us out of war" was a Democratic campaign line, and Wilson himself was careful never to promise that the peace would last. Trump made the promise personally, in the first person, over and over.
  • Who started it. Germany's return to unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann telegram pushed Wilson into war in 1917. No U-boats were sinking American ships off New Jersey in February 2026. Trump chose this war.
  • War was not the only issue. In 1920 voters were also punishing inflation, strikes and a slumping economy. In 2026, Gallup found voters rated the economy and health care slightly ahead of the war. The catch is that the war is what drove up prices, as Trump himself conceded.

Normalcy, anyone?

The lesson of 1918 and 1920 is that voters do not need a long memory, only an accurate one. Wilson's Democrats lost Congress in the middle of the war and the White House when it was over. They then spent twelve years in the wilderness. Republicans are now where Wilson's party stood in November 1918. They have lost Congress, the war is still on, and the president insists he had no choice.

There are two years until 2028. Trump could take the 1918 result as the warning it is, end the war and let the oil start moving again. Or he could listen to the people urging him to finish the job with another round of strikes on Iran. If he picks the second option, I suspect some Republican in 2028 will discover the political value of the word "normalcy." Somebody has to run on it. Harding did, and he was not even trying very hard.

items.title: Haircut No. 2: Anthropic IPO Talk Slides To $1.2 Trillion As AI Rout Crushes Odds Of A November Listing
items.content_text:
Haircut No. 2: Anthropic IPO Talk Slides To $1.2 Trillion As AI Rout Crushes Odds Of A November Listing

Keeps going lower.

Three weeks ago we reported that Anthropic IPO investors had marked the valuation from $2 trillion down to $1.5 trillion as the growth slowdown sank in. This morning, Bloomberg reports that the price tag has been cut again: after Thursday's AI bloodbath, some potential backers are now discussing a value as low as $1.2 trillion for the company, a person familiar told the news agency (deliberations are "ongoing," no final decisions have been made, and Anthropic declined to comment).

Put in context: in early October investors were floating a fair value "as high as $2 trillion." The low end of today's range is 40% below that peak, which is a lot of haircut for a company that, according to the WSJ, just pushed its annualized revenue run rate past $80 billion. And for some, even that's not low enough.

"Fair Value," Revised (Again)

The Bloomberg story fills in the timeline. After the company's October briefing on its latest financials, investors told the bankers on the deal that their estimate of a fair valuation had moved to around $1.4 trillion to $1.5 trillion. Then came Thursday, when the Nasdaq 100 plunged 6.4%, wiping out $2.3 trillion in market value, a record for a single day, and that number "shifted again." Which is why prospective investors are now "facing a weekend of uncertainty ahead of the kickoff of formal marketing."

The buy-siders Bloomberg spoke to are all over the map, though the direction of travel is the same:

  • BNP Paribas Wealth Management Germany's CIO Stephan Kemper expects the valuation to land at the very low end of the rumored $1.5-$2 trillion range, "maybe some 10% to 15% below that," which works out to roughly $1.3 trillion.
  • Gallo Partners' Michael Alfaro said before Thursday's rout that Anthropic needed to target $1.3 trillion to $1.4 trillion "in order to build a quality book." That was before the Nasdaq's worst day since Covid.
  • Sycomore's David Rainville: "If they set a valuation toward the bottom of the range, say $1.2 trillion, they shouldn't have a problem finding investors." Translation: at $1.5 trillion, they might.
  • And HSBC's Max Kettner thinks around $1 trillion "could be a more comfortable level."

Kettner's reasoning is worth quoting, because it's the one that should worry the underwriters most:

"I don't think we need the headline 'oh my god, it is a trillion dollar IPO,' because I think what's actually more important is the secondary. If we get a dynamic like we had with SpaceX, that you get it on secondary and then stock rips for a couple hours, but then it dumps, in the current environment you don't want to have that."

Kettner isn't alone at $1 trillion. Late on Thursday the WSJ reported that three major investors planning to take part in the offering think the $1.5 trillion valuation will likely need to come down, with one putting it "closer to $1 trillion." Executives and advisers are set to meet in the coming days, the raise could shrink from the planned up to $100 billion, and one investor floated a delay because it may be hard to convince institutions "burned in the recent selloff" to take a big AI risk again. At about the same time, Reuters reported that potential investors doubt Anthropic can start its roadshow next week and still list in November, something we discussed in "Is Anthropic About To Delay The Biggest IPO Ever?"

Here is how the "fair value" has evolved in the space of five weeks:

Note the dashed line: at $1 trillion, the IPO would price barely 4% above the $965 billion post-money of May's Series H. So much for the "biggest IPO ever" step-up.

$80 Billion Of ARR... And It Still Doesn't Clear

The awkward part is that the company itself is still growing fast. The WSJ reported this morning that Anthropic's ARR topped $80 billion at the end of October, against some expectations in the mid-$70 billion range, which probably helped this morning's premarket bounce in Nvidia and the memory names. Badly needed good press, and maybe a sign the August-September slowdown we flagged after investor day wasn't the start of a stall.

Some napkin math (approximate): at $2 trillion, buyers were being asked to pay 25x that $80 billion run rate. At $1.25 trillion, the midpoint of the new range, it's about 16x. In other words, the multiple has compressed by roughly 40% while the run rate went up. That's what a derating looks like.

On a trailing basis the math is still eye-watering. Against the roughly $35 billion Anthropic booked over the past four quarters, $1.25 trillion is about 35x sales. As Fortune noted this week, citing Jay Ritter's IPO data, anything above ~$1.41 trillion would mean more than 40x trailing revenue, a level reached by just 14 of 4,110 IPOs since 1980. And that's before you get to the $895 billion in committed spend disclosed in the amended S-1, roughly $70 billion of which is due in the next 12 months, or the October revenue line the filing left conspicuously blank.

Which brings us to the real problem: the company's numbers are no longer the only thing being priced. After Tuesday's Democratic sweep, the market is also pricing permitting risk on the data centers Anthropic needs to hit those numbers. Goldman estimates that the states likely to add restrictions hold about 45% of planned US capacity, and Anthropic's own Texas campus was already stuck on a $15 billion bridge loan before the election.

Polymarket Got There First

As usual, the prediction markets didn't wait for the Bloomberg scoop. Yesterday morning, with the Nasdaq rout just starting, we pointed out that the odds of an Anthropic listing were tumbling:

(The "by Nov 25" contract in that chart had slid to 69% from 86% a day earlier.) They kept tumbling. As of this morning, Polymarket gives Anthropic a 54% chance of listing by Nov 25 and 60% by Nov 30, down from 86% for both before the rout. Even the odds of an IPO at any point in 2026 have dropped from 93% to 73%:

The valuation markets moved even faster. Polymarket's "What will Anthropic's IPO valuation be?" contracts now make $1.25-$1.50 trillion the favorite at 43%, up from about 5% a week ago. The $1.50-$1.75 trillion bracket, which was a ~65% favorite right after the midterms, has collapsed to 32%, and the odds of anything $1.75 trillion or above are down to 16%. Bloomberg's $1.2-$1.3 trillion range straddles the bottom of the new favorite bracket, and the "below $1.25 trillion" tail has quietly gone from about 1% to 7%:

Nothing says "orderly price discovery" like the favorite outcome changing three times in a month.

1998 Or 2000?

Over at Goldman, the trading desks are split on what Thursday's crash means for the AI trade, and by extension for whoever ends up buying Anthropic stock. Goldman Delta One head Rich Privorotsky, who admitted "what I got wrong" on AI just one day earlier, posed the question everyone is asking in his morning note (available to pro subs):

"Is this a 1998 style liquidity crisis and buying opportunity, or March 2000 and the beginning of a structural technology unwind? I lean toward 1998. Russia's default/LTCM were the external shocks but US growth remained intact. Once liquidity returned and the Fed eased, markets recovered rapidly... The uncomfortable parallel with 2000 is the sheer scale of spending and uncertainty around returns. Are we liquidating a sound growth story or discovering its economics are wrong? I lean toward the former, but demand, utilization and returns need to hold."

Privorotsky lists four concerns behind the selloff: i) insufficient capital to finance the buildout, ii) insufficient revenue to justify the investment, iii) insufficient power and permitting capacity, and iv) an unsustainable aggregate spending trajectory. The market, he argues, "has latched onto number three, arguably the least important." Maybe. But the Anthropic IPO is a referendum on all four at once: it is a $100 billion capital raise (#1), priced off a run rate (#2), by a company that needs permitted, powered data centers (#3) to service nearly $900 billion in commitments (#4).

And Goldman's own credit strategists are hardly reassuring on #1. In her latest Global Credit Trader, "AI-Related Supply: Outlining the Directional Risks"  (also available to pro subs), Amanda Lynam notes that hyperscaler bond issuance has already hit $296 billion this year, well above Goldman's $250 billion full-year forecast, and warns that between now and early December the risks to spreads are "firmly tilted towards more widening." That is the backdrop against which bankers are trying to place what would be the largest equity raise in history, which is something we have been warning about since last October, when AI quietly became the largest sector in the bond market.

Meanwhile, the people who were supposed to anchor the book are licking their wounds. Goldman's derivatives desk says clients "had aggressively dumped protection" into Wednesday's post-midterm relief rally, leaving the market underhedged for Thursday's reversal, and tech-focused hedge funds have just wiped out their entire 2026 gain. Not exactly the crowd that will be clamoring for a $100 billion allocation next week.

And Then There's OpenAI

Anthropic isn't the only frontier lab finding out what the AI unwind does to private marks. Last Friday, the FT reported that OpenAI had slashed its funding target by $10 billion to about $20 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, a week after it trimmed the price from $1.4 trillion following a "thud" from Morgan Stanley's wealthy clients. Now the WSJ reports that OpenAI has secured just $11 billion of the $30 billion it originally targeted, and that's at the adjusted $1.25 trillion valuation.

Here's the punchline: just last week, the FT's explanation for OpenAI's struggles was that Anthropic's IPO was "absorbing both investor capital and focus." Well, if Anthropic prices at the low end of Bloomberg's range, the "hot" public listing would value the company below the $1.25 trillion OpenAI is struggling to raise money at privately. One of those two marks is wrong, and probably not the public one.

Size Down, Price Down... Or Wait Until 2027?

So what are Anthropic's options? Per Bloomberg, the company and its selling shareholders could start marketing with a conservative size and valuation and upsize on demand, the Cerebras and Figma playbook. Bloomberg helpfully adds that both "are now trading well below their IPO prices." The "less palatable option" is to delay: IPO filings must be public for at least 15 calendar days before formal marketing, and some issuers wait weeks or months, updating their quarterly financials along the way. For Anthropic, that would probably mean a Q4 refresh and a 2027 listing.

Our take: the bulls have a point that the business is growing (an $80 billion run rate is no small number), and Privorotsky may well be right that this is a liquidity event rather than a demand collapse. But his own 1998 analogy ended with the Fed easing. This time, Fed speakers Barkin and Hammack spent Thursday openly arguing for higher rates while the Nasdaq had its worst day since March 2020. In that environment, the more likely path is a third haircut or a delay, not a triumphant upsizing. As IG's Alexandre Baradez put it, "maybe it's better to go to the market when the valuation excesses have already been purged."

The question is whether they have been, or whether $1.2 trillion is just this week's number. For now, everyone wants to be in the room for the biggest IPO ever; fewer and fewer want to pay for the privilege.

More in Privorotsky's "Liquidation. 1998 or 2000." note and Goldman's Global Credit Trader, both available to pro subs.

items.title: Consumer Sentiment Unexpectedly Jumps, Fueled By Independents, Despite Growing AI Bubble Fears
items.content_text:
Consumer Sentiment Unexpectedly Jumps, Fueled By Independents, Despite Growing AI Bubble Fears

The UMichigan consumer sentiment survey unexpectedly jumped in November to a three-month high, boosted by modest improvements in Americans' views of their personal finances and the economic outlook.

The University of Michigan’s preliminary sentiment index increased to 51 in November from 48 in October; the median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of economists projected sentiment to hold at 48. Still, despite the improvement, the overall index remains just shy of the lowest prints ever recorded just a few months ago and during the early 1980s "hyperinflationary" period. 


The improvement was concentrated among independents, who reported the strongest consumer sentiment in more than a year. Curiously, sentiment across both Democrats and Republicans deteriorated in the days ahead of the mid-term election (The survey period included responses from Oct. 20 to Nov. 2). 

The improvement was widespread across both current conditions and expectations, with the two printing at 51.0 and 50.9, respectively, beating expectations of 47.0 and 49.0. Curiously, this happened despite another sharp drop in Democrat assessment of current conditions.

Cost of living concerns remain top of mind for many Americans. About 57% of respondents spontaneously mentioned that high prices had eroded their living standards - the highest since May.

Despite limited layoffs and strong economic growth, household finances have been squeezed as prices rise faster than wages. Democrats’ decisive victory in the midterm elections reflected deep voter frustration with the economy, particularly the high cost of food, gasoline and housing.

Inflation expectations in the year ahead improved but remained elevated. Consumers expect prices to rise 4.3% over the next year, down from 4.7% a month ago to a three-month low, and below expectations of a 4.6% print. They also saw costs climbing at an annual rate of 3.4% over the next five to 10 years, also a step down from the 3.5% in the prior month.

In addition to inflation worries, “consumers’ comments revealed growing anxiety over a possible AI bubble,” Joanne Hsu, director of the survey, said in a statement.

“The personal finances of consumers with the largest stock portfolios dropped 12% this month to their lowest reading since April, likely due to agitation in stock values in recent weeks, while all other wealth groups saw modest improvements,” she added.

A survey of current personal finances climbed to a four-month high in November, while Americans' views of buying conditions for durable goods rebounded from a record low.

items.title: Iran Reportedly Hands Out Iodine Tablets As Trump Locks Crosshairs On Pickaxe Mountain
items.content_text:
Iran Reportedly Hands Out Iodine Tablets As Trump Locks Crosshairs On Pickaxe Mountain

Summary:

  • Iodine Tablets Being Distributed  
  • Iranian Video Tells Citizens How To Survive Nuke
  • Trump Says US 'Locked And Loaded' For Renewed Strikes Against Iran

Iran Hands Out Iodine Tablets

The US midterms are over, and Democrats swept this week's elections. The question now is what the Trump administration will do about Iran's Pickaxe Mountain and Kharg Island.

This morning's diplomatic signals couldchange at a moment's notice. Meanwhile, The Times reportsthat the Iranian government is distributing iodine tablets to communities near nuclear facilities as Tehran fears an attack on Pickaxe Mountain may be imminent.

Here's how The Times described the preparations: 

However, the video appears to tell citizens how to survive a nuclear explosion at Pickaxe. The video, examined by The Times, asks viewers to imagine a nuclear explosion before listing the approximate distances to nearby cities: 17 miles from Natanz, 25 from Kashan, 117 from Isfahan and 223 from Tehran. It gives three instructions for survival: "Get inside, stay inside and listen for updates."

It also warns that an attack on an underground facility could throw large quantities of radioactive earth and rock into the atmosphere, allowing winds to carry contaminated dust for hundreds of miles. People near the site may have only ten to 15 minutes before the fallout arrives, it claims, while those in more distant cities could have several hours.

It is not just the video that is adding to the belief among Iranians that an attack is imminent. Iodine tablets are being distributed to communities near nuclear facilities as a precaution against possible radiation exposure, according to a health ministry official. "Yes, we are distributing iodine," the official told The Times. 

"During every war, we have tried to distribute it within a two-to-three-kilometre radius of nuclear facilities. Trump can no longer be trusted. He may go through with this crime."

If the Trump administration decides to escalate, a cyberattack or other less lethal means could disrupt operations at Iran's oil export hub on Kharg Island. Pickaxe Mountain poses a much bigger challenge. 

Pickaxe Mountain's nuclear facilities lie 80 to 100 meters underground, making them difficult to destroy even with the most powerful US conventional bunker-busting bombs. However, a B61-11 nuclear bunker buster could destroy the facility. 

Recall what Trump said last week: "There are 'one or two sites' left that need to be dealt with, including Pickaxe Mountain. We can do it in ten minutes. We have a plan for it, and we can execute it very quickly."

***

Trump Says US 'Locked And Loaded' For Renewed Strikes Against Iran

Authored by Tom Ozimek via The Epoch Times (emphasis ours),

U.S. President Donald Trump said that Iran cannot do anything regarding its nuclear program without approval from Washington and that he would soon decide whether to resume renewed military operations against Tehran.

Trump's remarks on Thursday came during an Oval Office exchange with reporters, who asked for comment on reports that Iranian negotiators are reviewing a new proposal put forward by regional mediators for a deal that would constrain Iran's nuclear program.

"It doesn't make any difference what they're looking at," Trump said. "They're not going to have a nuclear weapon; they know that. So do I."

Trump said that he would soon decide whether to resume major combat operations in Iran, clarifying that his preference would be for a negotiated solution rather than destruction of the Middle Eastern country.

"In Iran we are there for seven months, and we control everything that we've wanted to control, and now we'll make a decision: do we want to go further," he said.

"I think it'll take them 25 years to rebuild the country. I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I'll have to; you'll know soon enough."

For weeks, Trump has threatened to return to a full-scale bombardment of Iran after the midterm elections if Tehran remained unwilling to reach a negotiated settlement on terms acceptable to the United States, particularly regarding its nuclear program.

"We're locked and loaded," Trump told reporters Thursday. "If we have to do the rest of the Iran thing, we're very much locked and loaded."

Iran's top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, said earlier Thursday that Tehran had set seven conditions to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and enter negotiations with Washington.

"As long as they do not execute our seven conditions, we will neither open the Strait of Hormuz nor have negotiations," he said during a visit to Russia.

Tehran's demands include sanctions relief, the release of frozen Iranian assets, and paying war reparations.

Washington, meanwhile, insists that any initial talks address Iran's nuclear program.

On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance publicly questioned whether the Iran war was worth ​it and said it cost Republicans control ​of Congress in the midterm election.

Vance's remarks stirred debate about whether Trump remained willing to proceed with a potential resumption of major combat operations against Iran. The president's latest Oval Office remarks suggest that renewed military action remains under consideration.

Trump on Monday expressed optimism about a possible settlement with Iran as talks continued in Qatar, with Vance saying he and the president had discussed the matter and both "feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement."

"We're going to keep working at it," Vance said.

The U.S.–Iran conflict has spread regionally, with clashes between Iran-backed Houthis and a Saudi Arabia-led coalition in Yemen, Saudi Arabia, and parts of the Red Sea.

The Saudi-led coalition said Friday that its air defense systems intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis toward Najran, a major city in Saudi Arabia.

"Debris fell as a result of the interception, and damage assessment is underway," the coalition said in a Nov. 6 post on X.

Trump held a phone call with Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani to discuss the regional situation and efforts to de-escalate tensions, Qatar News Agency reported on Friday.

The two men discussed the latest international efforts, notably the initiatives led by the State of Qatar, to bridge the gaps between the concerned parties and support the negotiation process, to pave the way for reaching a comprehensive agreement that resolves the crisis and ensures security and stability in the region, according to the Qatar News Agency.

Al Thani highlighted the importance of continuing dialogue and embracing diplomacy as a means of resolving disputes, while calling for safeguarding freedom of navigation and energy supply security, the agency said.

Qatar has been mediating between Iran and the United States, with Qatari intermediaries shuttling proposals between Tehran and Washington.

items.title: Trump Proclaims Oval Office, Cabinet Room As National Monuments
items.content_text:
Trump Proclaims Oval Office, Cabinet Room As National Monuments

Authored by Travis Gillmore via The Epoch Times,

WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump signed a proclamation preserving two of the White House's historical rooms.

SIGNED: Designating the Oval Office as a National Monument, protecting the historic office for good. 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/x10uKg1AUe

— The White House (@WhiteHouse) November 6, 2026

The document declares the Oval Office and the Cabinet Room as national monuments, under the authority of the Antiquities Act.

"When we get the documentation fully done, legally binding, it'll make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space," Trump said during the signing ceremony.

The proclamation itself sets no vote for Congress: it says it does not diminish "the Congress's authority over Federal property," and nothing in its text stops a future president from rolling it back.

"So if they want to say let's not have an oval anymore, let's make it square, what happens is they have to go back to Congress, and hopefully ... the people in Congress will be smart enough not to let that happen," Trump said.

The Oval Office was not included in the original White House, completed in 1800. Earlier presidents chose a room in the main house to make their office, with Thomas Jefferson occupying the State Dining Room.

President William Howard Taft oversaw construction of the Oval Office in 1909. Architect Nathan C. Wyeth designed the historic oval-shaped room to symbolize the power of the presidency.

According to the White House Historical Association, President George Washington favored oval rooms for hosting guests.

The existing structure has looked the same since it was modified to accommodate President Franklin Delano Roosevelt in 1934.

"It will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump said. "We like the Oval Office, and it's a symbol like the White House itself. It's a symbol of our country and the greatness of our country."

His proclamation describes the room as one of "unmatched and unique combination of location, design, setting, materials, workmanship, and an association with historical events that are embedded in our national consciousness."

While the Executive Mansion and grounds are already federal property protected as a National Historic Landmark by the National Park Service as part of President's Park, Trump declared "the Oval Office merits specific recognition and protective management as a discrete historic structure of national significance."

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum is instructed by the order to create a management plan, which includes coordination with all relevant federal agencies, to review and consider any alternatives before allowing the substantial alteration or destruction of the rooms.

"It's where American history is made, and today will be preserved for the future," Benjamin Moss, White House staff secretary, said during the event.

The declaration preserves the rooms' core structural features, allowing incoming presidents to maintain tradition and decorate the spaces as they see fit, including "select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character."

"He can do whatever he wants to," Trump said. "He's got to be very careful."

Trump prioritized White House restoration projects in both terms, with expansion of a new ballroom a centerpiece of the improvements. Construction is underway on the approximately 89,000 square-foot structure with a 22,000 square-foot room for hosting state dinners and other events.

Other plans for Washington include the addition of a Triumphal Arch, a promenade from the Lincoln Memorial to the Potomac River, and the National Garden of American Heroes, with hundreds of statues honoring the past.

The president also renovated the Reflecting Pool, restored dozens of statues and fountains around the nation's capital, and repaired 2,300 light fixtures, according to a statement from the White House.

items.title: US Jobs Soar By 165K Blowing Away Estimates; Unemployment Rate Drops Putting Dec Rate Hike Back In Play
items.content_text:
US Jobs Soar By 165K Blowing Away Estimates; Unemployment Rate Drops Putting Dec Rate Hike Back In Play

In our preview of the October jobs report, we said that the labor data has rarely looked this solid going into a monthly payrolls report: claims near 57-year lows, the lowest October layoffs since 2023, JOLTS openings up 333K and ADP above expectations. If anything, the risk is to the upside of the 63K consensus, and the unemployment rate could well tick down.

Which, as we noted, was the problem as "a strong print gives Warsh, Hammack and Barkin all the cover they need to hike in December, right as the Nasdaq is coming off its worst day since March 2020. Goldman's rates desk thinks a single print can't take the hikes out." We said that we agree with this take, and added that the more likely outcome is a decent number that puts December back in play and adds a rates problem to what has so far been an AI problem. Given where positioning is, CTAs already selling and long-only "frozen (again)," that's not a recipe for a relief rally.

Well, moments ago, the BLS reported the October jobs and it came extremely red hot, enough to indeed put a December rate hike back on the docket, AI collapse notwithstanding. Here are the numbers:

October monthly payrolls rose by 165K, up more than double the 70K expected bounce, and the third highest print of 2026 (this was once again driven by private jobs, which surged by 159K, smashing expectations of 65K; government only accounted for 6K jobs in October).

The number was so hot it not only printed above the highest Wall Street estimate...

... it was a 5-sigma beat to the median consensus number.

Not only was October red hot, prior month revision were all higher: the August was revised up by 53,000, from +133,000  to +186,000, and September was revised up by 31,000, from +29,000 to +60,000. With these revisions, employment in August and September combined is 84,000 higher than previously 
reported. 

While the payrolls number was red hot, the monthly worker change blew it away, as 463K workers were added according to the Household survey, the third consecutive month of 400K+ workers added...

... which in turn helped the persistently lagging total worker series catch up every closer to the much stronger, in recent years, payrolls series. 

Just as remarkable is that after years of chronic underperformance by full-time jobs, in October the number of full-time jobs soared by 714K, the second highest monthly increase in 2026, while par-time jobs plunged by 242K.

The one blemish in the report was that after a year of declining foreign-born workers, in October we saw 809K foreign-born workers added, the biggest increase since Jan 2025, while native-born workers dropped by 64K.

It wasn't just the job numbers that came in red hot: the unemployment rate unexpectedly dipped back to 4.1% from 4.2%, and against expectations of an unchanged print.

Among the major worker groups, the unemployment rates showed little or no change in October for adult men (3.9%), adult women (3.6%), teenagers (13.9%), and people who are White (3.7%), Black (6.6%), Asian (2.8 percent), or Hispanic (4.7 percent). 

Both the labor force participation rate, at 61.9%, and the employment-population ratio, at 59.3%, changed little in October. These measures have shown little net change since January.  

And completing the trifecta of hot data was the average hourly earnings which beat expectations both MoM and YoY, with the former printing 0.4%, above the 0.3% expected, and the highest since Nov 2025, while the annual change in earnings disappointed expectations of the first sub-3% print since covid, and instead rose from the pre-revision 3.0% to 3.1% (then again Sept was revised higher to 3.2%).

The average workweek for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls remained at 34.4 hours in October. In manufacturing, the average workweek was unchanged at 40.5 hours, and overtime edged up by 0.1 hour to 3.1 hours. The average workweek for production and nonsupervisory employees on private nonfarm payrolls declined by 0.1 hour to 33.8 hours. 

Some more details from the report:

  • The number of long-term unemployed (those jobless for 27 weeks or more), at 2.0 million, changed little over the month. The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.6 percent of all unemployed people. 
  • The number of people employed part time for economic reasons increased by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October. These individuals would have preferred full-time employment but were working part time because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time jobs.
  • In October, the number of people not in the labor force who currently want a job changed little at  6.0 million. These individuals were not counted as unemployed because they were not actively looking for work during the 4 weeks preceding the survey or were unavailable to take a job. 
  • Among those not in the labor force who wanted a job, the number of people marginally attached to the labor force changed little at 1.6 million in October. These individuals wanted and were available for work and had looked for a job sometime in the prior 12 months but had not looked for work in the 4 weeks preceding the survey. The number of discouraged workers, a subset of the marginally attached who believed that no jobs were available for them, also changed little over the month at 448,000. 

Looking at the composition of the October jobs print, we find the following: 

  • Employment in professional and business services increased by 70,000 in October, well above the average monthly gain of 15,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment continued to trend  up in professional, scientific, and technical services (+33,000), in administrative and support and  waste management and remediation services (+28,000), and in management of companies and enterprises (+9,000). Professional and business services has added 269,000 jobs since a recent low in October  2025.
  • Health care added 42,000 jobs in October, higher than the average monthly gain of 31,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment gains occurred in hospitals (+16,000), home health care services (+11,000), and outpatient care centers (+5,000).
  • In October, transportation and warehousing added 25,000 jobs, reflecting growth in couriers and messengers (+17,000) and air transportation (+4,000). Transportation and warehousing has added 104,000 jobs since a recent employment low in February, with couriers and messengers (+71,000) contributing most of the gain.
  • Manufacturing employment continued to trend up in October (+19,000) and has increased by 101,000 since a recent low in December 2025. In October, job gains occurred in computer and electronic product manufacturing (+7,000), machinery manufacturing (+4,000), and primary metal manufacturing (+4,000).

Employment showed little change over the month in other major industries, including mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction; construction; wholesale trade; retail trade; information; financial activities; social assistance; leisure and hospitality; other services; and government.

And visually:

Since the numbers were red hot, top to bottom, it was expected that Treasuries dipped as the surge in US job growth led traders to add to wagers that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates when officials next meet in December. The declines on Friday pushed yields higher across maturities, with those on two-year notes — more sensitive to the outlook for the Fed’s rate path than longer peers — up by as much as seven basis points to 4.54%. The 10-year yield was four basis points higher at 4.87% after data showed the US added 165,000 jobs in October, topping forecasts. 

Traders maintained expectations of further rate hikes from the US central bank, pricing in a 70% chance of a quarter-point rate hike next month. All told, the market expects at least 40 basis points of additional tightening by September 2027, according to Bloomberg.

Developing.

items.title: DraftKings Crashes As "Aggressive Prediction Investments" Drive EBITDA Outlook Cut
items.content_text:
DraftKings Crashes As "Aggressive Prediction Investments" Drive EBITDA Outlook Cut

DraftKings shares crashed 24.5% in Friday's premarket trading after the sports betting operator slashed the midpoint of its 2026 adjusted EBITDA forecast to $225 million from $800 million. The mad dash into prediction markets overshadowed a 16% year-over-year increase in third-quarter revenue to $1.33 billion.

"In just a few months, we have become the clear number three Predictions exchange by Total Volume," CEO Jason Robins wrote in a letter to shareholders.

BofA Securities gaming analyst Julie Hoover attributed $475 million of the $575 million guidance cut to additional investment in prediction markets. The remaining $100 million reflected a lower adjusted EBITDA forecast for the core business.

Hoover wrote in her first take:

Q3 Miss and 2027 estimate reset

DraftKings (ticker: DKNG) reported Q3 revenue/EBITDA of $1.33/-316M vs. BofA $1.345B/-$100M and the Street's $1.393B/-66M. DKNG lowered their full year EBITDA guidance to $225M at midpoint vs. $800M, embedding $475M of incremental prediction market (PM) investment and $100M reduction to the core. For 2027, DKNG provided initial guidance of ~$800M-1B, including $300M of EBITDA loss related to PMs.

Bottom line: Shares of DKNG traded down -23% after the close on a bigger-than-expected 2027 numbers reset. Investors are disappointed by the magnitude of PM investment given the looming regulatory risk around sports event contracts. DKNG's desire to be best-in-class has driven its top-line success, but greater guardrails around spend, particularly in the current regulatory backdrop, are critical to drive the bottom line and stock. We reiterate our Buy rating with numbers reset, and PMs a potential source of upside. We lower our PO to $23 based on 14x 2027E EBITDA (11x core 2027E EBITDA).

DraftKings’ 2027 guidance for prediction markets calls for $700 million in net revenue and $500 million in gross profit, with operating expenses rising to roughly $800 million from about $675 million this year. Hoover estimates that higher fixed costs account for approximately $50 million of that increase, with another $75 million going toward marketing. The additional marketing spending was unexpected, although a projected high-single-digit decline in core marketing suggests some dollars may be shifting between the businesses. Given DraftKings’ prediction-market share and the market’s rapid expansion, the revenue forecast could prove conservative.

Core: Investing in iGaming, +6% revenue growth in 2027

The company is investing roughly $40 million in iGaming this year to support longer-term growth. Third-quarter iGaming revenue rose 2%, below her 8% forecast, primarily because of increased promotional activity. Renewed investment looks sensible following two years of market-share losses. The company’s 2027 core revenue and EBITDA outlook assumes 6% revenue growth, with iGaming expanding faster than online sports betting. Although marketing spending can move between the core business and prediction markets, the guidance implies that 75% of incremental core revenue will translate into EBITDA - an ambitious assumption given the competitive promotional environment.

Here's what the rest of Wall Street analysts are saying (courtesy of Bloomberg):

Bloomberg Intelligence

  •  "DraftKings' deep 2026 revenue and EBITDA outlook cuts on aggressive prediction investments create urgency to realize a targeted 20-month payback that defers prediction-market profit to late 2027 yet still implies a faster payback than for sportsbooks," Brian Egger writes

Morgan Stanley (overweight, PT $31)

  • The material reduction in outlook should weigh on the stock
    The forecast cut was driven not only by prediction market spend but also a weaker core

CFRA (buy, PT $40)

  •  Analyst Zachary Warring says profitability deteriorated sharply as DraftKings accelerated investment in its Predictions platform
  •  "For the nine-month period, the shift is even more pronounced: Adjusted EBITDA swung from a positive $276.8M to ($34.4M), underscoring the magnitude of Predictions-related investment"

Vital Knowledge

  • "DraftKings reported a big miss on headline EBITDA in Q3 due in large part to heavy spending as mgmt. builds the predictions business, and this issue will extend into 2027, w/an aggregate EBITDA guide mid-point of ~$900MM below the consensus of $1.1B," writes analyst Adam Crisafulli
  •  Says that while the company sounds very bullish about its predictions opportunity, this is coming at the expense of the core sportsbook business

According to Bloomberg data, 31 analysts rate DraftKings a Buy, eight rate it Neutral, and one rates it a Sell.

The consensus 12-month price target is about $32.25.

items.title: Voters In 8 States Approve Citizenship, Voter ID Measures For State Elections
items.content_text:
Voters In 8 States Approve Citizenship, Voter ID Measures For State Elections

Authored by Jack Phillips via The Epoch Times,

Voters in eight states backed ballot measures that sought stricter election rules during Tuesday's election, approving voter ID and U.S. citizenship requirements.

In West Virginia, South Dakota, Kansas, Alaska, and Arkansas, voters approved measures affirming that only U.S. citizens can vote in state elections. All but Alaska's were constitutional amendments, while Alaska's was a ballot initiative.

Voters in Ohio and Nevada approved constitutional amendments requiring photo ID to vote in person. North Carolina voters approved an amendment extending the state's photo ID requirement, already in its constitution for in-person voting, to mail ballots.

Voters in California and Colorado rejected measures that would have tightened voter ID rules. California's Proposition 39 would have required voter ID, and Colorado's Amendment 84 would have required an ID number for mail-in ballots.

In Arizona, a measure that would require voter ID and prohibit foreign contributions in elections was trailing but hadn't been called.

Other voting-related measures were on the ballot in several states.

Massachusetts voters approved a measure allowing same-day voter registration on Election Day. In Alaska, preliminary results showed voters narrowly rejecting a measure that would have repealed the state's ranked-choice voting system, open primaries, and some campaign finance disclosure rules.

California voters also weighed Proposition 5, a constitutional amendment that would change how statewide officials are recalled. Under current law, voters answer two questions on a recall ballot: whether to remove the official and who should replace them. Proposition 5 would eliminate the replacement question. As of Thursday morning, it was narrowly ahead, with the results not having been called yet.

About 7 in 10 registered voters nationwide favor requiring photo identification to vote, according to an October poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research. Support is higher among Republicans, but a majority of Democrats also favor it.

Before Tuesday, at least 15 states had adopted citizenship voting requirements in the past decade, including all eight states that voted on them in 2024 and Texas last year.

Aside from elections-related issues, dozens of other ballot measures were being considered by voters in a multitude of states.

In Arizona, voters approved measures restricting school sports teams and school facilities, such as bathrooms, by biological sex. In Colorado, measures to restrict school sports teams by biological sex and to prohibit gender transition surgery for minors were leading but hadn't been called, as was a similar sports measure in Washington state.

Arizona voters approved a measure to declare drug cartels terrorist organizations, and in Tennessee, voters passed a measure to grant more rights to the victims of crimes.

Alabama voters approved amendments requiring students to recite the Pledge of Allegiance daily, requiring public schools to play the national anthem weekly, and requiring schools to allow student-led prayer.

Voters in California appeared likely to reject Proposition 40, a one-time 5 percent tax on the wealth of residents worth more than $1 billion as of Jan. 1, 2026. Vote counting is ongoing, but "no" was ahead by about 11 percentage points as of Thursday.

Democrats won control of both the House and Senate in the midterms, giving them power in Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term. Democrats also won the governor's races in Georgia and Texas.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

items.title: Burger Bloodbath Intensifies As Yet Another Major Franchisee Goes Bust
items.content_text:
Burger Bloodbath Intensifies As Yet Another Major Franchisee Goes Bust

Another fast-food franchisee has filed for bankruptcy, becoming the latest casualty of mounting financial pressures squeezing restaurant operators across the United States.

Global Midsouth Holding Corp., a franchisee of Checkers and Rally's, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on October 28, just one day before a scheduled foreclosure auction involving one of its Tennessee restaurant properties, according to TheStreet.

The Memphis-based company reported $1.9 million in assets against $1.3 million in liabilities. Revenue fell from $860,000 in 2024 to $800,000 in 2025, underscoring the financial difficulties facing the business.

However, Global Midsouth isn't the only burger franchisee that went bust.

Meritage Hospitality Group, one of Wendy's largest franchisees, filed for bankruptcy in September after struggling with declining sales, rising beef prices, and mounting financial obligations.

The operator, which ran 314 Wendy's restaurants across 15 states when it filed, had already shuttered 60 underperforming locations. Another 60 restaurants could shut down by mid-November, according to court documents.

The bankruptcies come as the restaurant industry faces even bigger problems.

As we reported yesterday, San Diego-based Out West Restaurant Group, also known as Cerca Trova Restaurant Group, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection Monday in Delaware, putting 61 restaurants across five Western states into bankruptcy proceedings.

The company's debt has exploded from $269 million in 2020 to approximately $449 million in 2026, according to the Los Angeles Times.

"Guest traffic and earnings continued to decline, while food, labor, and other production costs continued to rise," CEO David Goronkin said.

California's rising minimum wages have been a major problem, with more than half the company's employees working in the Golden State. The COVID-19 pandemic also delivered another devastating blow, sending revenue plunging approximately 35%.

Outback parent company Bloomin' Brands said that it is preparing to swoop in. The restaurant giant has offered $26.3 million to acquire the struggling franchisee's assets, alongside up to $5.5 million in emergency financing. "This is an isolated situation involving the franchisee," a Bloomin' Brands spokesperson said. The 61 restaurants are expected to remain open during bankruptcy proceedings.
