Futures are showing signs of an early bounce, but the biggest rout in the Nasdaq 100 since the Covid pandemic has left investors wondering whether capitulation is already here or is still building. Thursday's selling pulled down everything from chipmakers to retailers, with 85% of S&P 500 members down on the day, but tech was the culprit: the SOX suffered a six-standard-deviation drop measured against moves over the past 20 years, a sign that investors are now cutting exposure at any cost after building oversized positions in anything AI-related. And while there was no obvious headline to trigger the crash, the catalyst is clear: data center opposition had been building one moratorium at a time, and the midterms tilted a broad swath of the regulatory map against the AI buildout (as we discussed in "Democrats Spent Year Demanding Data Center Moratoriums. They Own The Narrative. Will They Own The Fallout?").

“There’s a real sense of panic in the selling, and I suspect crowded positions, deleveraging and possibly forced liquidations are making things much worse,” said Dilin Wu, a strategist at Pepperstone Group. “This looks like more than just investors getting nervous about AI valuations.”

Semiconductor stocks in exceptional rout: such moves lower have happened only twice in the past 20 years.

Forced sellers may not be done. According to JPMorgan Market Intelligence, the move lower was "exacerbated by retail selling and forced liquidations", with retail sellers by over three standard deviations; levered ETFs are estimated to have sold $60 billion of equity exposure into the close, 90% of it tied to tech, and vol control funds still have about $50 billion to sell over the next few days (see also McElligott's "$47BN In Levered ETF Selling, $61BN In Vol Control"). Systematic funds are now short US equities, which means the good news, per the desk, is that positioning is a lot cleaner.

Volatility is off the highs, but Thursday's 11.6-point jump in the VIX to 28.18 was the third-largest one-day rise from a calm start since the index began in 1990, while the VVIX, the "vol of vol", jumped the most in eight years.

Only two VIX spikes have started calmer and gone further.

JPM's Market Intel desk under Andrew Tyler is sticking with its Tactically Bullish call, noting that when the NDX is within about 6% of all-time highs and drops 3.5% or more, the index tends to rebound about 3% the following week. JPM's Ron Adler, global co-head of equity HT cash trading, was more sober: "AI remains the fulcrum point of the market, and I think it's that straightforward," he wrote, adding that while a lot of the positioning pain has been taken, "right now, that's about all I have." Into payrolls, JPM's Michael Feroli sees 75k jobs vs a 65k Street estimate and the unemployment rate falling to 4.1%, but the desk warns that NFP may have asymmetric downside risk: a beat is fine but backward looking, while a miss will add to recession fears in a market now pricing "if AI fails or capex goes to zero."

The head of Goldman's Americas equities execution services summed up Thursday's floor: "Our phones are exploding with asks for color. Unfortunately we aren't seeing much." Over at Goldman's London desk, Rich Privorotsky called Thursday's session "a violent catch down" and asked the question everyone is asking: "Is this a 1998 style liquidity crisis and buying opportunity, or March 2000 and the beginning of a structural technology unwind? I lean toward 1998." GS derivatives strategist Lee Coppersmith notes the bank's Vol Panic Index surged to 9.57 out of 10, with Cboe trading more than 11 million puts, the largest put volume day on record; after the 15 prior signals above 9.5, the S&P averaged a 4.6% gain over the next three months. Meanwhile, Goldman's Ismail Abbas notes that "many of our AI related baskets just had their biggest down day since the launch of ChatGPT," and futures closed below the medium-term CTA threshold, with $7.5 billion of S&P for sale over the next week in a down tape. On the credit side, the most leveraged AI infrastructure bonds are now firmly distressed according to GS TMT sales, with CDS implying a more than 60% five-year default probability (as we previewed in "Blast Radius").

Bank of America's Michael Hartnett noted that through Wednesday, US equities had their biggest four-week inflows since June, with $92.3 billion pouring into US stock funds; the team remains "risk-off" until central-bank rate hikes end, the 10-year Treasury yield falls below 4.5%, and oil drops below $80. In politics, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries promises to "stop the stupid Trump tariffs," incoming Senate Finance chair Ron Wyden says he will reassert congressional authority over trade, and Trump blamed "Dumocrats" for the hit to Americans' 401(k)s (because of course he did).

In Europe, the Stoxx 600 is down 1.3%, off the worst levels after sliding as much as 1.7% earlier, as the global selloff wipes out the weekly gain and every sector trades in the red; media shares are the worst performers while tech sits toward the top of the pile as the selloff stabilizes, with ASML up 3%. The DAX is down 2.1% and the FTSE 100 drops 2.0%, while Spain's IBEX holds up best. JPM's desk sees buyers of semis and renewables and covering in MidEast shorts, while software, defense and luxury are under pressure; Bloomberg notes that Europe's diversified market has suddenly become one of the most attractive trades around as global investors seek to shed AI exposure.   • Intercos shares rise as much as 7.7% in Milan after the company said it expects a strong start to 2027. The manufacturer of cosmetic products posted 3Q revenue, adjusted Ebitda that grew year-on-year.

Asian stocks extended the global rout, with the MSCI Asia Pacific Index sliding as much as 5.3%, its steepest drop since March, and on course for its longest losing run since August 2023. Japan's Nikkei 225 tumbled 6% and is now more than 20% below its June record, officially in a bear market, with Tokyo Electron, SoftBank and Kioxia opening with double-digit losses. South Korea's Kospi plunged as much as 8.8%, triggering a 20-minute trading halt and briefly breaking below 5,000, before closing down about 6% as SK Hynix sank more than 10% and Samsung lost over 6%. Taiwan's Taiex tumbled as much as 9% and entered a bear market as TSMC slid 4.7%, prompting authorities to impose short-selling curbs and activate the national stabilization fund. China held up better, with the CSI 300 down about 1.6% and the Hang Seng off 1.3%, while the ASX 200 fell 0.5% thanks to its lack of tech names. Goldman's Asia desk says Taiwan was the most net sold market for a second week (-$1.2 billion) while China saw $815 million of net buying, adding that so far "the flow has been orderly, and we have not seen any significant signs of panic." Japan's GPIF reported a ¥5.25 trillion quarterly loss, its first in six quarters.

In FX, the Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index rose as much as 0.3% to a one-week high, with the greenback higher against all G10 peers as traders pivot back to treating it as a safety trade. Risk-sensitive currencies lead losses: USD/NOK is up 1%, the kiwi is down 0.9% and the Aussie fell 1% to 0.6862, its weakest since April. Cable dropped as much as 0.5% to 1.3382, its biggest drop since Oct. 14, a day after the BoE's hawkish hike, and EUR/USD slid to a 1.1167 low. The franc and yen are the most resilient, with USD/JPY around 157.8-158.3. Goldman's FX strategists note that "the broad Dollar has remained strikingly stable throughout the equity fluctuations of this week."

In rates, Treasuries hold modest losses, with yields 2-3bps cheaper across the curve and the 10Y around 4.86%, near the session high, after Thursday's haven rally sent the 2Y down 12bps to 4.46% and the 10Y down 5bps to 4.835%; ahead of payrolls, bond traders are positioned for further gains as expectations for more Fed rate hikes continue to fade, with swaps pricing about 18bps of tightening for December, or a 72% chance of a hike, down from 82% on Wednesday; the Bloomberg crowd-sourced whisper number for payrolls is 81k vs the 70k median estimate. Bloomberg's Ven Ram notes that haven flows into bonds "haven’t held up": German bunds gave up an early rally that pushed the 2Y yield down 5bps to 2.93%, its lowest since Aug. 31, with the 10Y Bund little changed at 3.24%, while gilts lag Treasuries by about 2bps as the market digests a BoE that was far more hawkish than expected and Bailey's warning that another hike is likely if energy prices stay high. The OAT-Bund spread stands at 154bps after widening almost 4bps on Thursday. Goldman's Arvind Giridhar thinks the asymmetry in reaction to NFP is to a miss rather than a beat, so "the front end remains a buy on dips." The IG dollar slate is empty so far after eleven names priced almost $22 billion on Thursday, pushing weekly supply above $74 billion, the fourth largest this year; Alphabet plans Hong Kong and Singapore dollar bonds after Apple raised $7.5 billion (at this point, a hyperscaler not selling bonds would be news).

“AI is mainly a US story. We shouldn’t see a 1-1 spillover to Bunds and other EGBs,” said Larissa de Barros Fritz, senior rates strategist at ABN Amro. “The theme for EGBs will remain sovereign risks, and we see AI themes as mainly a driver for UST into the year-end.”

In commodities, crude benchmarks pared the week's rebound, with Brent Jan futures slipping back toward $98 after peaking at $100.83 and WTI Dec up 0.5% at $90.94 after a $92.53 high, as markets digest a call between Qatar's Emir and Trump on de-escalating tensions in the region. That followed a morning in which the geopolitical premium had been building, with Iran claiming two tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz and an Iranian MP warning a US attack could send oil above $150; meanwhile, Kyiv hit a sixth Russian oil plant in a week, halting the Yanos refinery, and Aramco cut its prices. Dutch TTF is well off its highs. Spot gold falls 0.5% to around $4,069/oz but remains on track for its biggest weekly gain since August, even as Goldman cut its end-2026 forecast to $4,150/oz and end-2027 to $4,800/oz; silver rises 0.4% to $52 and LME copper is lower in a $13.64k-13.83k range.

DB's Jim Reid concludes the overnight wrap

What a week it's been. I'm not sure whether watching the last episode of Slow Horses last night or watching markets yesterday left me more exhausted after a huge slump in the most AI-exposed parts of the market. In fact, the scale of the moves ranked among the biggest in years, and the Philly semiconductor index (-12.25%) had its worst day since the pandemic slump in March 2020. And in turn, that cascaded elsewhere, with the S&P 500 (-4.36%) posting its biggest slump since the Liberation Day volatility in April 2025. So that drove a huge surge in the VIX index (+11.6pts), which also saw its biggest daily jump since the Liberation Day period, ending the session at 28.2pts, its highest since March. Meanwhile, several other points of recent stress crept back in, with Brent crude oil prices (+3.88%) paring a little of their losses from earlier in the week, whilst the Franco-German 10yr spread (+3.8bps) also widened again. So the risk-off tone was undoubtedly back.

The sell-off has spread to Asia but Nasdaq futures (+0.77%) are edging back up a bit after the -5.52% slump yesterday. However that hasn't saved Asia with the Nikkei (-6.28%) now more than -20% below its June record high and into bear-market territory. Elsewhere, South Korea's KOSPI (-4.39%) is also sharply lower after plunging as much as -8.8% in early trading, its lowest level since early February. The index was up more than +116% in late June and it's now up "only" just over +22%. The Korean Exchange temporarily halted stock and derivatives trading for 20 minutes earlier after the benchmark dropped -8%, triggering a circuit breaker. Meanwhile, losses elsewhere in the region have been more contained, with the Shanghai Composite (-1.27%), Hang Seng (-1.29%), CSI 300 (-1.58%) and ASX (-0.49%) all trading lower but not slumping. S&P futures are down around a tenth of a percent with Stoxx futures down around a percent having closed before the last leg of the US sell off last night.

These moves have come as investors continue to ponder the likelihood of tougher AI regulation after the midterms, with the most exposed stocks seeing a big impact. Indeed, the decline in the Philly semiconductor index now leaves it more than -38% beneath its peak back in June. And several names saw even bigger losses, with CoreWeave (-9.83%) falling to its lowest level since April 2025, with its 5yr CDS widening another +127bps to 1289bps. Meanwhile, Nvidia (-9.26%) had its biggest drop since January 2025 and is now slightly lower YTD, whilst Tesla (-10.77%) had its biggest drop since July.

What was striking about yesterday’s moves was there wasn’t a particular catalyst driving them. Of course, the midterm results were in focus, but these were already known the previous day, after which US equities saw a huge rally. While initially some more defensive portions of the market held in better, by the close only 73 members of the S&P 500 were higher on the day. This is broadly consistent with the last time the S&P 500 was down this much on 10 April 2025, when just 75 companies in the index were up on the day. So while the equal weight index (-2.89%) outperformed it clearly also suffered.

However the rotation trade over the last month has had a profound impact with S&P’s information technology (-15.89%) and communication services (-13.43%) posting sharp losses, whereas consumer staples (+13.96%) and healthcare (+11.24%) have posted equally sharp gains. But even though more than two-thirds of the index’s members have moved higher in the last month, the sheer weight of tech has dragged down the broader index.

With AI fears gathering pace again, that led to a fresh round of question marks as to whether the Fed would hike again in December. For now it’s still considered likely, but market pricing came down from 82% on Wednesday to 68% by last night’s close. And in turn, there was a strong rally for US Treasuries, with the 2yr yield (-11.9bps) down to 4.46%, whilst the 10yr yield (-5.3bps) fell to 4.835%.

Notably, all those moves came in spite of another very strong batch of US data. For instance, the weekly initial jobless claims fell to just 189k in the week ending October 31 (vs. 196k expected). And in turn, that took the 4-week moving average down to its lowest since 1969, at just 194.75k. Meanwhile, nonfarm productivity was also stronger than expected in Q3, growing by an annualised +3.6% (vs. +2.7% expected), whilst the Q2 number was revised up from +1.4% to an annualised +2.1% pace. So there was good news on both the labour market and on productivity, which sets the backdrop for the October jobs report at 13:30 London time. As a reminder, our US economists expect nonfarm payrolls to rise by +55k in October, with the unemployment rate remaining at 4.2%. But the next FOMC meeting isn’t until December 9, so there’s still another jobs report after this one before the Fed’s next decision.

As all that was going on, matters weren’t helped by a fresh rise in energy prices, with Brent crude (+3.88%) closing at $98.29/bbl. It moved back above $100 this morning but is just below again as I type. Clearly it was a lot higher last week, but given that the active contract was down over -16% over the first three days of the week, it was a reminder that positive headlines could only take prices down so far without a proper resolution in the conflict. That said, we did get a New York Times headline yesterday which said that Iran was reviewing a set of proposals from mediators, and they were willing to re-engage on nuclear talks.

Earlier in Europe, markets put in a comparatively resilient performance, reflecting the continent’s more limited exposure to AI and the fact that it closed before the last leg of the slump. For instance, the STOXX 600 was on course for a record high at one point, before it ultimately closed -0.38% lower. Clearly that wasn’t great, but compared to the slump in the S&P 500, it showed how tech was such a big driver of yesterday’s moves. Indeed, several European indices even managed to post gains yesterday, including France’s CAC 40 (+0.34%) and Spain’s IBEX 35 (+0.59%). Futures point to a weaker open but still notable outperformance in the last 24 hours.

The other big story in Europe yesterday was the unexpectedly hawkish hike from the Bank of England. The 25bp hike to 4% was widely expected, but the decision to hike was unanimous, and the one dissenter actually wanted a larger 50bp hike instead. Looking forward, Governor Bailey also signalled further hikes ahead, saying that “Unless progress towards resolving the conflict is made, or there is other news which softens the risk to inflationary pressures, a further increase in bank rate may be warranted”. Moreover, their latest inflation forecasts now saw CPI rising to +4.9% in Q2 2027. Our economists believe a December rate hike is now finely balanced. But given recent positive developments in the Middle East and the Bank’s near-term projections, they think a February rate hike is marginally more likely (with December likely delivering a 5-4 hold) but much can happen between now and then. For now they retain their view for one more hike with Bank Rate peaking at 4.25%. See their review piece here

10yr gilt yields were -2.6bp lower on the day before the announcement but then rose +6.8bps intraday as the market absorbed the hawkish messaging before a late flight to quality trade left benchmark yields little changed (+0.2bps).

For European bonds, there was more of a classic risk-off move, with 10yr bund yields (-2.2bps) falling back, in contrast to those on 10yr OATs (+0.7bps) and BTPs (+2.5bps). So that meant the 10yr Franco-German spread was back up +3.8bps to 154bps, slightly unwinding its big move lower the previous day. But unlike in the US, there wasn’t much of a shift in ECB pricing for December, with investors still pricing a 76% chance of a rate hike by the close, broadly unchanged from the 79% at Wednesday’s close.

Finally, COP31 (the UN’s Climate Change Conference) kicks off on Monday, and our analysts have written a preview on it for the DB Research Institute (link here). Among others, they expect AI’s climate potential and rising electricity demand to feature prominently in discussions, with a focus on clean-energy expansion to support its growing power needs.

Looking at the day ahead now, the main data highlight will be the US jobs report. Otherwise, we’ll get German industrial production and Euro Area retail sales for September, and the University of Michigan’s preliminary consumer sentiment index for November. From central banks, we’ll hear from the Fed’s Williams, Musalem and Bowman, along with the ECB’s Lane and the BoE’s Pill.

items.title: Tesla To "Wind Down" Cybertruck Production At Gigafactory Texas
items.content_text:
Tesla To "Wind Down" Cybertruck Production At Gigafactory Texas

"Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Elon Musk revealed on X early Friday morning. 

Musk described the Cybertruck as the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and said winding down production would mark the "end of an era."

US Cybertruck sales fell well short of Musk's goal of 250,000 units per year. Kelley Blue Book estimates that Tesla sold 38,965 Cybertrucks in the US in 2024, 20,237 in 2025, and 11,586 in the first nine months of 2026, for a total of 70,788 over that period.

"It doesn't make sense to keep it going when it's not meeting its targets," former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer told Reuters. "Every rational auto guy would say the same."

"It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla's balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves," Palmer said.

Electric pickups have struggled to gain traction with American buyers. Ford Motor understood, with the now-discontinued F-150 Lightning, and Dodge canceled plans for the Ram 1500 EV. GMC has experienced a sharp decline in Hummer EV sales as the broader EV industry languishes. 

However, Musk touted on the third-quarter earnings call that interest in Full Self-Driving software was "very strong."  

"Demand is growing rapidly for our vehicles. It's exceeding our production by a significant margin," Musk told investors. "The biggest driver for demand is full self-driving, and today there's really no competitor for FSD in any car that you can buy."

The Cybertruck did, however, stand out to US Special Forces, who described it as the most advanced truck ever built (read that note here).

Musk's focus is now on the nationwide Robotaxi rollout, which will require Tesla to ramp up vehicle production. As for the Cybertruck, one question remains. Could Tesla bring it back in the years ahead as a cheaper second-generation model?

Musk's other focus is SpaceX. He aims to bring rocket launch costs even low enough to make data centers in low Earth orbit viable, beyond the reach of the Democratic Socialist Party's push for ground moratoriums (at least for now). He also aims to take on AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile with a new mobile carrier that could launch in the coming year. The target for a broader commercial rollout is 2028. Also, let's not forget Optimus is coming...

items.title: Trump, Qatar's Emir Discuss Iran Peace Deal As Brent Suffers Biggest Weekly Drop Since COVID Crash
items.content_text:
Trump, Qatar's Emir Discuss Iran Peace Deal As Brent Suffers Biggest Weekly Drop Since COVID Crash

Brent crude futures briefly tumbled to $96 a barrel before rebounding to $98.50 as diplomatic efforts to end the nine-month war with Iran progressed toward the end of the week. President Trump spoke with Qatar's emir about Doha's efforts to broker a peace deal between Washington and Tehran. 

The Democratic sweep in Tuesday's midterms and Trump's subsequent comments that he had no immediate plans to strike Iran have eroded the war risk premium in crude. Brent is on track for its steepest weekly decline since the oil market crash of April 2020.

President Trump and Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani held a call "aimed at reaching a comprehensive agreement to end the regional crisis," according to a report from Arab Weekly. 

More color about this week's diplomatic signals from the London-based newspaper:

Iran sent the United States a nuclear proposal through Qatar, which Tehran says can be discussed only after Washington meets its seven demands, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday.

The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the United States was reviewing the proposal but declined to give further details.

Mediators have stepped up efforts to end the war between Iran and the United States amid fears that hostilities could resume after the US midterm elections. Trump on Tuesday declined to rule out restarting combat operations after the vote, while Iran is planning a wider retaliation if the war resumes.

Iran's top security official Mohsen Rezaei said earlier on Thursday, during a visit to Russia: "On the issue of diplomacy, we have announced seven conditions to the Americans. As long as they do not execute our seven conditions, we will neither open the Strait of Hormuz nor have negotiations."

Iran has called for the lifting of US sanctions, the release of frozen Iranian assets and war reparations, among other conditions. Washington, meanwhile, has insisted that nuclear issues must be included in any initial negotiations.

Separately, Iran's state broadcaster, IRIB, cited Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, who said, "Iran must see practical US actions with its own eyes, and once those actions are observed, the ground will be set to open a new chapter," adding, "It is Iran's right not to settle for paper commitments from the Americans before entering a new stage of diplomacy." 

On Thursday, UBS energy expert Dominic Ellis wrote that the collapse in crude's war risk premium this week reflects the prospects for peace and the potential for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen fully. But he warned that those hopes are colliding with the harsh reality that replenishing depleted global oil stockpiles could take considerable time.

Ellis pointed out that the conflict has drained nearly 700 million barrels from global inventories. Fundamentals still point to a severe global energy crisis that won't dissipate anytime soon.

Read the UBS report here. Our report earlier this week showed that US distillate stockpiles plunged below 100 million barrels for the first time since 2003.

items.title: Is Anthropic About To Delay The Biggest IPO Ever?
items.content_text:
Is Anthropic About To Delay The Biggest IPO Ever?

Backers want a lower price, the November timetable is in doubt, and executives and advisers are set to meet to review the deal...

Major institutional backers are pushing Anthropic to cut the $1.5 trillion valuation it had been targeting for its IPO, and one suggested pricing could fall closer to $1 trillion, the Wall Street Journal reported Thursday, after the Nasdaq Composite lost $2.5 trillion of market value in a single session.

Anthropic had aimed to raise up to $100 billion around the week before Thanksgiving, which would top SpaceX's June listing as the largest offering ever. According to the Journal, executives and advisers plan to meet in the coming days to review the IPO, and backers are debating whether to adjust the price range or push back the timeline. With a mountain of cash on hand, the company can afford to shrink the raise or wait.

Potential investors doubt Anthropic can complete its roadshow the week after next and still list in November, four people familiar with the discussions told Reuters. The roadshow had been expected to start the week of Nov. 9, with pricing the week after. Some now see $1.5 trillion as the high end of expectations, and Anthropic may need to offer a bigger discount because of its record of quarterly losses and its huge commitments to partners in the AI buildout. If the pressure on AI-related assets continues, the company could postpone until markets look sturdier, the sources said. Anthropic declined to comment.

Investors are also waiting on Anthropic's October revenue, which was left blank in its updated S-1, to see whether growth has recovered from its recent slowdown, two of the sources told Reuters.

The valuation has been marked down once already. After Anthropic told investors in October that third-quarter revenue grew 45% from the second quarter, down from more than doubling the quarter before, IPO investors marked it down from about $2 trillion to $1.5 trillion, as we reported.

Tech stocks suffered their sharpest selloff in a year after Tuesday's midterms handed Democrats the House and Senate, a blue wave that knocked the market's teeth in. The Journal tied the retreat to AI-skeptical lawmakers and local data center moratoriums; Reuters pointed to ballot efforts in many states to limit data center development. Meta president Dina Powell McCormick said Wednesday that building data centers will be "harder following the election results," Yahoo Finance reported.

Prediction markets have cut the odds of a November listing. On Polymarket, the odds of an Anthropic IPO by Nov. 30 fell from 84% to 58%, and by Dec. 31 from 90% to 73%...

In private markets, OpenAI has secured only $11 billion of the $30 billion it targeted in its latest round, at an adjusted $1.25 trillion valuation, according to the Journal.

As for those commitments, this week's amended filing put Anthropic's committed spend at $895.4 billion, more than $1 trillion all-in...

..., with $69.8 billion due in the next 12 months...

Buyers would also inherit Anthropic's philanthropy. Anthropic has already put 5% of its fully diluted stock into its own Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, managed initially by CEO Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela, Jack Clark and Buddy Shah, and the board may add up to another 2% every time the stock rises 50%. The co-founders, who stand to be worth hundreds of billions after the IPO, have each pledged 80% of their personal equity to charity. The employee donation-matching program alone produced a $2.0 billion non-cash charge in the third quarter, one of the two items that pushed Anthropic back to an operating loss.

And whoever buys in won't get much say. As we detailed when Anthropic's S-1 landed last month, a single Class F share owned by the seven co-founders carries 50.1% of the vote, the Long-Term Benefit Trust elects a majority of the board, and public shareholders will never hold more than 49.9% of the vote, one of the 10 biggest red flags we found in the filing.

items.title: Above-Average Returns: Why The Next Decade Differs
items.content_text:
Above-Average Returns: Why The Next Decade Differs

Authored by Lance Roberts via Real Investment Advice,

Sixteen years of above-average returns came mostly from rising valuations, and that is the one source that cannot be repeated from here.

Key Takeaways

  • Since the end of 2009, the S&P 500 compounded at 14.34% a year, or 11.41% after inflation. The long-run real average since 1881 is 6.72%.
  • Of that 11.41%, some 4.33 points a year came from nothing but the valuation multiple doubling.
  • Across 146 years, 140 of the 164 starting months with a CAPE of 25 or higher produced a below-average next decade. The 24 exceptions all fall in 2014 to 2016.
  • The highest CAPE ever to precede a decade this good was 26.95, in August 2016. Today's reading is 41.04.

In 2016, McKinsey warned that the "golden era" for investors had ended. Falling rates, fatter margins, and a rising multiple had done their work in creating above-average returns. Younger savers, the report said, would have to work seven more years or save nearly twice as much. Ben Carlson went back and graded that call this month. Since that spring, U.S. stocks have returned roughly 15% a year and more than tripled, European shares compounded near 10%, and a saver who took the advice and doubled their contributions now has a very comfortable problem. The call was wrong. Carlson's verdict is blunt and correct. Sometimes the three most useful words in this business are "I don't know."

"Strip the multiple out and the last sixteen years were ordinary. Every point of excess came from investors agreeing to pay more for the same dollar of profit."

I also have to take that same hit, as I have previously published my own versions of that caution, and the market ran anyway. Anybody claiming they called the last sixteen years of above-average returns is selling something.

Where The Above-Average Returns Actually Came From

While the bulls certainly have control of the narrative, there is a problem with treating that scoreboard as the end of the argument. The bears weren't wrong about the inputs. They were wrong about ONE variable. Which one matters is important because it will decide whether the case still stands today.

Let's start with the data. I pulled Robert Shiller's monthly series back to 1871 and broke real returns down into their specific components. Real total return splits into three pieces. What earnings were, what dividends were paid out, and what investors decided those earnings were worth.

Real earnings grew 4.91% a year. That's close to three times the 1.91% long-run rate. Dividends chipped in 1.96 points against a past norm of 4.25, because yields today are far thinner. Then there's the third bar. The CAPE ratio climbed from 20.32 at the end of 2009 to 41.04 in October, and that single "re-rating" of the same earnings stream, with no help at all from profits or payouts, added 4.33 points a year to what investors took home. Look at how much of the left bar it is.

Strip the multiple out and the last sixteen years delivered roughly 7% real, which is almost exactly the long-run average. Every point of excess came from investors agreeing to pay more per dollar of smoothed profit. Such is the anatomy of a "golden era."

That's the piece McKinsey missed. They had the right list of tailwinds, but they just assumed the "re-rating" had finished. But it hadn't, and it ran for another decade, producing the above-average returns that made the forecast look foolish.

Why Above Average Returns Can't Repeat From Here

Now run the same math forward. The multiple would have to add another 4.33 points a year for sixteen years. That takes a CAPE north of 83. Not 41. Eighty-three. No market on record has held half that.

Which raises the question that the decomposition doesn't answer. What drove the first doubling?

The discount rate did most of the work. Roughly half those sixteen years were spent with the funds rate pinned at zero, from January 2010 through December 2015 and again from March 2020 into 2022. The 10-year average yield was 2.20% from 2010 to 2021, compared with 4.71% for the entire Shiller record since 1871.

The Fed's balance sheet went from under a trillion dollars to a peak near $9 trillion. Argue all you like about whether the Fed led that or followed it. Either way, money was cheaper for longer than at any point on record, and cheap money lifts what buyers will pay per dollar of earnings while quietly flattering earnings themselves.

Here's the trap in that. The only thing that brings ZIRP and QE back is the crisis that justifies them. Either rates hold near 5%, and the multiple gets no help, or something breaks badly enough to put the Fed back at zero, which means the damage already happened. Baa corporates yield 6.47% today, and the maturity wall refinances at the new number, not the old one.

Going back to the Shiller data set, I tested every month from 1881 onward. For each one, I logged the CAPE, then the real total return over the next ten years. That gives 1,628 overlapping readings. They stop in August 2016, because any month after that doesn't have ten years behind it yet.

The pattern isn't subtle. Of the 164 starting months with a CAPE at or above 25, some 140 of them, roughly 85%, gave back a decade below the 6.72% long-run average. Go higher, and it gets worse. The 57 months above a CAPE of 30 averaged a loss of 1.02% per year, and the best of them posted a gain of 4.49%.

Before we proceed, we must discuss the caveat, because somebody will raise it, and they're right to. Two dozen of those expensive months beat the average. They ran from June 2014 through August 2016, starting CAPEs between 25.16 and 27.00, and delivered real returns of 8.86% to 12.02% over the decade that followed. So an expensive market has paid off. Exactly once.

Look at what that particular decade contained. It caught the back half of ZIRP, the 2020 emergency response, and the AI earnings expansion, and it finished with the CAPE at 41 instead of 26. The one time in 146 years that a high starting valuation was paid, it paid because the multiple expanded again from an already expensive base. That is the engine described above, and it's the engine that is most likely not returning anytime soon.

The overlap caveat matters a lot. When looking at those 1,628 readings, they were not 1,628 independent events. This is because the ten-year windows overlap, and the months within one episode repeat the same story. For example, the "expensive" months cluster into four episodes: 1901, 1928 through 1930, the long stretch from 1995 to 2007, and 2014 to 2016. Three ended badly. One didn't.

So call it three out of four, not 140 out of 164, and the honest reading is that expensive markets usually disappoint and occasionally don't.

26.95 - The highest starting CAPE ever to precede a decade as good as the one we just had. August 2016. Today we sit at 41.04.

Even the exception started from a valuation of 27, and it needed the multiple to run to 41 to get there. We're now being asked to believe the market can do it again from 41. Such is the "this time is different" bet, whether or not anyone phrases it that way.

"The bears had the right list of tailwinds. They simply assumed the re-rating had finished. It hadn't."

The Bullish Case Against The Next Secular Bear

While the data is clear, the bulls do have a serious answer to all of this.

The bullish argument is that above-average returns may remain for three primary reasons:

  • The current CAPE ratio of 41 is a broken yardstick, because the measure still drags the 2020 earnings collapse into its ten-year average.
  • It ignores the shift from capital-heavy industry to software margins, and accounting rules expense the very intangible spending that builds those fat margins.
  • Corporate buybacks also changed the cash math. A 2% "yield" in 2026 isn't the same as a 2% yield in 1962.

Every one of those points is fair. It's why real earnings grew at triple the old rate instead of reverting. I can't argue the AI capital cycle is a fiction either. The spending is REAL, and the profits so far are real.

Then there's the bull's best evidence, which happens to be mine too. The Fed raised the Fed funds rate from zero to more than 5% starting in 2022, and the CAPE promptly fell from 38.30 to 27.08, exactly as the discount-rate story would predict. Since then, that valuation multiple has climbed to 40.94 anyway, with the 10-year at 5.01%. The multiple rose into the most aggressive tightening in forty years.

The obvious answer is uncomfortable for both bulls and bears. A multiple that expands while the discount rate rises isn't resting on rates at all. It's resting entirely on what investors believe earnings will do, and today those estimates are very exuberant, as we noted recently.

"Corporate earnings just broke above a trend that had contained them for more than 90 years."

With expectations as high as they are currently, that foundation is much more fragile than a rate-supported multiple. If the earnings story disappoints, there is nothing sitting below the market to support it.

Here is where it gets interesting. Grant the whole case. Say margins hold higher and earnings keep growing near 5% real. You still don't get back to 11%, because the other two engines now run in reverse.

Stocks now yield 2.44% on smoothed earnings, and a 10-year Treasury pays 5.0%. That gap is the widest since 1999. For most of the previous market history, the discount rate was a tailwind, falling year after year and lifting what buyers would pay. It isn't doing that now. And the dividend engine can't climb back to 4.3% unless prices fall a long way first, which rather defeats the purpose.

However, there is a second channel that gets much less attention than valuations. Critically, it works through flows rather than math. From 2010 through 2020, the 3-month Treasury bill averaged 0.56%. It sat below a quarter point on 63% of all trading days. Cash paid you nothing to wait. For most of the previous decade, the entire market trade was built on the "TINA" trade. The idea that "There Is No Alternative" to risk assets was never really a thesis. It was a hostage situation. Money got pushed out of safe assets and into risk because safety had been priced at zero.

That entire scenario has now flipped with a 3-month Treasury bill paying roughly 4% today, while the S&P yields 1.06% in dividends, the lowest reading in the entire Shiller record. Cash pays roughly four times what stocks pay, with none of the drawdown risk. The same policy that once shoved money into equities can now pull it back out. That doesn't take a forecast to matter. It just takes a retiree doing arithmetic.

I will get this comment almost as soon as this article is posted:

"You're just repeating the mean-reversion call that's been wrong for a decade."

Fair enough. But I'm not making a timing call. A CAPE of 41 tells you almost nothing about next year. However, it tells you a great deal about the next ten.

What A Reasonable Investor Does With This

Start with the understanding that none of this discussion is a "forecast." Valuations are, and always have been, a horrible timing tool. Instead, let's examine the data in a grid. Start at a CAPE of 40.94. Add the dividend yield of 1.06%. Then vary the two things nobody can know. Where the multiple goes, and how fast real earnings grow.

Those are yearly real total returns. One cell beats the last sixteen years. It also needs the most expensive market on record to stay exactly that expensive for ten more years, while earnings grow at triple their old pace. Such is the wager now priced in.

None of this argues for selling everything and waiting in cash. As I've written before, full market cycles have two halves, and sitting out the first half can cost you more than the second half takes. However, the grid suggests that we should calibrate our expectations. For example, if your current plan assumes a 10% nominal return because that's the number in the brochure, you may be disappointed when your portfolio returns something nearer 3%. That gap doesn't show up as a bad quarter. It shows up as a retirement date that moves much further out into the future.

Secondly, the hard work is both practical and dull, and you will be fighting your emotions the entire way.

  • Save more than the plan requires.
  • Trim winners back to target weights instead of letting them grow into concentration.
  • Own duration while it pays 5%, since the rate hurting stock valuations is the same one paying you in the bond sleeve.
  • And decide now what you'll do at a 20% drawdown, because bear markets do useful work for anyone holding cash and a plan when one shows up.

Carlson is correct in his view that nobody knows what will happen next year, or the year after that. He is also right in that humility beats false precision. However, a forecast and a constraint are very different animals, and historically above-average returns from here run into the second kind. In other words, the math simply doesn't care whether anyone believes it.

items.title: Investigation Exposes America's Growing Cancer Crisis And Reveals Where It's Worst
items.content_text:
Investigation Exposes America's Growing Cancer Crisis And Reveals Where It's Worst

A growing cancer crisis is gripping younger generations across the United States as increasing numbers of Americans in their 20s, 30s and 40s are being diagnosed with diseases once overwhelmingly associated with older adults, according to an analysis conducted by the Daily Mail.

A 2025 National Cancer Institute study identified 14 types of cancer with rising rates among Americans under 50, while alarming new maps reveal where the disease is striking hardest. Roughly three out of four Americans diagnosed with colorectal cancer before age 50 already have advanced-stage disease, according to the American Cancer Society's 2026 statistics. Colorectal cancer rates among adults ages 20 to 49 have been climbing approximately 3% annually, while rates among Americans 65 and older have been falling.

The findings have left some of the nation's leading cancer researchers confronting an increasingly urgent question: What is driving this troubling rise in cancer among younger Americans?

Breast cancer rates are especially high among younger women in parts of the Northeast and East Coast, while colorectal cancer increases stretch from California and the Pacific Northwest to Florida.

Pancreatic cancer presents an even more troubling picture, with rates among Americans under 50 climbing nearly 3% annually and increases recorded across much of the South, Midwest and East Coast.

Researchers are investigating a growing list of suspects, including ultra-processed foods, obesity, pesticides, environmental chemicals and exposures that may begin in childhood.

A 2025 study by researchers at Mass General Brigham and Harvard Medical School involving 30,000 young women found that heavy consumers of ultra-processed foods faced a 45% higher risk of developing colon polyps, some of which can eventually become cancerous. Yet, there's a problem with blaming everything on America's deteriorating diet and expanding waistlines.

What is even more concerning is that researchers are investigating whether exposure to everyday chemicals during childhood could be contributing to cancers diagnosed decades later. Substances found in plastics, food packaging, cosmetics and household products are now under scrutiny for their potential effects on the body's hormones.

Additionally, researchers are examining whether exposure to certain pesticides could be playing a role. A study involving pesticide applicators in Iowa and North Carolina found that exposure to a commonly used herbicide was associated with a threefold increase in pancreatic cancer risk, although researchers have not established that pesticides are driving the broader rise in cancer cases, according to the Mail.

Doctors are increasingly encountering younger cancer patients who are otherwise remarkably healthy.

"It's remarkable to me how healthy some of these individuals are," University of Colorado cancer specialist Dr. Christopher Lieu told the Mail.

items.title: Butane's Perfect Storm Sends Prices To Decade Highs
items.content_text:
Butane's Perfect Storm Sends Prices To Decade Highs

Authored by Natalia Katona via OilPrice,

Butane prices are surging across the world. Northwest European November butane prices have reached $1,125/t by early November, their highest level in 30 years, having exceeded even the peaks following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. In Asia, the AFEI butane index stood at $1,180/t on November 3. US butane Belvieu prices have climbed to a 14-year high $920/t.

This surge in prices reflects several overlapping trends, with the most significant being a reorientation of global propane/butane trade flows since the US-Iran war kicked off in March. Before the conflict, the US supplied roughly 45-50% of global LPG exports and the Middle East another 30-35%. After the beginning of the Middle Eastern crisis, the Gulf countries' share subsequently collapsed to 11%, while the US substituted much of this shortfall and its share reached 65%.

Asia has absorbed much of that replacement supply. Middle Eastern producers previously covered around half of Asia's imports, offering relatively short voyages and cargoes suited to local requirements. In April-October, the US propane and butane supplied as much as 75% of Asian imports, drawing volumes away from other destinations, including Europe. That share eased to around 55% in October as deliveries from the UAE, Kuwait, Qatar and Saudi Arabia gradually recovered. Yet the broader restoration of Gulf exports has been stronger in oil, and the current flow of LPG shipments remains insufficient to loosen Asia's inevitable reliance on American cargoes. This is pulling US cargoes away from other regions. Subsequently, in October butane monthly imports into the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp (ARA) hub have fallen to a multi-year low of just 130,000 tonnes, down 34% from a year earlier.

However, replacing Middle Eastern supplies to Asia is complicated by their composition. 

US LPG exports are approximately 75% propane and 25% butane in outright terms, whereas Indian (and many other Asian countries) cooking-gas requirements typically favour a blend closer to 50:50, with butane helping maintain suitable vapour pressure in warmer climates. More American propane therefore cannot fully compensate for missing Middle Eastern butane.

India's exposure made the consequences particularly severe. At the outbreak of the crisis, roughly 87% of its LPG imports came from the Gulf, with the UAE and Qatar together accounting for half. Imports dropped from 2.03 million tonnes in February to 1.17 million tonnes in March, a fall of more than 40%. The government ordered refiners, including petrochemical complexes, to maximise LPG production and prioritise households. Some consumers switched to piped natural gas, although its higher cost and only partial indirect government support limited the relief. Recovering imports from the Middle East and strong reliance on US cargoes have given refiners more flexibility to ease emergency LPG production and restore output of other products, particularly petrochemicals.

China's demand comes from a different direction, as expanding capacity for gasoline additives and basic chemicals increases its feedstock requirements. Five new plants producing MTBE (methyl tertiary-butyl ether, which raises gasoline's octane rating, helping prevent engine knocking, with butane supplying its hydrocarbon component through several processing steps) opened in 2025, adding combined capacity of 3.4 million t/year and supporting demand for imported butane. Crucially, the gasoline using Chinese MTBE need not be consumed in China. Producers export the additive to other Asian markets, Europe and Latin America, allowing overseas demand to sustain butane purchases even when Chinese gasoline consumption is subdued. China produces butane domestically, but industrial expansion increases its need for supplementary imports.

This Asian demand is coinciding with another major factor that pushes butane prices up - the seasonal increase in Atlantic basin consumption. Winter gasoline specifications in the US and Europe require refiners to blend in more butane, whose high vapour pressure helps fuel vaporise and engines start in cold weather. The autumn switch into winter-quality gasoline typically strengthens butane demand between October and March, which means American producers are competing more actively with overseas buyers. US exports reached a record 2.4 million tonnes in May before decreasing to 1.55 million tonnes in October (still 12% higher than a year earlier). Asia received 840,000 tonnes, or 54% of October shipments, while Europe took only 105,000 tonnes, approximately 7%.

That distribution explains Europe's predicament: American exports are seasonally decreasing, just as Asian demand leaves less and less butane available amidst strengthening European blending demand. Operational disruptions have tightened US butane availability further, with force majeure at Energy Transfer's Nederland terminal in Texas and a compressor outage affecting butane loadings at Freeport last month.

Even Asia's ability to attract American cargoes is now approaching a commercial limit. US butane at $920/t, plus approximately $320/t in freight to India, produces a delivered cost of $1,240/t. The landed US butane versus AFEI butane spread is at $50-60/t, making the arbitrage commercially unattractive for American producers. For comparison, in April the spread reached minus $300-400/t, creating a huge incentive for US shippers to sell their LPG volumes to Asia. For additional shipments to become once again attractive, US prices or freight must fall, or Asian prices must rise further. Winter blending demand complicates the first possibility, while the last would deepen the burden on importers already struggling with expensive energy.

Continued recovery in Gulf deliveries can ease pressure across these interconnected markets, allowing Indian refiners to retreat from emergency LPG production and freeing more American cargoes for Europe. Yet that relief depends on maritime security in the Hormuz Strait, leaving buyers exposed to renewed US hostilities with Iran. Another escalation would force India back into the market for long-haul cargoes while Chinese industrial demand and European winter consumption would compete for the same supplies. America remains the obvious source of replacement volumes, but its own internal dynamics and the current economics of shipping suggest it cannot keep filling the Gulf's supply gap at prices buyers can comfortably afford.

items.title: France's Debt Crisis Could Trigger A Much Bigger European Meltdown
items.content_text:
France's Debt Crisis Could Trigger A Much Bigger European Meltdown

Authored by Alastair Paynter via OilPrice,

  • A budget deficit of 5.1% and public debt exceeding 115% of GDP raise concerns about France's fiscal sustainability and the eurozone's resilience.
  • Industrial decline, energy disruptions, political instability and growing nationalist movements are putting pressure on EU cohesion.
  • France's presidential election, Poland's political crisis and the rise of Central European nationalism could accelerate divisions within the bloc.

France's present economic woes signal serious trouble ahead for the coherence of the European Union. On Wednesday evening, the French National Assembly unanimously rejected the government's proposed budget, provoking further fears in the bond market. A couple of weeks ago, it was reported that the French government's budget deficit now stood at 5.1 per cent, the worst it had been for nearly a quarter of a century. Its national debt now stands at over 115 percent of its GDP. Last Friday, the credit ratings agency Fitch downgraded the outlook for France from stable to negative. How close might we be to a French default?

There are precious few good options for dealing with such a scenario. Permitting a country of France's magnitude to default would undoubtedly undermine international confidence in the Euro, at a time when most EU economies have been struggling under the weight of multiple pressures. However, the only possible means of preventing a sovereign default would be a bailout from the European Central Bank. This option would place an immense burden on Germany and would hit savers there hard. While bailing Greece out in 2010, 2012 and 2015 was considered a necessary course of action to stabilise international markets and save the Eurozone, the prospect of having to do the same for France could prove a bridge too far.

For its part, the German economy has also been under immense pressure for several years, particularly as the industrial sector has suffered under the dual burden of extensive Green regulations, enacted during the high water mark of climate politics during the late 2010s and early 2020s, and geopolitical crises such as the Russia-Ukraine war and the US-Israeli war with Iran and the turmoil in the Straits of Hormuz.

It appears increasingly possible that Marine Le Pen might win the French Presidential election next May. But even if that does happen, would she be able to meaningfully address France's economic woes or would she be forced to comply with the EU? She has at present promised to cut French public spending to below 50 per cent of GDP by 2032. Yet even relatively modest measures to cut spending tend to be met with fierce protest, making the issue a particularly thorny one for politicians of any stripe. France has of course for several weeks been rocked by widespread protests, rioting and looting as the social fabric frays. Regular politics appears to offer few solutions.

The instability of the political system is evident in the fact that five Prime Ministers have served under President Macron since 2022. It must be noted that this is not a uniquely French problem. In fact, the same effect can be observed both inside and outside the EU as a kind of 'vortex effect' seems to be in operation as the postwar era comes to a close and we enter a kind of interregnum before the new era emerges. For those taking the broader historical view, a number of political, economic and social cycles are coming to an end at roughly the same time. And while it is true that modern mass democracies tend to be characterised by a short political cycle and a high time preference among decision makers, these processes have sped up even more as governments repeatedly break down and instability mounts. The larger question is whether any leader can emerge who can break free from this vortex effect or whether the pattern is doomed to repeat until the system breaks down entirely.

The world has been moving away from globalism and towards a more multinodal, 'nationalist' arrangement. Yet despite this, even many of the major populist and nationalist political parties and leaders across the West are still operating within the general envelope of the postwar consensus. As the case of Italy under Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni illustrates, even in those countries where such parties have won elections and formed governments, significant change from the prior globalist status quo has not been forthcoming.

This makes it more likely that the present collection of nationalist parties across the EU and elsewhere does not in fact represent the final form that nationalist politics will take. It is quite likely that the longer the present period of turbulence persists, the more hardline political options will emerge. Certainly, if the present political establishment continues to double down on the failed strategic imperatives of yesterday they will only stiffen the very opposition they claim to oppose, running the risk of further and greater crises.

While the integrity of the Euro as both a concept and a practical reality remains the most pressing issue for the immediate coherence of the EU, it is important to keep an eye on other political pressure points too. For instance, the present political and constitutional crisis in Poland will prove a major stress test for the EU. The outcome of the conflict between pro-EU Prime Minister Donald Tusk and the nationalist opposition rallying around President Karol Nawrocki will provide an important indication as to how the globalist-nationalist dynamic could develop across the EU more widely.

Longer-term, all global indicators appear to suggest the ascendance of nationalism and the waning of globalism. The outcome of the Polish crisis could either slightly delay or accelerate this process in Europe. Poland is of growing geostrategic significance in Europe. Its economy is one of the few within the EU that has actually grown significantly over the last few years, while its central bank has in recent years pursued a policy of gold acquisition that now places the country amongst the top ten national gold holdings in the world, standing at over 630 tonnes. As I predicted in my risk report Europe 2026, the Central European region - comprising Poland, Czechia, Slovakia and Hungary - could over time begin to assume an even more significant regional power unit within Europe. This possibility would also be affected by the outcome of the present war between Ukraine and Russia, which will obviously have a major impact on the broader strategic landscape of the continent as a whole.

2027 could therefore see an acceleration of existing trends as multiple separate crises converge. The ability of governments to respond effectively to such a 'polycrisis' will be a major pointer to the durability or even survivability of supranational power structures, such as the EU, all of which were constructed in a very different epoch and context.

items.title: China's New 'AutoDNA' AI Lab Needs Humans For Just Two Chores
items.content_text:
China's New 'AutoDNA' AI Lab Needs Humans For Just Two Chores

Researchers at Shanghai Jiao Tong University have built a laboratory in which a team of AI agents designs and runs DNA experiments from a single typed prompt, with people stepping in only to restock reagents and service the hardware, according to a paper published this week in Nature.

The system, called AutoDNA, moves samples between instruments with robotic arms and can operate more than 20 types of equipment. A single project can involve thousands of operations, including synthesizing and sequencing DNA, Nature's news report said. "An experiment is designed and executed from start to finish by a team of AI agents, following a simple prompt from a human operator," it added.

The Nature paper reports four test applications. The system matched expert-optimized yields in enzymatic DNA synthesis, ran concurrent protocols 3.2 times faster, completed a full DNA data-storage cycle with exact recovery of the original digital content, and identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D cancer mutation. In one demonstration, the researchers had it encode a quote often misattributed to Stephen Hawking, "Intelligence is the ability to adapt to change," into DNA's four letters: A, C, G and T.

Labs have used automation for years, but usually for a single step such as mixing or heating. AutoDNA was designed around AI from the start rather than adding AI to an existing lab, said Haibo Chen, a computer scientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong and a co-author. "In many existing systems, human experts are still required to configure the instruments," he said. "AI is mostly added to handle just one part of the process."

Outside researchers were impressed. Milad Abolhasani, a chemical engineer at North Carolina State University, called the system remarkable for its autonomy and for how readily it takes in different lab equipment. "The future of science is going to involve a lot of autonomous labs," he said.

The work is one of several recent efforts to hand experimental biology to AI agents. Nature's news report lists a robot chemist that designs reactions and makes drugs on its own and an AI biolab at Anthropic among its related coverage. The AutoDNA code is on GitHub, and the sequencing data and agent outputs are on Zenodo, according to the paper's page.

items.title: Ukraine's Azov Brigade Admits Holding AWOL Soldiers At Residential House Amid Torture Allegations
items.content_text:
Ukraine's Azov Brigade Admits Holding AWOL Soldiers At Residential House Amid Torture Allegations

Authored by John Weeks via Antiwar.com,

A riot erupted Monday night outside a residential house in Ukraine's Petropavlivska Borshchahivka, a suburb approximately 12 miles west of Kyiv, after social media posts claimed the military was torturing conscripts in the basement and that medics were being denied access to the wounded.

Approximately 200 people gathered at the house. They threw eggs, water bottles, and bricks at police and National Guard soldiers. After they broke through the brick wall surrounding the house, they were dispersed with tear gas and live ammunition warning shots.

A confrontation broke out on Nov. 2 in Petropavlivska Borshchahivka, a village on the outskirts of Kyiv, where hundreds of civilians gathered near an unmarked facility with National Guard soldiers present following unverified reports that mobilized men were being unlawfully held... pic.twitter.com/DlEJ40Tr1O

— The Kyiv Independent (@KyivIndependent) November 2, 2026

A statement released that night from the 1st Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine confirmed that the house was a "military camp" operating as a "temporary deployment point of military unit 3121 of the National Guard of Ukraine, which belongs to the 1st corps of the Azov National Guard."

The statement said the camp was holding "mobilized servicemen" who had been "detained after committing an unauthorized abandonment of the unit...awaiting distribution to military units and further service." It said four of the detainees had "injuries" and dismissed the torture allegations as "unverified information."

"Azov protects the lives and health of its servicemen in extremely difficult conditions at the front. The unit is guided by the same principles in the rear: this applies to all servicemen of the corps and does not depend on the length of their service, " the statement said.

The Azov Battalion was founded in 2014 by Andriy Biletsky, out of his Patriot of Ukraine gang and fellow travelers from Right Sector, the coalition Nazi militia that had played a pivotal role in the 2014 Maidan coup. Since then, Azov has evolved into two sections, "The Third Army Corps," which Biletsky leads, and "The 12th Special Forces Brigade Azov" within the National Guard.

Both National Guard commander Oleksandr Pivnenko and Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov arrived at the scene to restore order and assure protesters that the allegations were false and that the four injured detainees had been taken to a medical center.

Ukrainian officials suggested an influence campaign might be at work, but admitted the reality of the deeply controversial mobilization tactics makes such potential campaigns easy to run.

As The Kyiv Independent put it, "While the events in Petropavlivska Borshchahivka show signs of a Russian information operation, their escalation is built on real, simmering tensions in Ukrainian society around the topic of mobilization."

Ukraine has been under martial law since Russia's "full-scale invasion" of 2022, which authorized forced mobilization. Draft officers have resorted to ripping military-aged men off the street and throwing them in vans or buses as a standard recruitment practice. Hundreds of draft officers have been attacked, and a few have been killed.

items.title: Is Russia Rehearsing An Attack In Orbit?
items.content_text:
Is Russia Rehearsing An Attack In Orbit?

Two Russian satellites are drifting toward the orbit of a second US-registered radar satellite run by Finland's ICEYE, weeks after a sibling spacecraft closed to within about 500 meters of the first, and one analyst says that earlier pass "looks like an attack rehearsal."

Greg Gillinger, a senior space analyst at Integrity ISR and a former US Air Force intelligence officer who has tracked the satellites, told Reuters that Cosmos 2612 has since moved about 400 km (250 miles) away from ICEYE's X36, and that two sibling Russian satellites are now drifting toward the path of X37, according to the Daily Mail's account of the interview. COMSPOC, a US space-tracking firm, said the two were becoming increasingly well positioned to approach X37. Both ICEYE satellites are US-registered, according to public space-object catalogues.

Gillinger said such a close approach would not be needed for intelligence collection or electronic interference, which points to a test of kinetic attack-related capability. "This is the most aggressive posture I've seen Russia take in terms of threatening satellites from another nation," he said.

How It Got Here

Russia launched six Cosmos satellites, 2609 through 2614, on a Soyuz-2.1b rocket in April. Between May 14 and 20, Cosmos 2610, 2611, 2612 and 2613 each raised their orbital inclination by 0.8 degrees, from 97.0 to 97.8, putting them in nearly the same orbital plane as X36, Gillinger wrote in a May analysis. He called a plane change that size rare in low Earth orbit because of the fuel it burns, and said X36, a roughly 90 kg satellite, likely lacks the fuel to dodge a co-orbital threat.

Cosmos 2612 began stalking X36 on Sept. 30, according to satellite tracker Marco Langbroek, as Breaking Defense reported. Between Oct. 15 and 19 it made a "deliberate series of maneuvers" and came within roughly 500 meters, LeoLabs said. "This is the most advanced and potentially dangerous uncooperative RPO we've observed," LeoLabs vice president Adam Marsh said, using the term for a rendezvous and proximity operation. LeoLabs also admits its observations do not establish hostile intent, and that its distance estimates may be uncertain.

Washington And Moscow

As we previously reported, a US delegation adviser signaled to the UN First Committee on Oct. 21 that the maneuvers had military implications, and Moscow called the US claims absurd. 

US Under Secretary of State Thomas DiNanno said Cosmos 2612 was "intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite" in conduct "consistent with on-orbit weapons operations." 

Russia's defense ministry did not respond to a request for comment, the Daily Mail's account says.

Moscow has said commercial satellites that help Ukraine could be targets. In October 2022, Russian diplomat Konstantin Vorontsov said "quasi-civilian infrastructure may become a legitimate target for retaliation." ICEYE's radar constellation has been a key imagery source for Ukraine, and Ukraine's military intelligence said in June 2024 that 38% of nearly 4,200 images from a donated ICEYE satellite were used to strike Russian targets, Gillinger's analysis notes. The Daily Mail adds that Western officials have warned the Russian activity around ICEYE shows capabilities that could be used against commercial constellations, including SpaceX's.

Not every expert reads it as a rehearsal. 

Germany's space commander, Maj. Gen. Michael Traut, said close approaches like this can serve inspection, observation or interference, depending on the spacecraft, and "we must therefore consider the entire spectrum of possible effects, ranging from temporarily disrupting a satellite's operations to permanently disabling it." He cautioned that the ability to make the maneuvers is not itself evidence of an attack being prepared.

ICEYE's US operations chief, Ann Stevens, said X36 "has been and will continue to be a productive satellite" and that the constellation is resilient to disruption. Washington has itself acknowledged putting weapons in orbit: as we noted, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said the US has deployed "on-orbit space control weapons."

Russia has not said what its satellites are for, and Traut says public orbital data alone cannot determine their purpose.

items.title: 从 Linux 到维基百科：志愿者如何构建互联网
items.content_text: Linux 和维基百科代表了一种被称为同侪生产（Peer Production）的模式——这一名字由法学教授 Yochai Benkler 提出。古典经济学认为，如果想要人们开展合作以及有效分配合作所产生的成果，那么最有效方式是通过私人营利性企业实现，即由这些企业在开放市场中销售商品或服务。企业雇用员工并支付报酬，而员工则通过合同承担义务，按照管理者分配的任务开展工作。员工劳动所创造的产品归公司所有，公司负责为产品定价、管理销售交易，支付员工薪酬以及分配经营过程中产生的利润。从理论上说，这些方法能解决几个关键问题：如何协调各方的利益动机、如何组织和安排工作任务，以及如何确保最终产出的成果能分配给有意愿且有能力支付费用的人。然而同侪生产为古典经济学传所依赖的行为模式提供了一种替代方案。在同侪生产中，无论是合同义务、经济激励，还是官僚式权威，都无法确保参与者一定会贡献自己的劳动，也无法保证这些劳动能有效组织。由此产生的成果属于公共资源（Public Commons），受到非排他性知识产权的保护。这意味着同侪生产所创造的资源无法直接在开放市场上进行定价。在理想形态中，同侪生产项目对自身工作的范围、领导者权威的合法性，以及值得投入精力的任务选择，都保持着完全的集体自主控制权。但在实践中，同侪生产往往只是以不同程度的形式得到运用，实施主体也包括一些并不完全符合上述所有定义标准的机构。

items.title: 特斯拉将停产 Cyber​​truck
items.content_text: 特斯拉 CEO 马斯克（Elon Musk）宣布将于 2027 年年中停产电动皮卡 Cyber​​truck。生产电动皮卡的工厂很可能转为生产电动出租车 Cybercabs。马斯克于 2019 年末宣布了外形奇特的 Cyber​​truck，预计售价低于 4 万美元，宣称它会和其主力电动汽车 Model 3 和 Model Y 一样随处可见。然而 Cyber​​truck 研发比特斯拉的其它车型更坎坷，为量产还修改了底盘结构，而 25 万年预售目标也根本无法实现。如今马斯克的粉丝将只剩下几个月的时间购买这款奇特的电动皮卡。

items.title: NASA 通过 AI 生成图像宣布 X-70 试验机
items.content_text: NASA 宣布了新试验机 X-70 Fractal，它展示了一幅生成图像——即并非实图，而是 AI 生成的。NASA 称，X-70 是载人飞行器，设计巡航速度为 0.75 马赫，最大飞行高度约 13700 米，航程 2778 公里。X-70 起飞重量为 4536 公斤，设计可容纳 900 公斤的机内外试验载荷。NASA 局长 Jared Isaacman 表示，这架试验机有望在两年内首飞。关于其具体设计细节和研发时间表目前知之甚少。NASA 公布的生成图像显示 X-70 与超音速侦察机 SR-71 非常相似。

items.title: 中国三季度 CO2 排放下降 3%
items.content_text: 根据 Carbon Brief 的分析，中国第三季度 7-9 月的 CO2 排放量同比下降 3.1%，为 2022 年以来最大降幅。今年至今中国碳排放量累计下降 0.5%。数据显示，中国第三季度石油消费量同比下降 4%，煤炭使用量同比下降 3%。第三季度 CO2 排放量下降的关键因素之一是燃煤发电量减少 3.3%。背后的原因是电力需求增长放缓，同时风能和太阳能未被利用的发电量也有所减少。太阳能、风能和核能的发电量同比增加了 110 TWh，超过了同期电力总需求增幅的两倍。

items.title: Silver Lake 和 PIF 磋商收购 Unity Software
items.content_text: 私募股权公司 Silver Lake 和沙特主权财富基金 PIF 在今年八月完成以 550 亿美元收购 EA 之后正在磋商收购游戏引擎提供商 Unity Software。Silver Lake 持有 8% 的 Unity 股权。在 Unity 发布最新财报前，收购财团论过约 250 亿美元的估值；财报发布后 Unity 市值升至约 215 亿美元。如果交易达成，Unity 将和 EA 一样私有化。Unity 的游戏引擎和开发者工具在游戏行业被广泛使用。Unity 于 2004 年在丹麦成立。自上市以来，公司业务已从游戏引擎扩大到广告技术和实时 3D 软件。

items.title: Salon 宣布终止出版
items.content_text: 有 31 年历史的 Salon 于 2026 年 11 月 5 日宣布从即日起停止出版。Salon 创办于 1995 年 11 月 5 日，当时的互联网与今天截然不同。一小群记者开始尝试创造一些与众不同的东西：他们希望创办一种具有鲜明风格、对世界充满好奇，并且坚信互联网能以全新的方式将新闻报道与读者连接起来的出版物。他们开创了一种全新的新闻报道形式，这种形式后来成为定义了一个全新的出版时代。

items.title: 摩托罗拉宣布第一款支持 GrapheneOS 的旗舰手机
items.content_text: 摩托罗拉宣布了第一款支持安全加固发行版 GrapheneOS 的旗舰手机 Signature 27，但售价高达 1600 美元。Signature 27 配备了高通目前最强大的移动芯片骁龙 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6，内存只有 12GB 没有 16GB 版本（目前内存供应紧张而且价格昂贵），存储空间为 512G​​B (UFS 4.1）；显示屏为 6.8英寸 Extreme AMOLED Duo，120Hz刷新率，12,000 尼特峰值亮度；电池 7000 mAh，90W 有线充电，15W (Qi) 无线充电，等等。

items.title: 微软画图应用曝出远程代码执行漏洞
items.content_text: 微软画图应用曝出了一个越界读取导致的远程代码执行漏洞，受影响版本从 11.0.0.0 到 11.2605.91.0 之前。画图应用被预装在每一台 Windows PC 上，最近一段时间微软为画图应用引入了越来越多的新功能，其中包括 AI 生成功能，它同时也给画图引入了新 bug。微软用户目前可能需要通过 Microsoft Store 官方应用商店下载修正后的版本，Windows Update 尚未推送新版本。

items.title: Kagi 开放搜索
items.content_text: 付费无广告搜索引擎 Kagi 宣布了最新更新，向所有人开放搜索，但免费用户搜索次数有限额。现在任何人无需注册账号可搜索 50 次，注册账号之后再增加 100 次。Kagi 还抨击了 Google 最近的一项决定：如果美国学校选择禁用 AI 那么它的搜索引擎也将会对学校关闭。Kagi 认为：教育不应沦为广告公司的人质，应当停止将企业利润置于教育学生这一核心使命之上。它呼吁美国学校可选择包括 Kagi 在内的其它搜索引擎。

items.title: 《尼尔：自动人形》释出更新游戏容量从 50GB 暴涨至 366GB
items.content_text: 2017 年发售的《尼尔：自动人形（Nier: Automata）》释出了最新更新，加入了对简繁体中文以及韩文的支持，但游戏的打包显然存在 bug，整个游戏文件的容量从 50GB 暴涨至 366GB。《尼尔：自动人形》共有八个 DLC，每增加一个 DLC，游戏的容量就会增加 40GB，也就是每个 DLC 都包含了主游戏文件。现在想要玩《尼尔》的中韩玩家最好先等待游戏开发商释出修正，除非你的 SSD 有几百 GB 的可用空间。

items.title: 印度金融机构遭黑客利用 AI 工具发动的网络攻击
items.content_text: 印度计算机应急响应小组（CERT-In）星期三发布安全通报，被称为“狡猾猎鹰”（Crafty Falcon）的黑客组织，已入侵非银行贷款机构、金融科技公司及加密货币交易所。攻击者利用公开可用的 AI 工具，实现高速自动化入侵。印度计算机应急响应小组形容这项威胁“仍在发生，且持续活跃”。该机构点名四款用于入侵的工具，分别是 ARTEX、PentAGI、Cairn 和 CyberStrikeAI。ARTEX 此前曾被用于攻击韩国银行。印度计算机应急响应小组没有说明这些攻击事件由谁发动，也未透露该组织的运作地点。该机构也没有称这些攻击由国家支持或主导，且其点名的攻击工具均可在网络上免费获取。

items.title: 同步导致电网呈现周期为一分钟的震荡
items.content_text: 今天的电网接入了数以百万计的数字控制设备，为了维持电力供需平衡，精准预测和实时控制必不可少。电力系统因此转变成为一种信息物理融合的基础设施（Cyber–Physical Infrastructure）。物理设备与数字控制系统之间形成了紧密的相互依存关系，在带来前所未有的效率与灵活性的同时也引入了新的系统性风险。根据发表在《Nature Energy》期刊上的一项研究，德国研究人员指出全球电力系统存在的一种由信息物理同步效应所引发的、周期为一分钟的相干振荡现象。除了故障和恶意攻击外，即使是良性的控制程序，当大量设备以协同一致的方式运行时，也可能产生系统层面的影响。在大规模信息物理能源系统中，非预期的同步行为可能引发反复出现且具有潜在放大效应的振荡现象。

items.title: 越南对足球直播盗版者判刑最高一年
items.content_text: 越南一家法院对 14 名参与盗版足球赛事直播网站 Bun Cha TV 的团队判处最高一年徒刑。4 名内容、编程和运营团队负责人被判处 12 个月徒刑，另外 5 人判处 10 个月监禁，2 人判处 8 个月监禁，3 名解说员被判处 10 个月缓刑。所有 14 名被告都承认了指控，配合了调查。Bun Cha TV 累计直播逾 15 万场体育赛事，通过博彩及赌博广告非法获利逾 200 亿越南盾（约 512 万人民币）。内容团队负责人获利逾 4.3 亿越南盾，解说员非法所得则在 3100 万到 4.8 亿越南盾不等。美国 MPAA 的代表称赞了这一判决。

items.title: 白宫网络监测到住宅代理活动
items.content_text: 安全公司 Layer3 Intel 报告，他们在分配给白宫的自治系统 AS2650 中监测到住宅代理服务的活动。住宅代理服务会将用户的网络地址租给其他人使用。Layer3 在 10 月 5 日-11 月 3 日期间观察到了 236 次住宅代理连接活动。住宅代理的源头被认为来自 Windows 11 设备安装的俄罗斯代理程序 Infatica。Layer3 Intel 指出，在30 天内有 26 天出现了源自白宫的代理出口节点流量，涉及 6 个 IP，大部分活动发生在傍晚，即下午 5 点至午夜之间。

items.title: Bazzite 45 释出
items.content_text: 基于 Fedora 的游戏发行版 Bazzite 释出了 v45。主要变化包括；基于 Fedora 45，更新 Open Gaming Collective(OGC)内核，支持罗技 TrueWheel 设备等等。过去几年 Linux 对游戏的支持有了显著改善，但对很多用户而言仍然需要自行配置。Bazzite 项目旨在让 Linux 桌面用户无需额外配置就能畅玩游戏，设计类似 Valve 的 SteamOS，但更适合通用桌面使用情景：SteamOS 主要支持 AMD GPU，Bazzite 包含了私有的 NVIDIA 驱动。

items.title: Google 和 OpenAI 的模型对特定口音有偏见
items.content_text: 研究人员调查了先进多模态模型如何评估面试、会议报告和英语口语能力测试中的语音，测试的模型包括了 Google 的 Gemini 2.5 Pro 和 Gemini 2.5 Flash，以及 OpenAI 的 GPT-Audio 1.5，开放权重模型 Qwen 3 Omni。这些模型对五种不同口音——美国、英国、中国、印度和尼日利亚——的英语语音进行了评分。AI 模型普遍将中国和尼日利亚口音的评分最低，印度口音居中，美国和英国口音的评分最高。即使内容完全相同，系统仍然认为美国和英国口音的表达方式和内容都更胜一筹。研究团队发现，明显的等级划分也体现在模型的解释中。研究人员说，模型反复声称中国和尼日利亚口音的英语使用者含糊不清或难以理解，但实际上它们非常擅长转录带有口音的语音，它们理解说话者，但它们只是基于口音，对说话者存在一种隐性的等级观念。

items.title: 富钾盐替换普通盐有助于每年预防数百万人死亡
items.content_text: 澳大利亚乔治全球健康研究院的研究人员评估了在 193 个国家将食盐供应转换为富钾盐的健康益处。他们发现，全球每年可预防近 300 万例死亡和 1000 万例心血管疾病和肾脏疾病新发病例。富钾盐是通过用氯化钾替代部分氯化钠（即普通食盐的主要成分）制成的。它在外观、味道和烹饪方式上都与普通食盐一样。2025 年世界卫生组织（WHO）认可使用富钾盐来降低血压和心血管疾病风险。全球范围内，30-79 岁成年人中有三分之一患有高血压，相当于约 14 亿人。心血管疾病（CVD）是全球死亡和残疾的主要原因，2023 年导致 1920 万人死亡，过去 30 年增加了近 50%。虽然潜在益处很大，但一个担忧是晚期肾病患者出现高钾血症（血钾水平过高）的风险。然而，研究发现，即使在晚期肾病患者中，益处也大于风险。

items.title: Swift 天文台从印尼上空重返大气层
items.content_text: NASA Neil Gehrels Swift 天文台于 11 月 4 日 7:39 a.m. EST 从印尼苏门答腊上空再入大气层，坐标为北纬 3.4 度、东经 98.6 度。天文台的大部分组件在重返大气层过程中烧毁，可能有部分组件幸存下来。Swift 天文台重 1.5 吨，于 2004 年发射升空，旨在研究高能伽马射线暴的起源。过去 22 年受大气阻力的影响 Swift 天文台的轨道高度在缓慢下降，过去两年的太阳活动加速了其坠落。今年 7 月 NASA 曾尝试了一次拯救任务，但任务失败。

items.title: 任天堂最大 ROM 芯片供应商准备退出
items.content_text: 任天堂 Switch 游戏机实体游戏卡带使用的 ROM 芯片供应也受到了 AI 热的影响。任天堂最大 ROM 芯片供应商旺宏电子在其第三季度财报中宣布它准备终止 ROM 芯片生产，脱离游戏行业。旺宏电子表示，ROM 芯片的产量在过去一年中缩减了 39%，目前仅占其业务总量的 5%。ROM 芯片正逐渐被利润更高、需求更旺盛的其它存储芯片所取代。这意味着任天堂未来只能依靠其它 ROM 芯片供应商如罗姆（Rohm）和蓝碧半导体（Lapis Semiconductor），意味着游戏卡带生产成本可能会进一步上升。任天堂已经承诺未来会继续提供实体游戏卡带，不会效仿索尼只提供游戏的数字版本。

items.title: 新型牙刷通过产生电对抗牙菌斑病原体
items.content_text: 一款新型牙刷可通过刷毛移动产生电能，进而可对抗产生牙菌斑的病原体。在为期 3 个月、涉及 115 名志愿者的试验中，牙刷在减少口腔中导致龋齿和牙周炎的细菌方面的效果优于常规的机械刷牙法。牙刷是人类对抗牙菌斑的最强战士，它每晚都能物理性地清除牙齿上的细菌生物膜。然而细菌总会卷土重来，因此每天早晨都会重新开始这场战斗。北京大学口腔医学院的研究人员研发出一种牙刷，其压电单丝刷毛在刷牙过程中弯曲时会产生电荷。这一过程会产生活性氧，进而能破坏牙齿上的生物膜。在实验室中，该装置能有效杀灭口腔病原体，如牙龈卟啉单胞菌（Porphyromonas gingivalis，可引发牙周炎）。研究人员还在真实口腔环境中评估了这种牙刷的实用性。他们将这种牙刷分发给总计 115 名志愿者，这些人都接受了相同的刷牙指导。根据对样本的基因测序和宏基因组测序结果，志愿者口腔中有几种口腔病原体的相对丰度有所下降。总体而言，与传统尼龙刷毛牙刷相比，这种牙刷能更好地控制牙菌斑、减轻牙龈炎症和出血。

items.title: distinct mechanisms for yelling from the gonads
items.content_text: Some evolutionary innovations are so useful that nature keeps on making them. There's the crab; everyone knows nature keeps making crabs. There's the ability to fly, whether by feathers, membranes, or chitin. And, of course, there's the indispensable trick of using one's genitals to scramble the sonar of hunting bats. No, your eyes are not deceiving you. Some moths have evolved the ability to make noise at bats using their genital structures.

items.title: The Scythians toked the reefer
items.content_text:
"Until now, the earliest evidence of cannabis use dated to around 2,500 years ago: charred marijuana remains found in eastern China that contained high levels of THC. That evidence, however, was indirect because it only showed the plant remains—whereas the newly found combination of seeds and human hair offers a "smoking gun of evidence" for humans using the plant to get high". (archive)

"It's easy to look at this stuff and say, 'Oh, the Scythians toked the reefer,'" Taylor jokes. "But in fact, it is a tremendously powerful snapshot into an interconnected world in which the people and cultures of the steppe were starting to shape life on both ends of a massive continent."

items.title: Stunning Map Shows Just How Much the Country Swung Left in Elections
items.content_text:
Want to see just how far left the United States shifted in Tuesday’s midterm elections? Look no further.

A map produced by Ground News using data from civicAPI showed just how far each U.S. county’s margin moved from the 2024 presidential election to the 2026 House vote. A whopping 94 percent of U.S. counties shifted left in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Jurisdictions in all 50 states reported an average 13-point shift toward Democratic House candidates. No state showed an overall shift toward the Republicans in the House, although there were a handful of districts that moved right.

The states that showed the largest shifts toward Democratic House candidates were New Jersey, Utah, West Virginia, and Wyoming. The states that saw the smallest leftward shifts were South Dakota, Vermont, and Oregon.

The map indicated that even in states where Democratic candidates did not win, such as West Virginia, Indiana, and Kentucky, there were still heavy leftward shifts among voters.

Voters under 30 swung sharply toward the Democratic Party, according to the AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters across all 50 states. Republicans appeared to lose most—if not all—of President Donald Trump’s gains with Hispanic and Black voters in 2024. Moderate and lower income voters also turned up to support Democratic candidates.

items.title: Trump Official Doug Burgum Has Been Pushing Data Centers for a Reason
items.content_text:
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has been pushing to build artificial intelligence data centers on public lands since he first joined President Trump’s Cabinet. A Friday report from ProPublica shows that Burgum might feel so strongly about the centers not because of worries about China or the future—but because he has somewhere between $18.1 million and $64.4 million invested in artificial intelligence companies.

Burgum’s 2026 financial disclosure document shows that the vast majority of his wealth is held with Arthur Ventures, the investment firm he co-founded. While Burgum’s Senate confirmation ethics agreement forced him to resign from Arthur Ventures, he still maintained his financial interests at the firm.
