The scale of the Democratic victories on Tuesday changes the actuarial math for the future of the Supreme Court. If Thomas and Alito had retired earlier this year and been replaced by younger conservative justices in their early-to-mid-fifties, Democrats would not have a natural shot at a Supreme Court majority until the 2060s. Tuesday’s results make it significantly more likely that the court will not get younger or more conservative until 2032 at the earliest. If both men step down for health reasons in the next six years and Democrats win the presidency in 2028, America could see its first liberal Supreme Court majority since the 1960s.

What if one or both of the justices change their minds in the next two months? That ship may have already sailed. The GOP majority in the Senate right now is 53 seats, with Vance available to cast a tie-breaking vote. But it is a brittle majority in functional terms and especially in judicial terms. Alaska’s Lisa Murkowski is not a reliable “yes” vote, having voted against Brett Kavanaugh’s confirmation in 2018. Maine’s Susan Collins voted against Amy Coney Barrett’s nomination in 2020. (She lost her seat on Tuesday in part for voting for Kavanaugh two years earlier.) Kentucky’s retiring Senator Mitch McConnell is in very poor health.

The GOP Senate majority will shrink by one seat a few weeks early when Sherrod Brown replaces John Husted on December 15 under Ohio law. (Everyone else gets sworn in on January 3.) Even if Thomas or Alito were now more inclined to retire in the next two months, in other words, the uncertainty about having enough votes to confirm a successor may be enough to deter them. None of this guarantees a major ideological shift on the Supreme Court in any direction anytime soon. But Tuesday’s Senate victories for Democrats have tilted the playing field in their favor for at least the next four to six years.

Preventing the conservative majority from replenishing itself could end up shaping decades of Supreme Court control to come. 2016 was a very, very bad election for liberals who care about the court to lose, as they have painfully learned in recent years. The 2026 midterms happened to be a very good one for them to win.

items.title: The Surreal Has Become Real in Texas
items.content_text:
The picture, so perfectly composed, takes on a certain unreality: James Talarico, Texas’s first incoming Democratic senator in over 30 years, sitting across from incoming Democratic Governor Gina Hinojosa (the first since 1990), clinking Whataburger cups at around 1 a.m. while onlookers cheer. “First stop post-win,” the caption reads. To me, it already looks like an old photo, the kind you see in grade school textbooks, where some long-gone hero, whose name and gist is in the glossary, beams in triumph—a momentous life that could happen then, but not now. It captures something optimistic and frankly foreign to Texas Democratic politics in my lifetime.

The best-case scenario promulgated by much of the pundit class was Talarico narrowly snatching victory from his opponent, Attorney General Ken Paxton, and Hinojosa valiantly crashing against the cold certitude of incumbent Governor Greg Abbott’s five-to-one spending advantage. Instead, Texas Democrats made history. They swept every single statewide office. They’re on track to control the state House for the first time since 2002 and flip all four of the Texas Supreme Court seats that were up for the taking this year, rewriting what’s possible in the Lone Star State overnight.

At Cactus Cove, a West Houston bar where area Democrats gathered, the night’s early tenor was uncertain. Everyone knew the odds—or at least, they had learned through each painful loss over the years that hope was a dangerous thing to have. Then came the results from the East Coast time zone: South Carolina, perhaps one of the most prototypically Southern states begrudgingly roped back into the Union, looked poised to select a Democratic senator for the first time since 1998. If they can do it, why can’t we?

As reality set in, people took to the streets. Cars parked outside the state Capitol in Austin and laid on their horns, waving the Texas flag. In the Rio Grande Valley, folks gathered in a strip mall parking lot for what’s called la pitada, an impromptu parade usually saved for Dallas Cowboys wins, hoisting large Hinojosa banners over a nearby pedestrian bridge. (Hinojosa, Texas’s first Latina governor, was born and raised in the Valley: puro pinche 956.) Tarrant County, the largest urban Republican stronghold in the state (Fort Worth), flipped both up- and downballot. Ditto Collin County, Paxton’s suburban Dallas home base.

In Houston, thousands of voters planted their “I voted” stickers on the memorial site where Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was killed by an ICE agent. This was regime change—it was not bloodless, lest we forget—which even those who hoped for it hardly expected to happen this way: slowly, then all at once.

No doubt Texas Democrats can thank national tailwinds for a good portion of their success last night, but Texas Republicans also had to contend with the slow erosion of people’s quality of life under their watch for the past 30-plus years. From the 1990s onward, they were the beneficiaries of a truly globalized economy: Allied with oil magnates, crossbred with neoconservative hegemony in Washington, and drawing boundless corporate investments at the expense of people’s everyday existence, all while blaming immigrants of basically every nationality for their own utter malfeasance.

Elon Musk burned at least $212 million to keep it that way (while reportedly seeking to purchase an entire state park). Pennsylvania billionaire Jeffrey Yass spent $12 million-plus to privatize Texas’s school system. The oil industry has for years “deferred” environmental fines while engorging itself on state grants, effectively reshuffling money back to itself, all under the auspices of GOP leaders.

Ken Paxton was in many ways the poster boy of this generalized—metastasized—corruption. The top of the ticket deserves most of the blame here; beyond his seeming inability to recoup his primary opponent’s country club Republican base, he also ran a “swagless” campaign, per Texas Monthly. But Abbott was part and parcel of the late Texas GOP, the sun around which apparatchiks obediently revolved. On my way to Cactus Cove last night, my rideshare driver was preoccupied by recurring calls from her aunt, who was trying to help her pay her electric bill, which she’d already restructured to pay in chunks. “It’s those new data centers,” she told me, exasperated—which Abbott had welcomed with open arms, no questions asked, until the backlash had reached a fever pitch. (Evidently, Amazon, Meta, and OpenAI’s endorsements for his “guardrails” on the industry didn’t win voters over.)

In truth, parts of the Texas GOP are now likely eager to cosplay as resistance fighters. It was becoming played out, the establishment constantly pretending to “fight” the establishment, year after year. Whatever comes post-MAGA, be it the proto-Rhodesian fringe à la Bo French, or something closer to Abbottism—selective populism with a plutocratic bent—Republicans will likely maintain a majority in the state Senate, and the right’s online media apparatus will, with renewed zeal, showcase just how ugly and conspiratorial it can be.

Life will be hell for Hinojosa and her fellow statewides. She and Talarico’s 32-ounce Whataburger drinks had better have been strong. The moment will last forever in photos, but one day it’ll only be a page in a textbook.

items.title: Trump Has Even Warped How We View Victory
items.content_text:
Well, we did it, America. Democrats have taken back the House and Senate. Not by a trickle. Not by a wave. By a “blue tsunami.” Liberals won in districts where the entire local Democratic Party once held its annual convention in a VW bus. With room for the band.

Democracy has survived. The republic has been saved. After two years of Donald Trump’s second administration, we can finally begin the long, arduous process of returning America to the deeply dysfunctional country it was before he arrived.

Democrats have promised sweeping change. And with their new congressional majorities, they finally have the power to hold hearings to determine why sweeping change just isn’t possible right now.

We are on the verge of restoring things that, until recently, were considered routine functions of a modern civilization. Scientific research. Public health. Educational opportunity. Foreign aid. The radical notion that government employees should possess some familiarity with the agencies they run. Imagine the possibilities.

One day, the Centers for Disease Control might once again be run by someone who believes in diseases. The husk of the Department of Education could return to the controversial business of education. Scientists at the National Institutes of Health might be allowed to conduct experiments without first determining whether the results would upset a podcast host.

Of course, Trump remains president. Which means that, for now, Democrats can investigate the wreckage, subpoena the wrecking crew, and introduce legislation that will eventually arrive on his desk for a ceremonial veto. There will be speeches. Emotional reunions with congressional oversight. Perhaps a commemorative postage stamp celebrating the return of basic competence. And we will applaud.

It’s déjà vu all over again. The Tea Party seized control of the Republican Party in 2009 before devolving into incoherence. MAGA took over in 2016 and descended into fraud and economic absurdity. But Trump has managed something even more remarkable: He has made mediocrity aspirational.

Ten years ago, health care was unaffordable. Housing was increasingly out of reach. Wages struggled to keep pace with the cost of living. Millions of Americans were one medical emergency away from financial catastrophe. And those were the good old days.

Now, after watching the federal government undergo the administrative equivalent of hiring arsonists to run the fire department, we’re preparing to celebrate the restoration of the very institutions that presided over those problems.

Democrats will assure us that real change is coming. Not immediately, of course. First, there will be committees. Then bipartisan working groups to determine whether the committees have been sufficiently bipartisan. By 2028, we may have a comprehensive framework for developing a road map toward the possibility of affordable health care.

The American people demanded transformational change. What they may receive instead is a carefully worded statement expressing deep concern about the need for transformational change. And a fundraising email. Because nothing says democracy has been saved quite like an urgent request for $5 to save it again.


To be clear, restoring competent government matters. But competence is supposed to be the starting point, not the destination. We’ve lowered the bar so dramatically that future presidents may be awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom simply for not tripping over it. And here’s the remarkable part. We’ll be deliriously grateful. I know this because of my bathroom.

Recently, water damage in my second-floor bathroom destroyed part of the ceiling in my office below. And the bathroom itself was a total loss. What followed was six months of insurance negotiations, contractors, estimates, delays, displaced belongings, and the general indignity of living in a house that resembled a storage facility with plumbing.

Then, finally, the work was completed. The bathroom was beautiful. The office ceiling was repaired. The stacked boxes were gone. My house was whole again. That first morning when I stepped into my newly renovated shower, I experienced an almost spiritual sense of joy. It was over!

Six months of frustration had culminated in this glorious moment. I stood beneath the warm water, overwhelmed with gratitude. And then a thought occurred to me. Before the bathroom declared war on the house, I’d been considering replacing the kitchen counters and cabinets. And wasn’t I going to get the roof inspected? It’s pushing 15 years.

Wait a minute. I had a perfectly functioning bathroom six months ago. I hadn’t gained anything. I’d endured six months of misery to return to a condition I’d previously taken for granted. Yet emotionally, it felt like one of the great achievements of my adult life. And to think, I was prepared to nominate my construction supervisor for president.

That’s when I understood American politics. We are a nation conditioned to celebrate the recovery of things we should never have lost while quietly abandoning our expectations of things we should have gained. Trump has created enough institutional wreckage to keep his political opponents occupied for years. He has made the restoration of yesterday’s disappointments look like tomorrow’s triumphs.

And Democrats are more than happy to accept the assignment. After all, repairing what someone else destroyed is easier to explain to voters than fundamentally reimagining what government ought to accomplish. You don’t have to convince anyone that a better world is possible. You just have to remind them that things used to be slightly less terrible.

Meanwhile, artificial intelligence and automation are transforming the labor market. Health care remains a financial obstacle course. Housing increasingly resembles a luxury product. Wealth inequality continues to widen.

We could be having ambitious national conversations about universal health care, universal basic income, affordable housing, and what a dignified human life should look like in an age when technology can produce unprecedented abundance. Instead, we’ll spend years celebrating the restoration of institutions that existed while those problems keep getting worse. And the politician who restores those institutions will be called a hero. The politician who proposes building something fundamentally better will be called unrealistic. Or a socialist.

We’ll congratulate ourselves for getting our bathroom back while a kitchen cabinet door hangs by one hinge and the roof leaks. And when someone suggests renovating the rest of the house, we’ll explain that now is not the time for unrealistic expectations.

Perhaps that’s Trump’s most enduring accomplishment. He didn’t just change the direction of the country—he changed what we consider a victory. But I understand the celebrations this week. I’ve stood beneath the warm water, steam fogging the mirror, marveling at the miracle of a functioning shower. Oh, to live in a world of hot showers.

items.title: The 2026 Midterms Put an End to “Stop the Steal”
items.content_text:
On election night, around 9:30 p.m.—before Texas turned blue, before the other flips in North Carolina and Iowa and on and on—the far-right podcaster Jack Posobiec happened to say something correct on X: “It’s going to get worse.” Posobiec came to prominence in late 2016 with Pizzagate, a conspiracy theory alleging a secret sex-trafficking cabal in the Democratic Party, and went on to become one of Stop the Steal’s strongest soldiers, taking a leading role in pushing what became another deadly conspiracy theory: that Democrats stole the 2020 presidential election. But there was precious little conspiracy-mongering from Posobiec and his cohort last night. Instead, there was a series of self-important and increasingly pathetic posts, as they witnessed their power and influence fade before their eyes. They were losers, and their leader quickly confirmed as much. In 2026, Stop the Steal has met an absolute dead end.

Heading into Election Day, after months of progressive groups organizing election defense and Democrats war-gaming election-interference scenarios, there was ample reason to believe we would be facing down another attempt to overturn an election result Trump didn’t like, although what exactly that looked like might be different this time. As the Brennan Center warned, “A new threat to free and fair elections has emerged: the federal government itself.” A redux might look more like a “white-collar January 6,” as the hosts of the podcast Posting Through It suggested earlier this week. Stop the Steal could be coming from inside the house.

Certainly there were bad signs. In January, there were Trump’s threats about canceling the midterms that press secretary Karoline Leavitt claimed were “jokes.” Trump appointed Ed Martin, a key 2020 Stop the Steal leader, as an acting federal prosecutor for Washington, D.C., after which he served in other Justice Department roles, until departing in August 2026, in order to, according to Trump, “go outside to fight Legal Battles for the upcoming Midterm Election.” Tina Peters, a leading election denier who was imprisoned in Colorado, met with Trump in the Oval Office with her attorney, who said he wanted Trump to essentially declare martial law. At the same time, it seemed that talk of a “stolen” election was down, with claims of a “rigged” election taking more prominence, noted Matt Cohen at Democracy Docket, a shift to narratives claiming that the law made it “too easy” for disfavored groups to vote. Old hand James O’Keefe, once of Project Veritas, tried to make a scandal out of Minnesota’s legal process by which a registered voter can vouch for an unregistered voter, but it didn’t seem to get much traction. It was almost comical how many high-profile Stop the Steal leaders were competing with one another to influence Trump to declare a “national emergency” in order to take over the election.

Then came Election Day. At first, Chaya Raichik of Libs of TikTok, the prominent right-wing X account that had pushed 2020 election conspiracy theories in the past, attempted to transform news of a handful of minor incidents into evidence of wrongdoing. She shared a CBS News post explaining that not all results may be known on election night, claiming, “Only someone who plans to cheat would say this.” But when she eventually posted news of Democratic wins, it wasn’t to suggest election theft or fraud. It was to do what she built her account on: point her audience at a name and photo of a trans woman, or a Muslim man, or a socialist. In this case, however, these posts were about newly elected state representatives and a U.S. senator.

Even the dedicated election-denier Kari Lake, who in 2022 refused to concede her loss in the Arizona governor’s race, broached election theft or fraud only as a question. “Americans, do you think our elections are honest?” she posted on X, at 12:38 a.m. Eastern time on Wednesday. “Did we properly deal with election fraud after the 2020 stolen election after the 2022 stolen election and after the ’24 rigged elections?”

As for Jack Posobiec, he chalked the election losses up to Trump’s Iran war. The morning after, JD Vance struck a similar note. In place of the stolen election conspiracy theory, there were concessions: They lost, they were admitting, and they lost for a reason.

There was one alternate conspiracy theory offered that may not have immediately read as such. The wins, as Chaya Raichik explained them, were because “Democrats imported millions of foreigners, handed them a bunch of free shit, and then registered them to vote.” This is the so-called “great replacement” conspiracy theory, as mainstream now as JD Vance. Raichik didn’t call for patriots to seize ballots or storm counting sites; instead she called on the state. “If we ever want to win again,” she posted, “we need deportations and denaturalizations ramped up on steroids.”

In this election, with wins so vast, there was simply no room for Stop the Steal. Even election deniers lost their races last night. There’s a victory in that—not so much because “democracy held,” as some said, but because people worked hard to make it hold. At the same time, as one particular narrative about stealing elections recedes, we can see more clearly the racism and xenophobia that was always a part of it. Such white supremacism should have been more obvious when (soon to be former) Texas Governor Greg Abbott hired a Stop the Steal guy, the Christian nationalist pastor Nate Schatzlein, as an “election integrity” adviser, only for him to be far more focused on scapegoating Muslims. Far-right influencer Mike Cernovich made it impossible not to see in an X post on Wednesday: “Republicans have a choice. Court the white vote or suffer personal defeat.”

Perhaps the bottom line, though, is that without Trump on board, there is no next step. Trump quickly claimed it wasn’t his loss, and did not contest the results. Without Trump, there was only one other figure to turn to. “God can override,” said the self-described prophet Julie Green on Rumble on Wednesday. “God can overturn. God can throw out. God’s also talked about martial law.”

items.title: The Blue Wave Disintegrated Red America
items.content_text:
The blue wave landed in the states too, with consequences that rival the changes coming to Washington. Sane, pro-equality policies can now be adopted for most Americans at the state level, and the number of states where a plutocratic, racist agenda can be easily enacted has drastically shrunk.

By winning control of the governor’s office or state legislature this week, Democrats will have trifectas in six additional states: Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. (A trifecta is control of both houses of the state legislature and the governor’s office.) That puts Democrats at trifectas in 22 states, whose combined populations are about 54 percent of Americans. That’s up from around 40 percent of Americans living in Democratic trifectas preelection.

Blue America can no longer be treated as synonymous with “the coasts,” since so many states where Democrats are setting policy are far from oceans.

And with Democrats winning gubernatorial races in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Texas, and the majority of seats in both houses of New Hampshire’s state legislature, about 24 percent of Americans will live in states (18) where Republicans control all levers of power. That’s down from around 40 percent preelection.

That’s huge too. Texas is the second-largest state by population, with 32 million people. Ohio is seventh (12 million). Georgia eighth at 11 million. Democrats winning the governorships in those states will have massive effects. Atlanta, Austin, Columbus, and other major cities will now have a governor who wants to work with them, not attack them. Texas’s Greg Abbott was perhaps the most MAGA politician in the country, infamously busing unauthorized immigrants to Northern cities without their consent. His defeat by Democrat Gina Hinojosa is perhaps the most important single election result this week.

Overall, to reiterate, 54 percent of Americans will live in Democratic-dominated states over the next two years, compared to 24 percent in Republican ones. (Some states still have divided governments.) That’s a big Democratic advantage, far bigger than they will have in Washington.

These state results really matter. Few major bills pass in Washington, even when one party has total control, because of the Senate filibuster. Now, with Democrats controlling the House and the Senate, Trump’s agenda is (thankfully) mostly dead. And issues such as education are largely decided by states anyway. What happens in blue trifecta states? Workers get higher minimum wages and paid leave. People struggling financially have easier access to unemployment benefits and Medicaid. Local public schools and transportation systems are better funded. Policies aren’t passed that make it harder to vote, get an abortion, or seek medical care that affirms your gender identity. The candidate who wins the most voters is quickly declared the winner of elections.

What happens in red trifecta states? Districts are gerrymandered to ensure that African Americans and other left-leaning groups have as little representation in state capitals and Washington as possible. Cities are stripped of powers to run their local police departments and schools and regulate businesses in their communities. Public schools are defunded while upper-income families get state-funded vouchers to pay for private schools that often discriminate against LGBTQ students. University professors are barred from speaking honestly about racial and LGBTQ issues. Elections that Democrats win are questioned.

Even if you don’t live in Red America, you should care about what happens there. Your fellow Americans are denied civil rights and economic opportunities—and no, everyone can’t and shouldn’t have to move to a blue state. Republicans use their redistricting powers to make it as hard as possible for Democrats to win control of the U.S. House—even though that failed miserably in the 2026 cycle.

States run by Democrats are far from perfect. They often have massive income inequality, public schools segregated by race and class, and super-high housing prices. And many state legislators and governors are unwilling to push policies that help lower-income people because they are carrying out the interests of corporations and the superwealthy.

But blue trifecta states are at least largely trying to create some version of multiracial equalitarian democracy. Having more of them is good. And seeing Republican trifecta America shrink, particularly the GOP losing control of Texas, makes 2026 a truly monumental election cycle.

items.title: Trump Throws Vance Under Bus as MAGA Crackup Over Losses Turns Vicious
items.content_text: Donald Trump fired quite a warning shot at JD Vance as the epic scale of GOP losses sank in. Asked about Vance and the political way forward, Trump employed his best mob-speak and declared that in 2028, maybe “a lot of people” will run for president, adding of Vance: “Maybe he won’t run.” Translation: If you distance yourself from me, your presidential ambitions are dead and others should feel free to run instead. This comes as Vance just posted a long statement blaming GOP losses squarely on the war. That’s a clear bid by Vance to repair relations with MAGA voters alienated by Trump by (subtly) getting distance from him. Meanwhile, Republicans are angrily pointing fingers squarely at Trump, with one declaring that he’s “optimistic for the future because Trump’s going to be gone in two years.” The infighting is growing truly vicious. We talked to international relations professor Nicholas Grossman, author of a good piece discussing the centrality of Trump’s war to GOP losses. We discuss Trump’s shivving of Vance, how Vance is trying to salvage his 2028 ambitions by hitching himself to the Tucker Carlson wing of MAGA, and why the GOP crack-up will get much worse. Listen to this episode here. A transcript is here.

items.title: The Secret Weapon That Went Pffft: The GOP’s Anti-Trans Attack Ads
items.content_text:
Republicans entered the 2026 midterms in a bad position. Donald Trump has completely taken over the party, effectively crushing anyone who doesn’t go along with his mad decrees. At the same time, inflation is up, ICE is brutalizing people across the country, gas and groceries are expensive, and the United States is trapped in a war with Iran that no one can figure out how to win. The President’s poll numbers were already abysmal and getting worse every month.

The Republicans desperately needed a topic to focus on in the election. They settled on demonizing transgender people, with more than a little help from Elon Musk.

Polling has shown that opposition to transgender women participating in sports and transition-related surgeries for minors are among the very few issues where Republicans enjoy a public opinion advantage over Democrats. Since 2020, the American Principles Project, a right-wing culture-war pressure group, has pushed the GOP to make transgender people its top target. A staggering 224 million advertising dollars were spent on anti-transgender ads by Trump in 2024, such as the “Kamala is for they/them” advertisement, which ran over 55,000 times.

The New York Times estimates that Musk has spent $474 million supporting Republicans in the midterms, even more than he spent in 2024. Just like in 2024, hundreds of millions went into advertisements attacking transgender people, or accusing Democratic candidates of being too supportive of transgender people in general. You would be hard-pressed to listen to a speech where Republicans didn’t mention “men in women’s sports” or, as Trump ungrammatically put it, “transgender mutilization.” Nearly every one of Trump’s stump speeches includes the ridiculous accusation that young children come home from school with a sex change.

The problem with this Republican strategy is that, while the American public wasn’t supportive of transgender people, most didn’t really care about the issue because it didn’t affect them or anyone they knew. Republicans found out that you can only wave a boogeyman around for so long before people stopped believing him/her/them.

Every poll I could find that asked voters what their top priorities were had transgender issues at the bottom. This makes sense, given that there are effectively zero transgender athletes competing at the NCAA or professional level in the United States (and the few who are competing are transgender men who were born female). No one performs “bottom surgery” on transgender youth. The only procedure being performed is breast reduction, and that is exceptionally rare: only perhaps 250 to 300 per year. A Harvard study found that 97 percent of all breast-reduction surgeries on teens were performed on cisgender (non-transgender) individuals.

What made this bet even worse is the YouGov polling that found that the public trusts Democrats (52 percent) on transgender issues more than Republicans (23 percent). In other words, the people who rated transgender issues as a top priority were more likely to be pro-transgender Democrats than anti-trans Republicans. The GOP bet that they could win an election based on fear and loathing directed at less than 1 percent of the population, on an irrelevant issue that Democrats care more about than the Republican base does.

The results were entirely predictable.

Tuesday night delivered an epic loss for the GOP. It was a curb-stomping for the ages; the sum of all Republican fears. Texas went blue. The House is projected to wind up with 255 seats held by Democrats. If Mary Peltola wins in Alaska and Scott Colom in Mississippi, Democrats will end up with an astounding 55 or 56 seats in the Senate. They came within a whisker of winning Florida and Louisiana, as well. By my own estimates, the polls underestimated Democrats by an average of about three points. This could be the worst loss we have seen in national politics since Ronald Reagan obliterated Walter Mondale.

It is impossible for anyone to say that Republicans made the right choice in focusing their campaign on transgender people. I suppose some (like Musk) would argue that loss would have been worse if not for the anti-transgender ads, but Republicans lost in basically every state where the ads were in heavy rotation, and hung on by the skin of their teeth in states no one thought would be competitive.

It’s also impossible to say that the few Democrats who threw transgender people under the bus profited from it. Some, like Amy Acton in Ohio and Annie Andrews in South Carolina, won in red states; on the other hand, they had comparatively weak opponents like Vivek Ramaswamy and Darline Graham. Ohio Democratic Representative Marcy Kaptur, who had some nasty things to say about transgender people in her political ads, brutally underperformed, being on track to win her district by only 6.8 points in a D+11 year.

It’s also difficult to say that supporting transgender people hurt Democratic candidates. Abdul El-Sayed doubled down on his support for transgender people on 60 Minutes on Sunday. He handily beat Mike Rogers by 7 percent in a campaign marred by rampant Islamophobia. Similarly, in Montana, Sam Forstag stood up for trans people during a mid-October debate with his right-wing opponent; he was projected to win his conservative district by two points at the time of writing. Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota was a staunch supporter of the transgender community, and she beat polling expectations by even more than the national average.

Polling suggests that when pressed on the issue, it’s Democrats, not Republicans, who were more likely to say transgender issues are a priority. Additionally, polling indicates that the public thought Republicans were talking way too much about this issue. Regardless of whether Democratic candidates threw their transgender constituents under the bus, however, Republicans still attempted to smear them with accusations of supporting trans people.

The only thing it did was anger a core Democratic constituency. Some Democratic candidates who did flip seemed surprised at how much anger and dissent their transphobic platform created. Dealing with the fallout was a distraction and headache for them and their staff in the waning days of their campaigns. Thus, one could also make the argument that had these candidates not done a heel turn, they would have done even better given the lack of evidence that this was the issue that drew in centrist voters.

I suspect that Democrats will be delighted if Republicans choose to make transgender people the centerpiece of their pitch to the American people in 2028 again. Republicans might do it anyway, if Musk and his hundreds of millions of dollars in support for the GOP are predicated on it.

In 2024, Republicans ran on transgender issues and mistakenly assumed they won because of it. They didn’t seem to realize that they rode into the White House on the back of public discontent over inflation under Joe Biden (which he handled better than any other G7 nation).

Since then, Trump has driven up prices everywhere with his tariffs and wars, while delivering tone-deaf “let them eat cake” speeches. The GOP hitched its wagon to Trump again, made that same bet on campaigning against transgender people in 2026, spending more money than it did on the 2024 election; and then found out the hard way that it was always the economy, stupid. As the kids say these days, Republicans FAFO-ed.

items.title: JD Vance Is the Trump Administration’s Biggest Weasel
items.content_text:
Where did things go wrong? That question is often top of mind after a humiliating failure, so it’s hardly a surprise that Vice President JD Vance is asking it after the Republican Party lost both chambers of Congress in the largest midterm defeat since Watergate. What’s surprising is how he’s answering the question.

In a lengthy post Wednesday on X, Vance spun the GOP’s massive defeat by blaming the administration he serves in—and the president he serves under, in particular—for launching a deeply unpopular war on Iran. The veep’s goal is barely concealed: He wants to succeed Donald Trump in two short years, and he doesn’t want the stink of Iran or the 2026 midterms on him. So he publicly threw his boss under the bus in an essay on Elon Musk’s hellsite. It has to be one of the boldest and most shameless things a vice president has ever done.

Vance, ever the clumsy retail politician, starts with an anecdote. He takes us behind the scenes to the days leading up to the midterms. The polls were looking bad then, though they ended up considerably underestimating Democratic margins, and the vice president wanted to know what was up. Was there any reason to hope?

Vance turned to the “smartest data guy I know” to ask if his party had any shot in hell. “No,” that man—who may or may not actually exist—allegedly responded. “We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us.”

This was “prophetic”—and not in a good way. “The main problem is not turnout,” Vance wrote. “The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.” Hence the blue wave. Hence the X post.

But here’s where it gets really interesting. Vance then goes to a pollster—maybe the second-smartest data guy he knows, maybe not. This person gives him a list of the priorities of the defectors: “The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were: (1) End the war (2) Focus on cost of living/inflation (3) Put America First (4) Change our relationship to Israel.”

That is essentially a repudiation of the president and his administration, which (1) Started the war and can’t figure out how to end it (2) Has not brought down the cost of living, and indeed has made it worse (3) Is putting Corporate America first (4) Has steadfastly defended Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

Vance then drops the hammer: “The reason we lost is the war.” The vice president attempts to temper this this by saying that Trump himself acknowledged as much last night. But that’s not really true. In an interview with the Wall Street Journal early Wednesday, Trump said Iran was a “piece” of why they lost. Vance is saying something altogether different: that the war Trump started, in part due to his close relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is why Republicans were just handed the worst midterm defeat in half a century. And not only that, Vance is all but saying that he opposes the war.

This borders on insubordination. Vance has been playing a weaselly game since the start of the war, offering tepid public support while his team anonymously leaks to the press about his supposed opposition. Whether he’s genuinely opposed to the war, or simply plotting his political future, is not clear. But he clearly understands that the war has turned a blue wave into a total wipeout and that he need to wash his hands of it if he wants to stand a chance in 2028.

But Vance’s decision to blame the GOP’s midterm collapse solely on the Iran war is especially interesting. “Everyone knows why we lost,” he wrote, referring to voters’ anger over the war. “And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” It’s undoubtedly true that the war and the resulting spike in prices—particularly oil and gas—played a major role in Tuesday’s results. But one could point to a host of other possible factors: the administration’s violent immigration crackdown, its self-destructive tariffs, or its alienation of longtime allies and coddling of dictators.

Vance doesn’t do that, however, and it’s not hard to see why: He’s walking a tightrope. He has to acknowledge the defeat, but he cannot see it as a rebuke of MAGA–America First. As wily an operator as he is, it’s too late for him to disown the movement: As Trump’s vice president, he is one of its main inheritors. So he is trying to rescue MAGA from the president.

The choice to single out Iran is notable because it’s an obvious area in which the president deviated from his campaign platform, which at least paid lip service to not starting endless foreign wars. It allows Vance to suggest—albeit subtly—that Trump betrayed his own movement. In his telling, the people want immigration crackdowns and (in the abstract) tariffs; they just don’t want wars and high prices. Another subtext of Vance’s post is that Trump is simply too erratic and incompetent to be trusted—and that Vance can be. (One delicious wrinkle is that the post was approvingly quote-tweeted by Donald Trump Jr., who, in a particularly Succession-y move, commented with several “100” emojis.)

It’s hard not to read Vance’s post in the context of a rather odd column Wednesday in The New York Times by Christopher Caldwell, one of the global populist right’s few interesting thinkers. Caldwell blames Trump for squandering the mandate he was handed in 2024, suggesting that the Republicans lost because Trump “chose swagger over rational argument. Instead of allowing his policies to have their effect, he squandered his energy humiliating his opponents.” He suggests, for instance, that Trump should have calmly, coolly laid out the case for sending goons to Minneapolis. It’s an unconvincing argument. Swagger and humiliation are central to Trump’s political appeal; rational argument is for RINOs and libs.

And JD Vance. Caldwell’s column makes more sense if you read it as being addressed to the vice president. Indeed, in some ways it lays out a conceivable version of what the last two years would have looked like if Vance had been in charge of this fascist administration. (Spoiler alert: It’s not pretty.) Vance is now making the case that he can give the people real Trumpism: the immigration and economic policies they want without all the chaos, incompetence, and buffoonery. That, ultimately, is what is so extraordinary about his X post: It’s a bid to take over the political movement Trump launched 11 years ago and fundamentally change its direction. It’s audacious, but also consistent with everything we know about JD Vance. He only has one loyalty, and that’s to his own ruthless ambition.

items.title: Providence Becomes Largest American City to Vote to Divest From Israel
items.content_text:
Providence, Rhode Island, became the largest city in America to divest from Israel on Tuesday night. And it did so with the help of Jewish voters.

Providence voters passed Question 7, a ballot measure that forces the city to end investments in “foreign countries conducting ethnic cleansing, apartheid, illegal military occupation, or genocide”—like Israel. 

The initiative, first submitted by the Providence for Palestine Coalition, received 75 percent of the vote, with 81 of 82 polling places partially counted. The measure does not name Israel specifically.  

David Morales, Providence’s recently elected democratic socialist mayor, campaigned in favor of the measure, and has promised to enforce it. His failed primary opponent Republican incumbent Mayor Brett Smiley campaigned against the issue alongside the Jewish Alliance of Greater Rhode Island. 

But not all Jewish Americans agreed, with many voters backing the measure. 

“Oh hey the ballot question to divest Providence’s pension funds from genocide and apartheid passed with 75% of the vote, and is winning in every single precinct, including across Providence’s very Jewish East Side,” organizer and New Republic contributing editor Aaron Regunberg wrote online. 

“The measure in Providence to divest pension funds from any foreign country committing human rights abuses is dominating in Jewish precincts,” Drop Site News editor Ryan Grim noted. “The narrative about Jewish voters told by the national media simply isn’t right.”

items.title: Republicans Forced to Reckon With How They Destroyed Their Own Party
items.content_text:
Republican lawmakers are being forced to own up to just how badly the midterm elections went for their parties—and it’s delicious.

Speaking at a press conference Wednesday, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis blamed Republican lawmakers for making bad votes, like opposing legislation that would ban stock trading, and for the botched release of the government’s files on disgraced sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Florida saw Republicans narrowly keep control of the government, but in Texas, DeSantis said, “not only did they lose a very highly publicized U.S. Senate race, they lost everything.”

“Let’s just be clear, that is going to hurt, not just for the next two years. That’s something that can reverberate for the next decade or more,” DeSantis said. “And if the Republican Party doesn’t have Texas as an anchor then we are not going to be viable nationally.”

Republicans may not be able to retake the Senate in 2028, DeSantis warned, and it was “probably not viable” to retake the House. This was the “worst-case scenario,” he added.

Texas Senator John Cornyn, who will be succeeded by Democrat James Talarico, declared that his party had forgotten what really mattered.

“Last night, Republicans lost the U.S. House, the U.S. Senate, and my home state of Texas, a conservative cornerstone for more than three decades, because our party forgot the basic rules of coalition politics: 1. Add, don’t subtract 2. Be likeable 3. Do what you promised 4. Character & integrity still matter,” he wrote on X.

Former Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney also weighed in on his party’s clear miscalculation.

“Bad policy, bad character make bad politics: erratic tariffs, impulsive Iran war, blanket pardons, apparent corruption, weaponized justice, ICE brutality, mountainous deficits, hiding Epstein, abandoning allies and coddling enemies. Hoping for a course correction, for the country and for my party,” Romney wrote on X Wednesday.

Earlier Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance opted out of a mea culpa, instead blaming Republican losses on President Donald Trump’s unpopular war against Iran. Strangely, even Donald Trump Jr. agreed.

items.title: Democrats Win Enough Seats Nationwide to End Electoral College
items.content_text:
With Democratic victories in state legislatures and governorships across the country Tuesday, the Electoral College could now be in jeopardy—even without a near-impossible constitutional amendment.

If passed by enough states, the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact would effectively nullify the Electoral College and, with it, the possibility of a candidate being elected president without winning the popular vote. Since the compact was introduced in 2006, 19 states have passed it, agreeing to assign their electoral votes to whichever candidate wins the national popular vote. That amounts to 222 of the 270 electoral votes that a candidate needs to win the presidential election.

On Tuesday, Democrats took control of state legislatures and governorships in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Arizona, Wisconsin, and Nevada, all states that haven’t agreed to the compact. If all five vote to join, then the total number of electoral votes apportioned based on the national popular vote jumps to 283.

That all depends on whether Democrats in these states think that the compact is a priority. Democrats in Michigan failed to pass the compact when they held a trifecta from 2023 to 2024, and Nevada’s Democratic governor vetoed the compact in 2019, saying that it would hurt the state’s role in presidential elections.

There are also potential constitutional issues. In Article 2, Section 1, Clauses 2 and 3, the Constitution says that states can appoint electors “in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct.” But in Article 1, Section 10, Clause 3, it also prohibits interstate compacts without the consent of Congress.

The Democratic takeover of Congress would seemingly make this moot, and in theory, if the compact comes to a vote in the House and Senate, it wouldn’t even need the president’s signature. But Democrats still don’t have a filibuster-proof majority of 60 votes in the Senate, and with their dwindling national popularity, Republicans would undoubtedly try to block nullifying the Electoral College. After all, four of the five presidents who have won the presidency while losing the popular vote were Republicans, including President Donald Trump in 2016.

items.title: Trump Rages Wildly Over Losses—and Accidentally Reveals How MAGA Dies
items.content_text:
In the most predictable outcome ever, Donald Trump blamed everyone but himself for the blue tsunami that flipped the Senate and House on Tuesday night. No one was spared: Fox News, the GOP candidates, his own consultants—all of them, he fumed, brought about this epic catastrophe for his party.

But Trump’s fury has proven illuminating. Because the logical extension of his own claims is that the MAGA movement will almost certainly not be sustainable going forward, at least not in anything like its current form.

“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” Trump seethed as the results came in. This statement is true in only one sense: The Trump coalition really didn’t show up to the polls, and by his own accidental admission—since he’s now a lame duck—it never will again.

The MAGA coalition basically disintegrated on Tuesday night. Democrats flipped at least five Senate seats in states Trump carried by double digits, which could rise to seven if Democrats win in Alaska and Mississippi. Trump’s 2024 gains among Latinos and young voters—which were central to claims that MAGA had become a multiracial, multigenerational working-class realignment—evaporated.

Indeed, exit polls show that Democrats won Latinos and young voters nationally by extraordinarily lopsided margins. Democrats almost reached parity with Republicans among non-college voters. Democrats increased their vote share among working-class whites by 14 points relative to 2024. They won white women, notably reversing Trump’s 2024 victory among them.

Meanwhile, Democrats forged deep into MAGA country. Many Senate seats they flipped—Iowa, North and South Carolina, and possibly Alaska, where they’re favored—are among the more rural states in the country. Importantly, throw in Texas, and many of the biggest wins were in the South. Democrats recaptured places like Mahoning County in Ohio, the archetypal Obama-Trump county and the epicenter of Trump’s capture of ancestral unionized working-class Democrats. En route to winning well over 250 House seats, Democrats flipped districts in Iowa, Wisconsin, and Appalachian North Carolina. The public rejection of Trump and his agenda was monumental and decisive.

Yet as the bad news rolled in, Trump raged at … Fox News. He insisted that Fox “bears responsibility for these losses” because it sometimes features the “Dumocrat opposition” on the air. He fumed at Fox for its history of publishing polls that displease him. He even called in to Fox to complain.

In all this, too, you can also see a deeper revelation of MAGA failure. Fox has functioned as a major disinformational support system for Trump and the MAGA movement. As Matt Gertz of Media Matters details, it has propagandized on behalf of his Iran war, sanitized his ethnic cleansing campaign, and hidden his corruption and self-dealing from public view, among many other things.

Central to this has been the maintenance of plausible deniability. Fox does feature Democrats and does have a sterling polling operation. That’s all fine, but it’s also allowed Fox to obscure its role as a propaganda operation for Trump and his movement. The Fox-Trump alliance has in a sense operated as a bigger experiment in running totalitarian-style state propaganda on behalf of a dictatorial presidency.

This whole project failed spectacularly on Tuesday night. Trump’s criticism of Fox is actually an attack on Fox for not doing enough to deceive its viewers. And that’s true as far as it goes: Fox could not deceive them to the degree that Trump and MAGA needed it to. It could not sell them on the idea that the war was worth fighting—or on the notion that Trump’s economy and presidency have constituted world-historical successes.

Every indication right now is that the constellation of policies loosely described as “Trumpism” helped unleash this disaster on the GOP. As Ron Brownstein writes, exit polls showed public opposition to his tariffs and his personal corruption alike to be broad and deep. All signs are that Trump’s mass deportation campaign helped drive away Latinos. Tariffs, white nationalism, and the freedom of Dear Leader to pillage the public to his heart’s content are all key pillars of MAGA. Adam Gurri adds the essential point that this massive electoral rebuke was nothing less than a repudiation of the authoritarian consolidation at the core of the whole MAGA project. No amount of propaganda and lies from Fox could make any of it palatable. Nor will they be able to, going forward.

In this context, it’s notable that Trump also privately raged at his own advisers over the losses. As The New York Times reports, Trump “vented his frustration at political aides and accused them of giving him bad information about polling in the lead-up to the elections.”

What Trump really means by all this is that his MAGA agenda cannot fail. It can only be failed. Only the messengers for it—Fox, GOP candidates, his own consultants—can possibly be to blame if it faces national rejection. His presidency has deeply alienated national majorities, but to Trump this simply cannot be so by definition.

The natural heir of MAGA is of course JD Vance. But as Jonathan V. Last writes, Vance’s only hope of getting the 2028 GOP nomination is to keep Trump happy. If so, he can apparently only go so far in admitting to the Trump presidency’s record of extraordinary failure in order to recalibrate. If he even edges in that direction, he very likely cannot be MAGA’s standard bearer.

Note that Trump already fired a warning shot at Vance along these lines:

Trump on JD Vance: "Maybe he won't run" https://t.co/tRgmtAE3Yu

— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) November 4, 2026

Yet as Tuesday’s thrashing suggests, the MAGA agenda cannot appeal to anything close to national majorities in its current form, either. Maybe someone out there can pick this lock. But if Trump’s sound and fury signifies anything, it’s that it’s very hard to see where this movement goes from here, or what must happen for it to endure.

items.title: Trump Says There’s No Way Democrats Are Going to Impeach Him
items.content_text:
President Trump couldn’t seem to care less about Republicans losing control of the House and Senate to Democrats on Tuesday night.

The president offered brief remarks on the GOP carnage following a baffling ceremony at the construction site of his controversial White House ballroom.

“Sir, you held 30 rallies across the country, gave your final speech in front of the Reflecting Pool,” a reporter asked, referencing the way Trump centered himself in so many of the failed House and Senate campaigns. “Do you have any regrets about the way you closed out the campaign?”

“No, look if I were on the ballot we would’ve won. You saw the people, they were packed. Thousands and thousands of people at every rally. And if I was on the ballot we would’ve won.… There was such love at those rallies, it was incredible. We weren’t able to transfer the love to candidates.”

Q: Do you have any regrets about the way you closed out the campaign?

Trump: No. If I were on the ballot, we would have won pic.twitter.com/sTRgHpBjTQ

— Acyn (@Acyn) November 4, 2026

When asked if he was concerned about the prospect of impeachment from a Democratic-controlled Congress, the president replied, “Not even a little bit.”

“I think it would destroy the Democrat Party if they did that. It’s impeachment for no reason. What, for having a successful country? Our country is more successful now than at any time in its history.”

“Watch the beam go up,” he suddenly declared, before pointing to a large piece of metal being hoisted into the air over the construction site.

Q: Are you concerned about impeachment?

Trump: Not even a little bit. I think it would destroy the Democratic party if they did that. Impeachment for what? Having a successful a country? pic.twitter.com/mIGZdMNwvv

— Acyn (@Acyn) November 4, 2026

The president also said he would’ve “done nothing different” regarding the Iran war—despite acknowledging it lost Republicans the election, as Vice President JD Vance noted. He also said that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s job was safe for the moment, even as other reports reveal Trump has been considering firing him and blaming him for the Iran war.

Q: When will the war end?

Trump: Whenever I want it to. pic.twitter.com/srCL3IV8rw

— Acyn (@Acyn) November 4, 2026

items.title: Trump Prepares to Dump Pete Hegseth Over Midterms Destruction
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump may soon give Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth the axe after Republicans lost massively in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

CBS News reports that the president has been asking advisers if Hegseth should keep his job due to the Iran war going so poorly, a fact that swayed many voters. NBC’s exit polls showed that 74 percent of voters saw the Iran war as a crucial or major factor in how they voted. Hegseth was already in the hot seat before the midterms, with many in Congress calling for his impeachment, including outgoing Republican Representative Thomas Massie.

Hegseth was reportedly hoping Tennessee Senator Marsha Blackburn would be elected the state’s governor so that she could appoint him to fill the seat. That way, he could have a graceful exit and avoid the mess of being impeached or fired. Blackburn did win her race, but Hegseth would still face competition from other hopefuls such as Republican Representative Tim Burchett, who campaigned for Blackburn.

If Hegseth goes, one of CBS’s sources said that Florida Governor Ron DeSantis could be a possible replacement, and could get a speedy confirmation by the lame-duck Republican Senate before the end of the year.

Trump hasn’t made his decision yet, however, and some of CBS’s sources in the White House think that he might direct blame at other military leaders, such as Admiral Brad Cooper, head of U.S. Central Command, or Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Dan Caine. White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement that Hegseth had Trump’s full confidence, praising military efforts in Venezuela and the Iran war while also touting Hegseth’s attacks on “DEI and woke ideology.”

Speaking to reporters Wednesday, Trump gave Hegseth a vote of confidence, saying outside of the White House, “I think he’s doing a very good job.”

When asked if he wanted Hegseth to fill Blackburn’s Senate seat, Trump said, “I actually think he’d be very popular if he did that, but I haven’t heard that at all.”

items.title: These Are the Faces of the Democrats’ Election-Night Ecstasy
items.content_text: The polls and pundits were wrong—just not in the way that Democrats feared. A party faithful that was moderately confident of winning back the House of Representatives, while praying that the Senate was also in play, instead witnessed a historic electoral tsunami on Tuesday that wiped out Republicans even in red states like Texas, Iowa, South Carolina, and Kansas. The Democrats’ shock, and joy, was something to behold.

items.title: Republicans Tried to Steal House Seats. It Backfired Big Time.
items.content_text:
Republicans tried to upend Democratic election odds by redrawing congressional districts across the country, but even that wasn’t enough to dam the blue wave.

Despite making new maps to boost Republican candidates in Florida, North Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Alabama, and Utah, voters in those states by and large still chose Democrats to represent them.

For more than a year, local legislators in the Lone Star State were explicitly pushed by Donald Trump and his allies to forgo tradition and create a new congressional map for the 2026 election. State Republicans complied, carving up five historically Democratic districts into supposedly MAGA-friendly inventions.

But the plan backfired spectacularly. Republicans lost four of the five supposedly GOP-friendly seats they had created, as well as another two of their own.

Alabama voters also rejected the state GOP’s gerrymandering efforts, opting to send Democratic Representative Shomari Figures back to Congress.

Earlier this year, Governor Ron DeSantis redrew 20 of Florida’s 28 U.S. House districts. At the time, four newly created districts were expected to turn red. But they didn’t, and Florida Democrats remain poised to retain their targeted seats. Representatives Jared Moskowitz, Kathy Castor, and Debbie Wasserman Schultz were able to fend off Republican challengers, while first-time candidate Pia Dandiya outcompeted Republican nominee Casey Askar. The results for Florida’s 9th congressional district have not yet been called, though Democratic Representative Darren Soto has a slight lead.

Democrat Ben McAdams turned the tide in Utah’s redrawn first congressional district, besting Republican nominee Riley Owen by a margin of 47 points.

Ohio voters not only stuck to their Democratic incumbents despite similar redistricting efforts, but the liberal party also gained two more House seats (with potentially a third on the way, according to the Ohio Capital Journal). Democrats won big in Ohio’s gubernatorial and Senate races too, electing Dr. Amy Acton and Sherrod Brown, respectively.

Democrats enjoyed a landslide victory in North Carolina, despite voting under a new map that should have easily handed an additional House seat to Republicans by massively reconfiguring congressional districts 1 and 3. At the time of publication, just four out of 14 races have been called by the Associated Press, though Democratic Representative Don Davis was leading by more than 4 percent with 99 percent of the district votes counted.

Voters outright rejected a new congressional map in Missouri, where Republican leadership had prematurely decided to rely on a redistricted map during its primary election in August, effectively stripping many Missourans of the opportunity to elect their congressional nominees. The courts ultimately ordered Missouri to use the state’s original 2020 congressional map for Tuesday’s election. After the votes were tabulated, Democrats had gained an additional House seat.

Meanwhile, in Louisiana, the top two performers in the state’s 6th House district are headed to a December runoff race. They include Democrat Chauna Banks and Republican Blake Miguez.

But it wasn’t a unanimous Democratic victory. Tennessee’s decision to carve up Memphis into three separate congressional districts effectively thwarted the city’s historically Democratic vote. At the time of publication, Republicans were projected to win in three of four House races in Tennessee, while Democratic nominee Victoria Broderick peeled ahead by just fractions of a percentage point in Tennessee’s 4th congressional district.

items.title: Trump Brags About Ballroom After Republican Annihilation in Election
items.content_text:
President Trump’s first public speech after a disastrous, resounding midterm election defeat was about the White House ballroom, as he offered the American people deranged ramblings about the only thing he actually seems to care about.

“I doubt there’s a ballroom in the country [with] a 50-foot ceiling,” Trump said outside the construction site of his ballroom on Wednesday, just barely more than 12 hours after Democrats took control of both the House and the Senate in a resounding rejection of his administration’s policies and ideology.

You’d think a president would offer words of encouragement to his party or righteous anger in such a desperate moment. Instead, Trump went full lame-duck mode. “There has never been anything built like this, and it’s for the country, and it’s free, we got it free of charge, thank you very much.… When it’s completed it’ll be the best anywhere in the world.”

Trump on ballroom: The kitchen is going t be top of the line. There has never been anything built like this and it is for the country. When I was in China, we went to the great hall of China, and it is incredible. This is actually larger. pic.twitter.com/S4nQ9MDTrt

— Acyn (@Acyn) November 4, 2026

The president appeared with Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.

“Why does Trump spend time on the White House? Well, first of all, it’s very little time. Second of all, I like it. It’s good. For me it’s relaxing.… I love construction,” Trump continued. “That’s what I do, I like beautiful things.”

Trump went on to speak about the ballroom’s kitchen, staircase, roof, and marble veining.

It’s incredible that Trump—who seemed particularly calm at the event—can simply act like nothing happened, after his own unpopular decisions in office resulted in a midterm sweep that could cripple the Republican Party for the next decade. His own vice president, JD Vance, admitted that their war on Iran, the cost of living, inflation, and the administration’s close relationship with Israel lost them the election. But rather than address any of that, the president would prefer to talk about buttresses.

items.title: JD Vance Throws Trump Under the Bus for Republicans’ Election Wipeout
items.content_text:
Vice President JD Vance is desperate to save himself from the blue wave—even if that means letting President Donald Trump drown.

Just hours after Democrats seized control of Congress and swept state elections across the country, Vance promptly threw the president under the bus.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X Wednesday, blaming the Iran war without mentioning Trump by name.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” he wrote. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

In the early days of Trump’s military onslaught, Vance had expressed some reluctance about the president’s war plans. But that quickly gave way to the spineless sycophantism we’ve come to expect from the vice president.

In his post on Wednesday, Vance claimed that Republicans’ main problem is that many people who supported Trump in the 2024 presidential election had flipped to support Democratic candidates.

Vance claimed that a pollster—”one of the smartest people I know in politics”—found that voters would return to supporting the GOP if they ended the war in the Middle East, focused on the cost of living and inflation, “put America First,” and changed the U.S. relationship with Israel.

Trump’s eight-month-long “six week war” in Iran has proven to be a major political liability. His military campaign has resulted in the deaths of 22 U.S. service members, and hundreds more injured. Trump’s war is responsible for the deaths of thousands of Iranian civilians, including 120 schoolchildren. The president also oversaw the destruction of multiple U.S bases in the Middle East, a series of deadly military morale issues, and the depletion of the U.S. weapons stockpile, leaving the country more vulnerable to foreign threats.

The war effort has already cost American taxpayers an estimated $47.1 billion. That’s enough to pay for one year of Medicare coverage for 5.84 million people, based on previous figures from the Center for American Progress. That doesn’t include the skyrocketing price of gas and consumer goods thanks to the war.

In the words of Dwight D. Eisenhower: “Every gun that is made, every warship launched, every rocket fired signifies, in the final sense, a theft from those who hunger and are not fed, those who are cold and are not clothed.” It seems that Vance is finally catching on to just how damaging this war has been.

items.title: Democrats Take Over Total Control in Four States With Trifecta Power
items.content_text:
Democratic candidates flipped control of multiple state legislatures on Tuesday, clinching electoral trifectas in Wisconsin, Minnesota, Michigan, and Pennsylvania.

It was a wildly successful night for Democratic candidates in Congress, but Americans also voted to install Democrats in their state governments across the country.

In Wisconsin, Democrats flipped both the state’s Assembly and Senate. In the state’s Senate, Democrats flipped to an 18–15 majority, an exact inverse of the chamber’s current makeup. In the state Assembly, Democrats secured a 53–46 majority. And Democratic candidate David Crowley was elected to the governor’s office, securing the party an electoral trifecta for the first time in 16 years.

In Minnesota, Democrats clinched majorities in both chambers of the state legislature. In the House, the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party has won 72 of 134 seats thus far, surpassing the 68-seat majority. In the state’s Senate, the DFL party held onto its 34-seat majority. When coupled with DFL nominee Senator Amy Klobuchar’s victory in Minnesota’s gubernatorial race, Democrats have achieved trifecta control of the state’s government.

In Michigan, Democrats flipped the state’s House of Representatives. In the 110-seat House, Democrats ousted at least five Republican incumbents to secure at least 50 seats. In the 38-member state Senate, Democrats ousted two GOP incumbents, growing their majority from 20 to 23 seats. Democratic candidate Jocelyn Benson was elected to the governor’s office, securing the Democrats’ electoral trifecta in the state.

In Pennsylvania, Democrats also achieved a trifecta by flipping the state’s Senate for the first time since 1993. Ahead of the election on Tuesday, Republicans held a 27–23 majority in the 50-seat state Senate. Democrats flipped three seats on election night. Democrats also increased their majority in the state’s House of Representatives from 103 to 111 seats.

In North Carolina, Democrats flipped control of the state’s House of Representatives for the first time since 2010. As of Wednesday morning, Democrats held 66 seats in the 120-seat House. They needed to flip 12 seats to retake a majority, and by the time all the votes are counted, it’s possible they will have flipped 20. Going into the election, Republicans were just one seat short of a supermajority in the chamber.

As if that wasn’t enough, a few other states appeared to still be on their way to turning their state legislatures blue.

In Texas, the House races remained too close to call on Wednesday morning, but the Democrats were closing in on control of the lowest chamber for the first time since 2003. As of Wednesday morning, Democrats needed to flip at least 14 seats but had already flipped six seats, and they were leading in at least a dozen more Republican-held districts. Meanwhile, Republicans maintained control of the state Senate.

In Arizona, Democrats were poised to take control of the state legislatures for the first time in 60 years and potentially achieve yet another electoral trifecta for the Democratic Party.

items.title: Transcript: Trump Presidency on Life Support as Blue Wave Drowns MAGA
items.content_text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the November 4 episode of the Daily Blast podcast. Listen to it here.


Greg Sargent: This is The Daily Blast from The New Republic, produced and presented by the DSR Network. I’m your host, Greg Sargent.

In a stunning rebuke to Donald Trump, Democrats have won control of the House by a large margin, and they’re on track to win a majority in the Senate. It’s an absolute wipeout. And critically, Democrats have regained enormous ground in areas of the country that they’ve long struggled with: the South, the parts of the Midwest that Trump conquered, the Great Plains, Texas. This will change our political geography and deal a truly crippling blow to the MAGA movement, and render Trump a significantly diminished figure.

We’re talking to New Republic editor Michael Tomasky about all of it. Mike, what a night.

Michael Tomasky: Incredible. I had never seen a night like it. And you know, at my age, probably will never see another night like it. Amazing.

Sargent: It really is. Let’s start with the Senate. As of this recording, Democrats easily won North Carolina and Georgia. Michigan appears to be holding. They’ve now flipped South Carolina. They’re on track to flip Maine, Ohio, and Texas, and probably Kansas as well. That would seem to put Democrats at a minimum of 53 seats, assuming it all holds, probably 54. What do you make of that, Michael?

Tomasky: I thought it would be around 53 or 54. So it’s just what I expected, I guess. But it’s even more, because there’s still Alaska. And if all of these dominoes have tumbled in one direction, the remaining dominoes are likely to tumble in the same direction. So it could be 55 or something like that.

And it’s not only that, Greg, it’s the margins. These aren’t close. Ohio was kind of close. It looks like Maine is sort of close. But Talarico’s winning by a lot, and a lot of these other races, they’re just not close. And it’s just as you said, it’s just a stunning, stunning rebuke of Trump and MAGA, just all across the board.

Sargent: A big story here seems to be the Democratic inroads in the South, right? Democrats held Georgia. They just elected the first female Black governor there. They’re on track to taking Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas. They just flipped the House seats in Kentucky’s sixth district and in North Carolina’s 11th district, which is in Appalachia.

Those are both House districts that Trump won by double digits. They held a bunch of House seats in Florida that have been gerrymandered. Michael, this was unthinkable a decade ago. I think Trump did this, right?

Tomasky: Yeah, absolutely. And we have him to thank. So we finally have something to thank him for.

Yeah, the margin again—the margin in Kentucky six, the Democrat won by nearly 10 points. And Kathy Castor in Florida, they redrew her district. She’s a Democrat from the Tampa area. They redrew her district to finish her off. She won very comfortably.

The Democrat in the new 22nd district won pretty comfortably. But it’s all Trump. And, you know, he has brought the MAGA movement and the Republican Party crashing onto the rocks. Absolutely crashing onto the rocks.

Sargent: I think North Carolina’s 11th actually tells that story pretty well, so it’s maybe worth dwelling on. North Carolina’s 11th district is in the western part of the state. It’s in Appalachia. It’s got Asheville, but there’s a lot of rural territory there. It’s basically Trump country. It really is Trump country.

And that’s the place where Donald Trump lied about the disaster response. And I think that really pissed off a lot of people out there. And Democrats were telling me for a long time to keep an eye on that district for this reason.

And Jamie Ager, who’s a farmer—his family has been farming in the region for generations. He’s absolutely North Carolina 11 through and through. He won this by double digits. I mean, that is an enormous flip. It’s just unthinkable. This is Appalachia, Michael.

Tomasky: I know. I know. It’s just incredible. And again, the margin, double digits.

And speaking of Appalachia, Pennsylvania—Scott Perry, one of the MAGA-est of the MAGAs, up to his eyeballs in January 6, he was from that part of Pennsylvania that’s known as Alabama, in between Pittsburgh and Philadelphia. He lost by double digits, if I’m not mistaken. Got swamped.

So it just—everywhere you look, I mean, I’ve been, as I’m sure you have, I’ve been following this through different means. I’ve been watching TV, I’ve been looking at my computer, I’ve been looking at my social media feed, I’ve been on email chains with friends. And results are coming in from all those things, just hitting me as we speak.

And everything that comes in is like, oh my God, he won. Oh my God, she won. Oh my God, he won by nine. Oh my God, you telling me she won by 11 points? Are you kidding? And it’s just been like that nonstop.

And I can’t think of one piece of negative news. I mean, the Florida results—but people didn’t really expect the Democrats to win Florida, Jolly or Nixon, and they came awfully close.

Sargent: They did come awfully close. And as we said earlier, there were some positive stories out of Florida, which is that the Republicans were unable to gerrymander out these Democrats.

I want to dwell a little on Kentucky six for another reason. Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear, this is a big deal for him. And it’s got major 2028 implications as well. Andy Beshear told us all that Kentucky six could be flipped.

I think there was a lot of skepticism, for good reason. Again, this is a place Trump won by double digits, but he kept insisting it would happen. And now it’s happened.

I’ve got to think that gives him a bit of a leg up. And these big inroads in the South, they’ve got me thinking about Southern governors running for president. That vibe is coming to mind kind of heavily now, right?

Tomasky: Yeah, yeah, it is. And you know, it’s going to change the character of the House Democratic caucus. If there are going to be 245 or maybe even 250 House Democrats from these places where there haven’t been Democrats, Greg, since—well, since 2010, 2008, or 2006, I guess, was the big election that swung so heavily in the Democrats’ direction.

And the Democrats really expanded their map in that year. And that was in the wake of, you know, the Iraq War and Hurricane Katrina, and President Bush, the second Bush, took a real pummeling.

And then after 2010, when Obama was president for two years and the economy hadn’t recovered and the Republicans regained all those seats, the Democratic map contracted.

And for a long time, it looked to me and to you and to, I’m sure, a lot of people listening to us, like it was never going to expand back into places like western North Carolina. But now it has. And it’s a great opportunity for the Democrats to try and make that permanent.

Sargent: Yes, there’s going to be a major opening for Democrats to reconnect with some of these rural voters, some of these small-town voters, churchgoing voters, in these places.

I want to pick up on your point about Obama and the Blue Dogs, because it did seem like the Blue Dog Democrat was extinct. But now NBC is projecting, at least at my last hearing, NBC’s projecting 244 House seats for Democrats, as you say, could go higher. But that means we’re going to see some Democrats in some really, really unusual places.

I don’t have a clear picture where that’s going to be right now, but I think maybe they’re going to win some districts in South Texas, which are historically a little tough for them. They’re going to be in Appalachia.

They’re going to probably win, I think, that one in Virginia, which is a pretty rural district as well. It’s not Appalachia, it’s eastern Virginia. You know the one I mean, I think, right?

Tomasky: Yeah, the first. Yeah.

Sargent: Yeah, right. They’re going to flip that, aren’t they?

Tomasky: It’s a close race right now, but they have a good chance of doing it, yeah.

Sargent: Yeah, and then they’ll get the Virginia Beach seat, which is more of a swingy area. But you’re going to see—I think you’re going to see them flip some seats in Iowa, right? They’re going to have a lot more Democrats in rural areas, right?

I don’t know if they’re going to flip Wisconsin’s third, which is Derrick Van Orden, major MAGA guy, but I’m sure it’s very competitive as of this moment. But point is, they’re going to get into places like Iowa, rural Iowa, they’re going to get into South Texas, they’re going to get into western North Carolina.

And there’s going to be like a new rural caucus of Democrats, although I think they’ll be a little different. It’s a different time now than it was even as recently as 2008.

Tomasky: Yeah. Yeah. And I hope that means there are going to be a lot more Democrats in the caucus that you might call moderate. But I don’t know that they’re so moderate on economic issues.

I think a lot of these people are pretty populist on economic issues, and are ready to take on Trump and his friends, and the Elon Musks and Peter Thiels and people like that, and transfer wealth back to working- and middle-class people in a pretty serious way. I hope the caucus is ready to do that en masse.
