And that’s a place where I think there’s potential for common ground between some of the progressives and some of the new folks, who might not call themselves progressive on some social issues or cultural issues, but I think probably are fairly progressive on economics.

And I think if the Democrats, if Hakeem Jeffries, can just keep them focused on that stuff, I think they can speak with one voice on a lot of these economic concerns, and flip some opinions about them in rural and exurban parts of the country.

Sargent: And I think another thing that makes that essential is that, if you think back to the Blue Dogs, those were some of the people who kind of forced a more moderate Obamacare to emerge.

Tomasky: Yeah.

Sargent: Right? In those days, the Blue Dogs were a little bit more in the Joe Manchin mold, who kind of acts like a populist but isn’t really an economic populist. He’s really kind of, you know, center-right on economics, interestingly.

And I agree that now all of a sudden you’re going to have a lot more unity on this one thing. Maybe not on other things, right? But you will have unity on economic issues.

And that will be, I think, potentially—there’s a long way to go, right? But if they can win the presidency in 2028, then you can really start to see some really big economic proposals emerging, I think.

Tomasky: I think that’s right. And yes, the context is really different. You know, in 2010, 2012, those kind of Blue Dogs were very cautious economically, and they took corporate money, and they didn’t want to be aligned with the progressives at all. I hope and sense that that has changed some now.

The anger over the data centers, the anger over crypto and AI, and the fear of what AI might do to this country and to working people, and just the power that people like Elon Musk and Peter Thiel and the others have over our political system and our society at large—I hope and believe that that’s got most Democrats united in opposition to and anger about all of that stuff. And I think they’ll act on it. I hope.

You know, it’s going to take the leadership of Jeffries and Schumer to make sure that they do. But there’s a great opportunity for them, if they do that, heading into 2028, to show the country what their priorities are and what they want to do.

Sargent: Absolutely. So let’s talk about the Midwest. Just two years ago, Trump won all of it, winning the three blue wall states of Pennsylvania, Michigan, and Wisconsin. And of course, he had already turned Ohio and Iowa into red states. But now Democrats are on track to take the Ohio Senate seat. They’ve won the Ohio governorship as well. Amy Acton won it. The Senate seat in Iowa, as of this recording, looks very plausible as well.

I think a big question now is whether states like Ohio and possibly Iowa kind of revert a bit back to swing states after Trump, right? I think people forget that Barack Obama won Ohio and Iowa twice. He won them both twice. It seems plausible that Trump’s conversion of them into red states was a bit of a unique and fleeting event, possibly. What do you think of that?

Tomasky: I agree. Hopefully they’re, like, snapping out of some trance and waking up from some fever dream that they had. Trump, I suppose, to a certain kind of person, mostly white person, said things that seduced them, about the economy and about American society. And, you know, it just takes people a long time to snap out of that.

And it always just amazed me, to watch these interviews with people after the 2024 election, and they say they voted for him because, you know, he said he was going to lower prices, and they believed him.

I mean, I always just thought, how can you believe, first of all, this charlatan? But second of all, a president doesn’t have the—a president can’t say, hey, you can only charge $3.89 for a gallon of milk. A president just can’t do that. Yet these people bought this.

And it was all part of some big—like, I can’t say it any better than the word trance, that people got lulled into. But tonight they snapped out of it. And they emphatically snapped out of it, as you say, in Ohio, Iowa, Kansas, where Adam Hamilton was declared the winner, and other places.

By the way, Kansas has been in the Union since about 1860, and has had senators since 1861. In all that time, he’s only the fourth Democratic senator they’ve ever elected in the history of the state. So I think that that section of the country is just—whatever Trump did to them, whatever drug he put them on, it’s leaving their system now.

Sargent: I hope you’re right. It’s the “cultural heroin” that JD Vance referenced. And I think that that’s interesting, because JD Vance understood at one time, right? He really understood this trance that you’re talking about.

Tomasky: Yeah.

Sargent: He called it cultural heroin. He saw the people around him in his home state of Ohio, site of Hillbilly Elegy and all that. He saw those people slip into that trance and understood that it was a toxic force back then. And then of course he recognized that it was a route to fulfill some sort of ambition of his.

I think it’s more complicated than that, but basically JD Vance started to buy a certain vision of, I don’t know, the liberal cathedral or whatever they call it, whatever the new right calls it. You know, he started to think that the left is really some sort of major threat that required a tribune-like figure like Trump to break. And he hitched himself to that.

And I think after tonight, that’s going to have looked like a colossal mistake, a colossal miscalculation. I don’t see how Vance manages to kind of escape this wreckage now. What do you think of that?

Tomasky: Yeah, this wipeout really weakens him, because he has tied himself, he’s lashed himself, so aggressively to the MAGA mast. And how does he wriggle out of that? I don’t know that he can.

So it opens up the Republican field, I think, in 2028. I think you’re absolutely right about that. I would still, for now, call him the front-runner, but we’ll see how this shakes out over the next few weeks and into next year.

And one of the things that I’m really interested in watching, Greg, particularly when the new Congress convenes, is, I bet we’re going to see Republicans a lot more willing to criticize Trump.

Sargent: Yeah.

Tomasky: I mean, he’s down and it’s easy to kick a man when he’s down.

Sargent: Yes. And I think they really don’t have any reason to let themselves get pushed around by him anymore, do they?

Tomasky: Right. No, no, they don’t. So it’s going to be really interesting to see.

I think it now possibly portends a much more wide-open 2028 Republican field, right? Don’t you think?

Sargent: I do.

Tomasky: I mean, it was Vance versus Rubio, we thought, or so the conventional wisdom thought. But I think now you get governors, you get Sarah Huckabee Sanders in there, you get a couple senators, and I don’t know, there could be a dozen people.

Sargent: Right. And JD Vance has been prancing around as if MAGA is still culturally ascendant, as if it’s still a real dominant force in American life, I think. And they didn’t really realize what was happening right under their noses, the degree to which MAGA and Trump were deeply alienating the country, both with policy but also with affect, right? Also with the constant stream of hate, the constant rage, the constant derangement.

Everyone’s just had it, and all these Democratic candidates stepped into that breach and sort of created a new politics, I think, almost a decent values-based politics. Which, I mean, look at Talarico. He talks about religion all the time.

Amy Acton talks about her difficult childhood. Every one of them is talking to voters and saying, you don’t need to live this way anymore, you know? This is not what we should be. And it seems to have worked. I think that is a big part of what happened.

Tomasky: I agree. And I think the authenticity of so many of the Democratic candidates in this cycle is something that shouldn’t go unremarked, and is something that, you know, I may do a little reporting on, and may encourage you to do a little reporting on too.

I mean, you know, in so many places you looked, they had a candidate who was from the area, went to college in the area, joined the Navy, or owned a farm, or was a fifth-generation farmer, or, you know, a third-generation small business, you know. It was just a series of people like that, who weren’t your typical Democratic cookie-cutter maybe grew up there but went away to some fancy law school and became a lawyer and moved back to the district in a quasi-opportunistic fashion to run for Congress.

That’s an all too common Democratic story. But these were, like, homegrown people in many, many districts. And they were right for the moment. And I think that probably ties into what makes them a little bit more economically populist too, because, you know, the struggles and the pain of the people in the district are more real to them.

Sargent: I think we might be seeing the birth of a new Democratic Party, Mike.

Tomasky: Wow. That would be good. That’d be a good thing. We need it.

Sargent: We do indeed. Mike Tomasky, let’s all try to get some sleep, man.

Tomasky: Yeah, I’m pretty jazzed. I’m going to be up for a little while. No—Josh Turek, projected winner. Just now.

Sargent: There you go. Iowa two. The whole Midwest.

Tomasky: Yeah. Amazing.

Sargent: It is. Mike Tomasky, awesome to talk to you.

Tomasky: Likewise, my friend. Thanks.

items.title: Every Democratic Socialist Who Won a National Race This Election
items.content_text:
The Democratic Socialists of America are here to stay. One of the most contentious—and misunderstood—political groups in the country rode a wave of popular support to groundbreaking victories this election.

First reanimated by the 2016 Bernie Sanders campaign and reaffirmed since then by a lack of imagination and initiative from the Democratic Party’s center, the DSA left wing is now firmly entrenched within the Democratic machine. Eleven DSA House and mayoral candidates won Tuesday after running on platforms emphasizing affordability, ending U.S. aid to Israel, and expanding access to health care. As a whole, with down ballot races included, DSA-endorsed candidates won 149 of the 294 races they ran in, with 37 races still undecided. Eight of them will be in the U.S. Congress next year. Here are the biggest victors:

Nithya Raman — Mayor of Los Angeles

Janeese Lewis George — Mayor of Washington, D.C.

David Morales — Mayor of Providence, Rhode Island

Angela Gonzales-Torres — House of Representatives, California

Melat Kiros — House of Representatives, Colorado

Donavan McKinney — House of Representatives, Michigan

Darializa Avila Chevalier — House of Representatives, New York

Claire Valdez — House of Representatives, New York


Chris Rabb — House of Representatives, Pennsylvania

Rashida Tlaib — House of Representatives, Michigan

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — House of Representatives, New York

This story has been updated.

items.title: Democrats Won Control of Congress. Here’s What They Can Do Now.
items.content_text:
A blue wave has washed over the nation, as Democrats retake both the House and the Senate and voters across the country offer a resounding rebuke of President Donald Trump and his far-right administration. Democrats have flipped both the House and Senate, and New York Representative Hakeem Jeffries will become the first Black House speaker. Meanwhile, Democratic Senate candidates flipped seven seats previously carried by Trump and the GOP. But now that the Democrats will control Congress in January, what can they do? And will they actually do it?

Impeachment

Let’s start here first, since it’s at the top of everyone’s mind.

Democrats now have the numbers to impeach Trump or any of his Cabinet members. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has headed the disastrous, destructive, and expensive war on Iran, is reportedly the Democratic majority’s top target.

The impeachment process can begin in the House of Representatives with a simple majority, which Democrats now have. The trial then moves to the Senate. To actually convict and remove, they will need a two-thirds majority in the Senate, which means the Democrats will need some Republican votes.

While impeachment of Trump is certainly a possibility, there is a greater likelihood that Democrats will be able to convict and remove someone like Hegseth, who has been losing Republican allies over the course of the Iran war.

Investigations

The Democrats could also open a wide array of investigations into the Trump administration, much like they did last time they controlled the House in 2018.

This is certainly the most corrupt administration in modern history. Some top investigation targets could include:

The Epstein Files

This issue won’t be going anywhere, especially with a Democratic-controlled Congress. The party has called for a renewed push to reopen investigations into the world of infamous sex predator Jeffrey Epstein—and the Trump administration’s botched rollout of the files. Just last week, House Judiciary Democrats released a report on the cover-up, noting that “DOJ and FBI shut down investigations and withheld evidence while claiming no basis to prosecute or even investigate any additional Epstein co-conspirators.”

The UAE chips affair

In May, a firm of Emirati royal Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan gave $2 billion to World Liberty Financial Group, a crypto company controlled by the families of Trump and his Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff. Two weeks later, the Trump administration completed a deal to give the United Arab Emirates hundreds of thousands of the world’s most valuable AI chips—in an extremely questionable display of ethics.

Jared Kushner

Last month, a new book reported that the president’s son-in-law had his phone hacked during the first Trump administration, which revealed Kushner’s control of foreign slush funds filled by the leaders of the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Israel. The report exposed how Kushner appeared to make deals with those governments to violently transform Palestine, Iran, Lebanon, and the greater Middle East region.

Trump selling early access to Truth Social

Trump and his aide Natalie Harp were sued in September over the “Truth API” program, which offers Truth Social users early access to posts from government officials in exchange for $100,000 a month. Watchdog groups alleged that Trump is using the media company that he uses as a personal bulletin board to run a pay-to-play scheme, offering crucial information that affects global markets and policy decisions to whoever can afford it.

Heavily Impede the Trump Agenda While Pushing Their Own

At a bare minimum, any Republican bill or policy is all but guaranteed to die in Congress, as Republicans will need Democratic votes every time to pass anything. The Democrats’ majority allows them to go on the offensive, and it has been reported that they have a “First 100 Hours” agenda focused on ending Trump’s antagonistic and expensive foreign tariffs, reviving expired Affordable Care Act health care premium subsidies, and reversing almost $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts. They could also make efforts to impede the Iran war.

Unfortunately, to make their bill veto-proof, Democrats will need a two-thirds vote in both the House and Senate, meaning they will need Republicans to join them. Whether Trump will veto will depend on his own temperament, as he may be likely to reject legislation from a Democratic Congress in his lame-duck era, regardless of how popular or bipartisan it is.

items.title: Hakeem Jeffries Says Impeachment and Getting Even Aren’t Priorities
items.content_text:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries isn’t interested in seeking impeachment charges against President Donald Trump.

Speaking on MS NOW’s Morning Joe Wednesday, Jeffries laid out his priorities for his party’s newfound leadership in the House of Representatives.

“The American people don’t want us to get even. They want us to get things done on their behalf because life is way too expensive,” Jeffries said.

Hakeem Jeffries on Morning Joe: The American people don't want us to get even. They want us to get things done on their behalf because life is way too expensive.

We ran on affordability, we won on affordability, and now it's our job to govern on affordability. pic.twitter.com/b5ieQUbMRO

— Clipping Wings (@ClippingWings) November 4, 2026

Ahead of the election results, Jeffries similarly made clear that impeaching Trump was simply not a priority.

“I’ve made clear from the very beginning that our top priority is going to be to drive down the high cost of living,” the House minority leader said on Fox News Sunday.

While it’s clear that Democrats have more than their fair share of damage to undo, it’s not clear why they’d need to draw the line at impeaching the most corrupt president in American history. While we’re at it, why not pick off his Cabinet of cronies one by one?

If anything, voters have delivered a clear mandate against Trump’s entire reign of corruption. After two years of Republican control in Congress, and Trump’s disastrous leadership, voters don’t just want to get even—they want everything.

items.title: This Is the Battle That Will Define the Democrats These Next Two Years
items.content_text:
The midterm elections are over. Yes, some returns are still being counted, but the outcome was clear before midnight on Tuesday. Democrats across the country crushed their Republican opponents, in many cases by running on “top versus bottom” economic populism. Victorious candidates—including James Talarico in Texas, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, Troy Jackson in Maine, and Sherrod Brown in Ohio—pledged to take on the corporate corruption that has rigged the game against regular Americans. This message worked, even in Republican-leaning districts where Democrats were badly outspent, like Michigan’s 7th, which Sunrise co-founder Will Lawrence managed to flip despite over $23 million in Republican outside spending, the most faced by any House candidate this cycle.

With these electoral triumphs, Democrats have seized the initiative. Now they have to decide what to do with it—and already we are seeing very different answers to this question.

On one side is Team Small Potatoes. Senator Brian Schatz of Hawaii went on CNN recently to articulate this uninspiring view. “I do not think it is time to propose things that the president of the United States is guaranteed to veto,” said Schatz, who is in line to be the Senate’s next Democratic whip and is a favorite to eventually succeed Senator Chuck Schumer as leader. “I think that’s a bit of wasted energy. If we want to be more aspirational, if we want to make more bold policy changes … that’s for 2028. Right now it’s about stabilizing the country itself.” Soon-to-be Speaker Hakeem Jeffries signaled a similar perspective in August when he preemptively announced his opposition to Medicare for All.

On the other side of the debate is Team Go Big, who are refusing to cede ground to the Small Potatoes crowd. Congressman Greg Casar, who is chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, went so far as to directly respond to Schatz’s statement, saying he “100% disagree[s].” Casar warned that Democrats “cannot be the party of nervous lawyers who just tinker around the edges” or they will “sleepwalk into President Vance 2028.” On election night, Senator Bernie Sanders similarly declared that holding Trump accountable is not enough: “At a time of massive income and wealth inequality, we must do more. We must aggressively fight for working families.”

These arguments raise an obvious question for Small Potatoes advocates like Schatz: Why, exactly, is it “wasted energy” to propose and pass legislation that President Trump might veto? Democrats have a wide array of extremely popular economic policies at their disposal: anti–price gouging laws to bring down the cost of food and housing, an excess profits tax on Big Oil to crack down on fossil fuel profiteering, paid sick leave and family leave and vacation leave, a congressional stock-trading ban, a data center moratorium and AGI kill switch—the list goes on. What is the downside to daring Trump to veto bills like these that are supported by 70 to 80 percent of Americans?

As Congressman Ro Khanna posted in response to Schatz’s statement: “Make him veto Medicare for All. Make him veto a $25 living wage. Make him veto free childcare. Make him veto Block the Bombs to Israel.” If Trump does veto these popular policies, great—that demonstrates which side is fighting to bring down prices and end corruption, and which side is standing in the way. And it provides the clearest possible pitch for why voters need to put a Democrat in the White House in 2028.

While Team Go Big’s approach is all upside, Team Small Potatoes’ strategy has very real costs. Though Tuesday’s election results represent a major backlash to Trump’s garbage fire of a second term, the Democratic Party is still severely unpopular, and many working-class voters do not trust it to fight for them. If Democrats’ response to winning big majorities in both the House and Senate is to timidly spend the next two years focused just on “stabilizing the country,” as Schatz suggested, they will once again be aligning themselves with the status quo.

Americans are furious with the status quo. Democrats already tried a “nothing will fundamentally change” strategy—not once but twice, in 2016 and 2024. Both of these bad bets threw the door open to the fascists. To repeat this catastrophic mistake again—after an election in which voters sent such a clear message that they want change—would be madness.

Of course, there’s another reason establishment Democrats might not Go Big in tackling corporate profiteering and corruption: Many don’t want to. They oppose passing these policies not because Trump will veto them but because they’re scared of having to vote on bills their corporate donors hate. The problem is that they, like Trump, are on the wrong side of supermajority issues—which doesn’t matter if a bill is never brought to a vote but becomes quite uncomfortable when you actually have to pick a side.

We need to be crystal clear about this dynamic. There is no political rationale for failing to advance incredibly popular policies. The Democrats who oppose these populist measures are not trying to improve their party’s political position—they’re trying to protect their own pro-corporate interests, at the expense of the Democratic Party’s future prospects.

Voters don’t want small potatoes. They have made abundantly clear that they aren’t looking for leaders who will just manage a broken system. They want leaders who will change it for the better—who will go big. That’s the lesson of this week’s blue tsunami, and if Democrats don’t heed it, they will blow a historic opportunity that this party may not get again for decades to come.

items.title: Mike Johnson Quits Republican Leadership After Midterms Humiliation
items.content_text:
House Speaker Mike Johnson is stepping down from Republican leadership.

The Louisiana Republican announced on Wednesday morning on an all-staff call that he will not run for House minority leader for the new Congress next year, following Tuesday’s historical Democratic landslide takeover of the House of Representatives.

It’s not clear yet if Johnson has anointed a successor to lead the Republican caucus. Representative Jim Jordan, chair of the House Judiciary Committee, has already thrown his hat into the ring and announced he’s running for House minority leader. According to Punchbowl News, Jordan’s pitch will be that new blood is needed and that he specializes in investigations.

The current number two Republican in the House, Representative Steve Scalise, also announced that he is running for caucus leader.

“Scalise will be announcing his run for Republican leader for the next Congress today,” a source told The Washington Sun. “His number one goal will be to lead the conference back into the majority. He is a proven and tested leader who is ready on day one. He’s spent his career unifying Republicans and he is prepared for the big legislative and oversight battles ahead. The conference knows him, how he fights, and that he’s a trusted leader.”

Johnson’s tenure has been marked by his unwillingness to stand up to President Donald Trump, repeatedly playing dumb about new developments from the White House. Under Johnson’s watch, Trump took away congressional authority from controlling funds and levying tariffs, and Johnson supported—either openly or by inaction—every piece of Trump’s agenda. That proved to doom Republicans on Tuesday, and Johnson’s successor will have to choose between protecting Trump by fighting against an overwhelming Democratic majority, or actually trying to help the American people.

This story has been updated.

items.title: “Trump Did This”: Republicans Reckon With Midterms Wreckage
items.content_text:
After the Democrats’ historic landslide victory on Tuesday, Republicans are looking for whom to blame, and uncharacteristically, they are openly pointing the finger at President Donald Trump.

“It sounds a little ironic,” Republican Bobby Charles, who lost Maine’s gubernatorial election, told Politico, “but I am nevertheless optimistic for the future because Trump’s going to be gone in two years.”

The chair of the Licking County Republican Party in Ohio, Matt Dole, told the publication that “there’s a little bit of a reckoning in the Republican Party about where they go.”

“I think you’re going to see a part of the Republican Party advocate for a return to normalcy, which is not repudiating Trump’s ideology and policies, but will repudiate Trump’s style,” Dole said. Licking County is a staunch Republican county in the Buckeye State.

Trump himself was defiant, calling Fox News around midnight to complain that the network’s polls showed that he wasn’t popular. In response, host Bret Baier pointed out that “tonight, actually, the results are pretty close to what the Fox polls showed.”

Trump disagreed, saying, “Well, I don’t know about that,” and he maintained that he had the “greatest two years in the history of the presidency,” despite the disastrous Iran war and faltering economy.

White House adviser Alex Bruesewitz said poor candidates were responsible for Republican losses, slamming them as “uninspiring, lazy, and thoroughly ineffective communicators.” He specifically mentioned Georgia Representative Mike Collins’s failed Senate campaign. But an unnamed Republican operative told Politico that candidate quality was a “lazy excuse.”

“This is more than just one lazy candidate here. I mean, the chair of the … NRCC is losing his election,” the operative said, referring to Representative Richard Hudson losing North Carolina’s 9th congressional district to Democrat Richard Ojeda, the first Democrat to represent the district since 1963.

“We are beyond candidate quality. It’s a bloodbath,” another senior Senate GOP official told Politico. “Trump did this.”

items.title: 10 States With Data Centers on the Ballot All Voted to Ban Them
items.content_text:
Election Day 2026 revealed just how much of the country loathes Silicon Valley’s data center projects.

Communities across the nation voted on 41 data center-related ballot initiatives on Tuesday. The measures were introduced in California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota, Ohio, and Wisconsin.

At least 33 of those municipalities voted to keep data centers out, according to votes tracked by Data Centers on the Ballot. At least six localities specifically voted to ban data center construction and halt the development of all planned facilities. Just one measure in Harwood, North Dakota, counted as a victory for the industry, as voters decided against restricting data center construction

The vast majority of the data center-related ballot initiatives were introduced and decided in Ohio, which has recently become a buzzing hub of activity for tech companies looking to build the water-zapping facilities. Over the last year, some of Silicon Valley’s most prominent AI firms have poured millions of dollars into races across the state and on both sides of the aisle in an apparent effort to influence the region’s politics.

Exactly why AI-backed money was funneled into the Ohio race boils down to a perfect confluence of factors across the state. Ohio has relatively cheap land, plentiful resources, and enough power plants to fuel the data centers required to support the AI industry’s seemingly imminent boom.

But the same can be said for many other regions in the country. In Kansas, where land is similarly cheap and plentiful, voters adopted some of the most restrictive proposals on the table. One such measure banned the construction of “high-impact data centers” (facilities that use more than 100,000 gallons of water per day) for 10 years, stipulating that the decision could only be reversed by public vote, according to an analysis by Multistate.us.

Mounting evidence that the public actually hates data centers doesn’t bode well for Donald Trump, who has spent months attempting to convince Americans to let the industry build as he cozies up to major tech executives.

Recent polling indicates that the vast majority of Americans, including Republicans, have no interest in permitting the tech industry to build AI facilities in their backyards. An August survey published by Heatmap revealed that 75 percent of the public opposes data center development in their communities.

More jurisdictions are expected to take a stance on the issue in the coming weeks. Voters in Arkansas and North Dakota will vote on whether to finance or prohibit data centers on December 1 and December 15, respectively.

items.title: What Democrats Just Accomplished in Ohio Is Remarkable
items.content_text:
If you’ve ever lived through a heat wave or drought, you know there’s a sound when the rain finally breaks. The atmospheric shifts as the first, fat drops fall, yes—but then as it all cuts loose, whoops from the streets. It is the sound of relief. This is the sound of America’s blue tsunami from a Southwest Ohio pizza parlor.

First, a trickle of positive results: With a fraction of the vote in, gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton was way ahead, as was Sherrod Brown in Ohio’s Senate race. People cheer, then wait. Later in the night, a deluge: A group of Democrats, ostensibly gathered to support three candidates at a different Montgomery, Ohio, tavern, cheered over the Georgia governor’s race, called for Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms. Then Annie Andrews took South Carolina’s Senate seat. Dems secured control of the House—a wave of screams.

Though MS NOW was still waiting, a voice across the tavern shouted that Bloomberg and NBC had called it: Amy Acton had won the governor’s seat. A statehouse rep in the room won reelection, so did a judge. Within a minute, another shouted message: Dems were on track to win multiple new seats in the Ohio House, breaking the supermajority. It started to be hard to hear why everyone was bursting into elated cheers. Talarico won in Texas! On the TVs in the tavern, Acton’s image filled the screen, final confirmation she had won. Thunder. Relief.

Vivek Ramaswamy spent $79 million (including $41.3 million of his own money) to lose a governor’s race in which the billionaire showed himself to be so out of touch, he thought it would help his campaign to dig Acton’s estranged mother out of the cobwebs for an unconscionable attack ad that drew resounding disgust from across parties (with the notable exception of Donald Trump and JD Vance). The grossest campaign in America lost last night. Ohio, which hasn’t swung left in a governor’s race since 2006, just did.

I suspect, though, that the result, while certainly part of a national referendum on Trump and Republicans who’ve kowtowed to him at every level, is also a reflection of Democratic candidates who activated an impressive grassroots campaign. Every time Ramaswamy skipped across the state (or out of state) in his private jet or invested millions in cartoonishly evil attack ads, Acton was on a family farm, or on a union picket line, or at a diner, leaning in to talk to voters regardless of party. And down-ticket candidates did the same. Ohio was won by making the race not about party but about Ohioans, writ large, winning.


Ohio used to be a key swing state, but highly effective gerrymandering has carved us into right-locked districts that have produced increasingly extreme candidates and a Republican supermajority in the statehouse. Ohio has had a Republican trifecta (governor’s office and both chambers of the statehouse) for 28 years since 1992, and in that time, Ohio’s schools have suffered (now forty-fifth in the nation for our state share of public school funding). Ohio’s economy ranks thirty-ninth, and we’re thirty-fourth for health care. Our infrastructure and water scores low too. The relative security of Republican seats surely contributed to our dark money–fueled FirstEnergy bribery scandal, which landed former Ohio speaker of the House Republican Larry Householder in prison for racketeering.

Sizable sums wash in and out of the state, but not often to benefit the common good. Tens of millions in PAC money was donated from outside billionaires, such as Elon Musk and Jeffrey Yass, to sway votes for Ramaswamy. (Over 95 percent of Acton’s donations totaled $100 or less.) A projected $11.6 billion was spent on Ohio’s midterm election this year, with more than half a billion on the U.S. Senate race alone.

Our gerrymandered maps and millions of dollars have been invested in chopping up Ohio to ensure Republican power. And in some parts of the state, the partisan divide still strains.

In rural Shelby County, Democratic Party Chair Christopher R. Gibbs has been busy trying to help Democratic candidates understand rural voters who regularly feel ignored, sidelined, and taken for granted. I met him on a family farm whistle-stop for the Acton campaign. Gibbs, who used to be the county’s Republican chair, left the party in 2019. It “no longer shared my core values.”

Anecdotally, Gibbs says in Shelby, one of the reddest counties in Ohio, there is a visceral hate for Democrats, based on locals’ perception of national Dems. But data centers, a significant rural issue, isn’t yet partisan. Over 200 data center projects are planned or under construction, and 21 initiatives were on the ballot yesterday (the most nationally). Both Acton and Ramaswamy campaigned on tighter rules around data centers after, in May, current Governor Mike DeWine ordered a pause on tax exemptions on the centers—which had already surpassed $2 billion in 2025. Across the state last night, a number of data center bans passed.

Electoral maps and MAGA aside, Ohioans may have been united by practical realities. I passed a gas sign that read “$4.17/gallon” for regular unleaded, yesterday driving between polls. Big Tech has planted data centers that slurp up our energy, land, and water. About one in eight Ohio families lives under the poverty line and, according to the United Way, another 23 percent live above the poverty line but can’t afford basic expenses.

We are, collectively, done. And the billionaires could not buy this election.


Acton often talks about how people in Youngstown who didn’t have much would share with those who had less. Desperation communicates across boundaries, if we can really see each other. Maybe the current state of the country and Ohio has finally made enough of us too tired to hate each other.

At my own polling location, in Wyoming, Ohio, hometown of the Democrats’ incoming lieutenant governor, David Pepper, two middle-aged women stood side by side just off the lawn outside our community Civic Center. One held blue handouts of the Democrats’ slate; the other held the pink Republicans’. Voters swept in and out. It was nice to see the two chatting volunteers, holding opposing slates, getting along so well. I said so. The woman holding the Republican slate said of course they were friendly, they live in the same neighborhood.

But the stakes were still obvious.

I ran across voter Michael Robinson on my way to grab a bagel. His hair is dappled with grey, and his hoodie was adorned with an “Ohio Voted” sticker. The sticker is important. His mother-in-law insists upon photographic evidence, though Robinson wouldn’t miss a vote. His parents and grandparents lived in Washington, D.C., before the majority-Black city was allowed to vote in presidential elections. His paternal grandfather grew up in South Carolina as a sharecropper who could not afford the poll tax. Robinson, an Ohio resident for 26 years now, was born in the Nation’s Capital, and at 18, voted in the District’s first home rule election in 1974. He tells me his grandmother drilled into him that education and the vote were the two things no one could take away, “That’s how you have power … that’s what they wanna take away.” (A voter ID requirement passed today in Ohio too.)

In the Cincy suburb of Montgomery, Ohio, two men, each holding slates of opposing parties, chatted in a friendly way at a church entryway, a polling site. A father and young daughter come out, and the Republican asks, “Is it her first time voting?” It was indeed her first time tagging along. She got a sticker. Everyone cheered. At the other entrance, though, from the Democrats, I hear the police were called earlier because a man was berated by a volunteer for a Republican candidate after voting. A Republican volunteer tells me it’s been a beautiful day. She says, “It’s up to how God turns the hearts and minds of men. But I do hope they choose his values over their own desires.”

I know it’s not what she meant, but I kind of suspect many would say they did.

Outside Norwood Community Center, shortly before polls closed, I open my car door to Rihanna. There was no line, but the music was pumping. The DJ, Bizzy Bizz (Rodney Hayes), is part of DJ at the Polls, a good-vibes-only, nonpartisan get-out-the-vote effort. Under the thump of “This Is What You Came For,” Bizzy Bizz tells me that it has been an incredible day. After the past few years, the positivity he’s seen at the polls, people coming together to vote, “honestly, it’s restored my faith in humanity.” As the music plays, this, he says, “this is what this nation needs.”


People who are stressed over how they are going to stock their kitchen cabinets have been subjected to a dizzying demonstration of disqualifying behavior from candidates who seem to have lost the plot on human decency. Congressman Max Miller, who represents a Northeast Ohio district, has been accused of domestic abuse. Despite a delay in speaking out, our other senator, Bernie Moreno, whose daughter happens to be Miller’s estranged wife, finally did pipe up, saying Miller needs “psychological help,” that he holds his breath whenever Miller has custody of his granddaughter, and calling for Miller’s resignation from Congress. Miller’s opponent, Brian Poindexter, a union organizer and ironworker, was named the presumptive winner overnight.

Longtime U.S. Senator Sherrod Brown lost his seat in 2024, after $251 million in attack ads that largely weaponized trans rights and lied about Brown’s positions. This time, as he ran against Jon Husted, a widely debunked attack ad claimed that “Sherrod Brown supports sex change surgery for minors.” However, the woman in the ad who claimed she got surgery without her parents’ consent as a minor is actually from Texas (not Ohio) and was 19 when she had her double mastectomy. This time, many Democrats, including Brown, have strategically pivoted from getting bogged down in a culture war over trans rights, either pointing out the inaccuracies in such ads or redirecting away from the vanishingly small handful of trans youth in Ohio school sports. (It’s debatable whether it’s better to have your identity weaponized or ignored, both for political ends.) Instead, Democrats’ energy has largely focused on pocketbook issues, which affect almost all of us (yes, including trans Ohioans).

At 11 p.m., CNN called it for Ohio’s Senate race: Mr. Brown is going back to Washington. The tavern where I was watching results erupted. The local TV news happened to cut away and fill the screen with an image of Amy Acton. More cheers. A chant of “O-H, I-O.”

Acton took the stage in Columbus behind a “Governor-Elect Acton” sign, saying the state had chosen “unity and decency over division and hate. The healing begins today.” As Acton took the stage for her acceptance speech, for a moment, I had the heart-pounding sensation of witnessing a local girl done good.

I grew up a couple miles down a long cross-county road from where Acton grew up, once she and her brother settled in with their father. This was after she spent time hungry and homeless, living in a tent over winter in Youngstown, after escaping her sexually abusive stepfather and a mother who skipped town with him after his indictment for Acton’s abuse. We come from this place, where steel still runs in people’s veins, generations since the mills closed, decades since opportunity was anything people could count on. A place where those who could were often coached to go away to school, get out. Acton, with Brown, held her last campaign stop in her old high school. “I’m a scrappy kid from Youngstown,” she said before hundreds as the high school gym erupted in applause.

Her reprise, this entire campaign, has been a stubborn fixation on the issues “99 percent of Ohioans can agree on.” She talks like she was aiming for, not a blue wave, but enough to drink for everyone.

As we were each growing up, our corner of the state was a Democratic stronghold, but give a place a couple generations of broken promises of change, grown kids moving away, and those who stayed staking a sad, fierce loyalty to a place of want, and the region was ready for a new promise-peddler when Donald Trump ran in 2016. Youngstown’s Mahoning County switched from reliably blue to red.

But Acton and Brown both won there last night.

When people vote, they choose a person to represent them in government, but they also approve the person who publicly represents their interests, their values. They represent us as a people.

When Acton started campaigning, she was bothered that on the internet, young people used phrases like “That’s so Ohio” as a catchphrase for things that were bad or cringe. Acton suffered as a child in Ohio, but her ambition and effort were also rewarded in Ohio. She learned in the great public schools that have been quietly underfunded and now are being siphoned of over $1 billion per year for private school vouchers. She served the state over Covid, and even after enduring the brunt of blowback, she put her hand up for more service as governor.

She had the cruel indignity of campaigning to serve this state and getting sideswiped by her mother, a woman who has failed her over and again. As the nation has looked to Ramaswamy with a collective “WTF,” Acton told me recently that since the attack ad, she has been stopped at event after event by survivors whose worst moments were dredged up by Ramaswamy’s disgusting campaign ploy. The swipe could have derailed most people. Others might have become overwhelmed by the disclosures of abuse, but what Acton took from it was that there are more survivors of sexual assault in the state than most people realize.

Ramaswamy’s campaign tried to destroy her; Acton’s empathetic heart found an additional policy front.

When I was young, people called Ohio purple, a reliable mix of red and blue. As went Ohio, so went the nation. For a long time, we’ve been painted red by state and congressional maps, and a lot of us got used to officials who extracted their power and influence from the state but failed to see us, on rural farms now in the shadow of data centers, or striving for more in the three C’s (Cleveland, Columbus, and Cincinnati), or for kids growing up in towns where almost everyone struggles. If they saw our dreams, it was just to exploit them. A lot of pundits may tell the story of 2026 as a blue wave, but from here in Ohio, it looks more like the first gulp of an enormous storm, skies cracking open after a long, hard drought.

items.title: 3 Out of 4 States With Abortion on Ballot Vote to Increase Access
items.content_text:
Much like 2022, the 2026 midterm elections proved the majority of voters support reproductive rights and abortion access.

Four states had abortion on the ballot. Nevada and Virginia voted in favor of allowing abortions within state lines. Missouri voted against repealing a constitutional amendment supporting abortion access that was introduced via a ballot initiative in 2024. Idaho was the sole exception on Tuesday as voters sided against a citizen-initiated statute that would have enshrined abortion access as a statutory right.

Nevadans, Virginians, and Missourans voted 63 percent, 62 percent, and 55 percent, respectively. Idahoans, meanwhile, voted by 56 percent.

Since Roe v. Wade was overturned by the Supreme Court’s conservative supermajority in June 2022, abortion has become a nonstop losing streak for Republicans, pitting the party’s long-standing policies against their increasingly dire ramifications.

States that enforced aggressive abortion restrictions saw medical brain drains, with large swaths of medical professionals moving elsewhere. Other states with such rules witnessed the horrific reality of allowing the legislature into the doctor’s office (see: the case of Adriana Smith, a Georgia nurse who died in 2025 but nonetheless was forced to remain on life support as an incubation chamber after doctors discovered a nine-week fetus in her abdomen. Her family had no say in that matter).

The bad PR has led to a quiet stripping of pro-life policies from conservative platforms across the country, with the GOP futilely attempting to ditch the “pro-life” branding altogether in an effort to skirt more electoral losses.

National surveys indicate that the vast majority of the country supports abortion access. In a poll published by the Pew Research Center in March, 60 percent of respondents said abortion should be legal in pretty much all cases, while only 38 percent said it should be illegal in most cases.

items.title: So Who’s Running the Party Now: Progressives or Moderates?
items.content_text:
You’re reading The TNR Blue Book. Get daily scoops, strategy, and developments inside the liberal ideas factory delivered right to your inbox. Sign up for free.


Inside Washington

Democrats have won a massive majority in the House, and amid the celebrations, different factions of the party will be clamoring to claim credit for the blue tsunami. Was it the progressives, the centrists, or even the Bernie dogs who carried the party to victory? And which faction will be calling the shots come January?

The answer, to some extent, depends on who you ask. “A Democratic majority is really going to be built on the back of moderate candidates in the House,” said David de la Fuente, deputy director for politics and research at the centrist group Third Way. He pointed to moderate candidates who eventually won on Tuesday night, like Jared Moskowitz in Florida’s 25th congressional district or Bobby Pulido in Texas’s 15th congressional district.

Meanwhile, Usamah Andrabi, the communications director of progressive group Justice Democrats, argued that progressives brought the energy and policy platforms that turned the tide. “The mandate from voters across this country is for this majority to look like what many Democrats finally learned to campaign on, which is taking on corporate interests to deliver on an affordability agenda that actually helps working class communities,” he said. “They finally listened to the left.”

Andrabi pointed to Justice Democrats’ massive wins this cycle; it was their most successful year by far. The group is poised to send at least seven leaders to Congress, including Donavan McKinney in Michigan, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez in New York, and Melat Kiros in Colorado. These electeds will be joining fellow progressive firebrands like Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Rashida Tlaib, and Greg Casar in Congress. As it stands, the Congressional Progressive Caucus currently has 101 members, while the New Democrat Coalition, which includes more centrist lawmakers, touts 114 members. While it’s too soon to say definitively how those numbers will change, the Congressional Progressive Caucus PAC suggested that the caucus might be adding “over 20” new members, according to an email the group sent previewing a later press call.

“Typically, the Congressional Progressive Caucus is bigger than the New Dems when Republicans control the House, and the New Dems are bigger than the progressives when the Democrats control the House, and that’s because, essentially, the New Dems tend to be the majority makers,” de la Cruz said. The term “majority maker” comes from former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who famously called the moderate-to-conservative Blue Dogs the “majority makers” for their success in unseating Republicans and contributing to the Democratic majority.

But some progressive candidates overturned that orthodoxy on Tuesday. In Michigan’s 7th congressional district, Sunrise Movement co-founder William Lawrence prevailed despite running in one of the most competitive districts in the county, and facing the most Republican spending of any House candidate this cycle—more than $23 million. Similarly, in California’s 22nd congressional district, Randy Villegas declared an early victory over Republican Representative David Valadao, a testament to the size of his win (usually, California results trickle in slowly).

Trying to tally up the number of seats that will soon be held by progressives versus moderates creates another problem: “It suggests that there’s just a kind of monolithic progressive ideology and a monolithic centrist ideology, and in my experience, it’s not quite that simple,” Democratic strategist Oliver Libby said.

This year, that question became even more complicated with the emergence of a number of so-called Bernie dogs—candidates endorsed by both the Blue Dogs and Senator Bernie Sanders. Those candidates include Sam Forstag in Montana’s 1st congressional district, Rebecca Cooke in Wisconsin’s 3rd congressional district, Brian Poindexter in Ohio’s 7th district, and Bob Brooks in Pennsylvania’s seventh district. All four won.

A more useful way of analyzing the Democratic majority—and predicting what they might do come January—could be to look directly at what policies they ran on, regardless of how they identify ideologically. That could help reconcile the simultaneous successes of moderates, progressives, and Bernie dogs, the Progressive Change Campaign Committee suggested in an Election Day memo. These winning policy platforms—including anti-establishment fights against data centers and surveillance tech, oversight of AI companies, and affordable health care—could ultimately provide a roadmap for Dems in 2028 and beyond.

—Emma Janssen


Outside Washington

The humble “I Voted” sticker could turn out to be one of the enduring images of this election. On October 19—the first day of early voting in Texas—Ronaldo Salgado cast a ballot and placed his voting sticker on Houston’s makeshift memorial to his father, who was shot and killed by an ICE officer this summer. Amid a historic rise in early voting, hundreds of other voters proceeded to follow Salgado’s lead, leaving “I Voted” stickers or other messages at the memorial to Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. On Tuesday afternoon, MPR News and other outlets reported that the practice had spread to Minneapolis, with local affiliate Fox 9 reporting “dozens” of “I Voted” stickers at the memorials for Alex Pretti and Renee Good, both of whom were shot and killed by an ICE agents in January.

Elsewhere:

  • James Talarico, Gina Hinojosa, and Nathan Johnson won the Senate, gubernatorial, and attorney general races in Texas last night—breaking a 32-year Dem losing streak in statewide races. But if we’re talking long losing streaks: No Democrat has held a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission—an underappreciated body with huge and little understood power to regulate the fossil fuel industry—since 1990. On Tuesday, though, Democrat Jon Rosenthal claimed victory over Republican Bo French, a candidate so prone to nakedly racist rhetoric that even Karl Rove denounced him in The Wall Street Journal in September and vowed to vote for Rosenthal.
  • As of publication time for this newsletter, the race in New Jersey’s 2nd congressional district has not been called. Multiple outlets have reported, however, that four-term Republican Representative Jeff Van Drew has conceded to Democrat Zack Mullock. This is another race that longtime watchers of Democratic politics are going to be talking about today—particularly if a formal winner emerges. You can read more about this race—Van Drew, who used to be a Democrat, “has certainly earned the everlasting animosity of Democrats in the district,” Micah Rasmussen said—in Emma Janssen’s prior TNR Blue Book reporting here. Just a few weeks ago when this was written, analysts that she talked to still thought a Mullock victory was a long shot. Early Wednesday morning, Mullock led by nearly 8,000 votes, with 92 percent in.

—Heather Souvaine Horn


In Closing

Political Trivia Question of the Day  

If Scott Colom wins in Mississippi, he’ll be the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction, when two Black men were elected to the Senate from the state. Can you name either? (Sign up for The TNR Blue Book to find the answer in tomorrow’s newsletter.)

—Michael Tomasky

items.title: Washington State Votes to Keep Making Millionaires Pay Their Share
items.content_text:
Washington voters decided to keep their state’s millionaire tax on Tuesday.

Fifty-eight percent of Washingtonians voted against Initiative 645, an effort to repeal the state’s millionaire tax led by right-wing donors and PACs, including Let’s Go Washington. The PAC, headed by conservative hedge fund executive Brian Heywood, was the most active group in the $13.1 million failed effort to overturn the 9.9 percent tax on income over $1 million a year.

“I can’t tell you how many people have left the state,” Heywood told The Guardian in October. “My business partner moved to Arizona. I probably know 50 people that are deca- or centi-millionaires that have left the state.”

The millionaire tax, which was signed into law in March, uses the funding to expand eligibility for the Working Families Tax Credit, allowing 460,000 more households a cash rebate of up to $1,330.

items.title: Congrats to the First Muslim Senator, First Gay Senator, and More
items.content_text:
Americans made history Tuesday night. Amidst the seasonal pandemonium of ballot counting and number crunching, the country elected several political firsts.

Michigan elected its first Muslim senator, choosing Dr. Abdul El-Sayed over Republican candidate Mike Rogers. El-Sayed ran a shrewd campaign, canvassing across the state and overcoming a nasty strain of Islamophobia while holding earnest, intelligent conversations with conservatives and liberals alike.

Halfway across the country, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won her bid for Georgia’s gubernatorial office, making her the first Black woman to hold a governorship in U.S. history. Her winning campaign platform promised to push back on the White House, to find relief for inflated gas and grocery prices, to eliminate state income tax for public school teachers, and to impose a moratorium on data center development.

In Illinois, voters chose to send Juliana Stratton to the Senate. Stratton’s admittance to the upper chamber in January will mark the first time in U.S. history that three Black women have served in the Senate simultaneously. She joins Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland. The previous record was set in 2025, when Blunt Rochester and Alsobrooks joined the 119th Congress.

Nearby, Ohioans elected Dr. Amy Acton as their first woman governor, besting billionaire tech entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy. Ramaswamy’s final campaign push centered around a disturbing ad that featured Acton’s estranged mother declaring that something was wrong with the 60-year-old Democrat.

She wasn’t the only gubernatorial first. Deb Haaland, who served as secretary of the interior under former President Joe Biden, became the first Native woman to be elected governor when New Mexicans cast their ballots Tuesday.

The diversity achievements also extended to Texas, where civil rights attorney Gina Hinojosa became the first Latina governor in the nation.

Other candidates that broke the mold include former Minnesota state Representative Peggy Flanagan, who became the first Native woman to be elected to the U.S. Senate. The Native community’s groundbreaking moment could be made that much sweeter by a win for former Representative Mary Peltola, who is currently fractions of a percentage point behind Republican Dan Sullivan for Alaska’s Senate seat as the Last Frontier continues to tabulate its ballots.

Delivering a speech from St. Paul, Minnesota, Flanagan noted that her victory signaled a breakthrough in the nationwide fight against Donald Trump’s MAGA movement.

“You said no more war. No more health care cuts. No more taking away food from children and seniors. No more selling this country off to the highest bidder. And no more masked goons shooting our neighbors,” Flanagan said, according to the Minnesota Reformer.

And nearly 50 years after Harvey Milk was elected as the country’s first openly gay lawmaker, New Hampshire elected former Representative Chris Pappas as the first openly gay man to become a U.S. senator.

items.title: Maryland Democrats Land Massive Win on Voting Maps
items.content_text:
Maryland voters approved a ballot measure Tuesday amending the state’s Constitution to allow Democratic-led congressional redistricting.

The measure, known as Question 3, passed 60 percent to 40 percent, with 77 percent of votes counted.

The measure does not enact a new map, but gives Maryland state legislators greater powers in drawing congressional district boundaries. Maryland has eight congressional districts, and all but one, the 1st district, are represented by a Democrat. The state Constitution currently requires compact districts that respect “natural boundaries,” and the 1st district, represented by Republican Andy Harris, is mostly confined to Maryland’s eastern side of the Chesapeake Bay.

Republicans fought the ballot question in court, but in September, the state Supreme Court allowed the amendment to be put to a vote in November’s elections. In the weeks leading up to the election, Maryland’s Democratic Governor Wes Moore campaigned for the measure, and former President Barack Obama lent his endorsement, filming a video ad urging voters to approve it.

Missouri also voted on redistricting Tuesday night, and the Show Me State’s residents blocked a Republican-led effort to gerrymander the state in favor of conservatives.

Last year, Donald Trump began pushing Republican-led states to gerrymander their districts in order to prevent a Democratic majority in Congress from investigating him. This set off a gerrymandering war, and Republicans successfully put new maps in place in seven states: Texas, Louisiana, Alabama, Florida, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Ohio. That was helped by the Supreme Court gutting the Voting Rights Act in April, allowing Southern states to eliminate majority-Black districts.

Until now, Democrats only had one successful redistricting effort in California and a favorable ruling from a federal judge in Utah, who rejected a Republican-drawn map in favor of independent redistricting reform approved by voters in 2018, creating another Democratic district. For 2028, it appears that Democrats are on their way to picking up another congressional seat in Maryland.

items.title: Swing State Voters Reject Trump-Backed Effort to Steal House Seats
items.content_text:
Missourians blocked a new congressional map pushed by the state’s Republicans and President Donald Trump Tuesday by nearly 62 percent of the vote.

Proposition A would have redrawn the state’s map to favor Republicans and push Democratic Representative Emanuel Cleaver, whose district currently comprises most of Kansas City along with nearby suburbs, out of office. The vote follows months of television ads mostly opposing the new map drawn by Republicans last year, according to St. Louis Public Radio.

Republicans tried to force their new map through before the midterms, but the Supreme Court halted their efforts in an unsigned order in September. In the months since then, Democrats successfully canvassed across Missouri in an effort to defeat the measure, while Republicans, who were hoping to have the map in place already, had less enthusiasm.

Trump began pushing for rapid redistricting last year in an effort to keep a Republican majority in Congress and prevent Democratic investigations of himself and his administration. That set off a gerrymandering war, with Republicans successfully getting new maps in place in seven states: Texas, Louisiana, Alabama, Florida, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Ohio. The effort was helped by the Supreme Court gutting the Voting Rights Act in April, allowing Southern states to eliminate majority-Black districts.

Democrats were only able to respond with one successful redistricting effort in California, and picked up a seat in Utah thanks to a federal judge rejecting a Republican-drawn map in favor of independent redistricting reform approved by voters in 2018. In Missouri Tuesday, voters sided with Democrats, but the redistricting fight will continue there and across the country for 2028’s presidential election.

items.title: Trump Tries to Blame Everyone But Himself for Democratic Sweep
items.content_text:
Donald Trump demanded that the midterm elections be another referendum on his popularity, but now he can’t seem to accept the results.

The president called in to Fox News around midnight to complain about the conservative media behemoth’s polls, which reflected Trump’s tanking approval ratings.

“And then I read at Fox that I’m not popular. The Fox polls are terrible. You ought to get yourself a good pollster ‘cause your polls are the worst,” Trump said live on air.

Host Brett Baier pushed back: “But tonight, actually, the results are pretty close to what the Fox polls showed.”

But Trump wasn’t willing to confront reality. “Well, I don’t know about that,” he snipped.

Democrats won big all over the country—even in historically deep red districts—taking control of both chambers of Congress in the process. Despite the obvious blow, Trump told Fox News that he had the “greatest two years in the history of the presidency.”

An NBC News exit poll found that more than half of voters saw the election as an opportunity to rebuke Trump and his MAGA agenda, which has thus far included an aggressive foreign policy that tied Americans to a wildly unpopular war with Iran, economic tariffs that vastly inflated the cost of living, and a militaristic deportation scheme that has pitted federal agents against the general population.

Republican candidates saw the writing on the wall months ago, but were unable to successfully peel their campaigns away from the president’s influence. Instead, the president urged voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.” By late Tuesday, Trump was already trying to rewrite history.

In a separate interview Tuesday night, Trump told Politico’s Dasha Burns that his party would have won big if he was on the ballot.

“I wasn’t on the ballot, and we didn’t get the people out, but I wasn’t on the ballot,” Trump said. “If I was on the ballot, we would have won. We would have won it all very easily.”

“But Mr. President, you told voters that you were on the ballot, to vote as though you were on the ballot,” Burns reminded him.

“I said, ‘Think about me being on the ballot,’ but they didn’t agree and they didn’t like the candidates in most cases. Just one of those things,” Trump said.

He then offered that he didn’t want to blame any one individual, but that he watched the results roll in with “great interest” and that he “learned from it.”

“What did you learn, sir?” Burns pressed.

“Well, we’re going to work with the Democrats, to make sure things go well for our country. They’ve already called and—I have the right to veto everything, but I don’t want be just sitting there vetoing everything,” Trump said. “We have a lot of friends in the Democratic Party.”

items.title: Elon Musk Spirals Over His Failure to Buy Elections
items.content_text:
After wasting almost half a billion dollars supporting Republicans in the midterm elections, tech oligarch Elon Musk is having trouble digesting the Democratic landslide.

Musk took to his X platform in the early hours Wednesday morning, offering some lame observations as his preferred candidates were trounced. At about 1:12 am, Musk posted, “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” before following that up with, “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time 🤷‍♂️” a minute later.

A couple of hours later, he commented, “Interesting” on a repost of exit polling purporting to show that voters supported the Trump administration’s immigration policies, but massively opposed the Iran war.

It’s not clear where that polling is from or whether it is credible, but in any case, Musk appears to be trying to cope with the negative results as best as he can. Stocks in his Tesla and SpaceX companies are plummeting Wednesday despite other tech companies doing well in early trading. His plan to merge SpaceX and Tesla might now hit some obstacles in a Democratic-controlled Congress, which has already signaled that investigations of the tech oligarch are on the way.

Plus, Musk moved his companies from California to Texas to escape Democratic oversight, only to now have a Democratic governor in the Lone Star State, Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned against Musk. She also called for a moratorium on new data centers and an end to tax breaks for the industry. Now Democrats in Texas, as well as across the country, have him and other tech barons in their crosshairs.

“They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” posted Democratic Senator Ed Markey Tuesday night.

items.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s Victory Is Historic for These Two Reasons
items.content_text:
Abdul El-Sayed’s election is a watershed moment in American politics. The victory of a devout Muslim, particularly in a fairly white, moderate state like Michigan, is another step toward America becoming a truly multicultural democracy. And the triumph of a progressive candidate in a swing state, despite intense opposition from Republicans and centrist Democrats—particularly his primary opponent Representative Haley Stevens—suggests that conventional notions of what kinds of candidates are “electable” should be further discarded. 

El-Sayed is the first Muslim American ever elected to the Senate. There will probably never be a large number of Muslim senators, since followers of Islam are only around 1 percent of the U.S. population. But being Muslim is arguably a bigger barrier to success in America, particularly in electoral politics, than being Black, Latino, female, gay, or a member of another group whose members often face discrimination. Anti-Muslim sentiment in America is actively stoked by the political right and in many ways tolerated by the rest of our society. In a recent Pew Research Center poll, 42 percent of American adults said that Muslims have a negative impact on the United States, 43 percent said Muslims are less patriotic than other Americans. Fifty-one percent said that Islam encourages violence more than other religions, including 76 percent of Republicans and, yes, 29 percent of Democrats. 

In Michigan, 39 percent of voters said that a candidate being Muslim makes them less likely to vote for that person, according to an October survey conducted by the Institute for Public Policy and Social Research at Michigan State University. In contrast, only 10 percent said they were less likely to vote for female candidates. These numbers likely vastly underestimate Islamophobia, since some who hold these views might be leery of acknowledging them to a stranger calling from a polling company. 

Islamophobia has been a powerful force affecting the most important political figures of this era. In his 2008 campaign, Barack Obama, who spent some of his childhood in heavily Muslim Indonesia and whose middle name is Hussein, repeatedly emphasized that he is not Muslim, no doubt aware that Islamophobia is even more widespread than anti-Black racism in America. Obama’s successor, Donald Trump, rose to power in part by promising during his first campaign to limit the number of Muslims entering America, casting their mere presence as a danger to the country. 

Trump won in 2016 even as the media openly called his proposal a “Muslim ban.” And in both of his terms, Trump’s administration has intentionally restricted immigration from majority-Muslim countries, with little pushback from Dems, the national media, or voters. 

El-Sayed was facing both that backdrop of anti-Muslim sentiment and specific tensions around his religion throughout his campaign. Trump and Republicans constantly implied he was supportive of terrorism and potentially even a terrorist himself. The news media repeatedly asked El-Sayed about the Muslim Brotherhood and other issues related to his faith that were not relevant to the Michigan primary. 

A significant bloc of Democrats slammed his relationship with political commentator Hasan Piker, and his positions on Israeli-Palestinian policy, namely El-Sayed describing Israel’s war in Gaza as a genocide, calling for a suspension of U.S. military aid to Israel, and questioning the idea of a state where Jewish people always have political control over Palestinians. Some claimed he was insufficiently concerned about antisemitism. 

Perhaps these Democrats would have celebrated a pro-Israel Muslim candidate, or at least a candidate who sidestepped the issue. But it’s hard to disentangle these critiques from El-Sayed’s faith. American Muslims are deeply concerned about Israel’s actions in Gaza over the last three years, so expecting Muslims politicians to soft-pedal that issue is asking them to essentially deny their Muslim identity. The party establishment also regularly undermines and lodges antisemitism accusations at Zohran Mamdani, Ilhan Omar, and Rashida Tlaib, three of the other most prominent Muslim politicians in America. 

A week before the election, former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, both a party elder and supposedly deeply committed to fighting Republicans, blasted El-Sayed over his Israel views and hinted that he would lose because of them. The party got fully behind El-Sayed only two days before the election, after Stevens’s shocking decision to actually endorse Republican Mike Rogers. 

El-Sayed overcame all of that. The main reason he won is that Democrats everywhere did, as the election was a backlash against Trump. But that doesn’t take away from the importance of his victory. Obama won in  2008 in large part because of hatred of George W. Bush and the Iraq War, but America electing a Black person president was still a major step forward in our democracy. A Muslim candidate winning a swing state shows that many Americans, particularly Democrats, truly want us to be a nation based on our shared ideals and values, not a country dominated by white people, men, and/or Christians. 

The resistance to El-Sayed, from both Republicans and some Democrats, of course, wasn’t just about religion or Israel policy. El-Sayed has long been aligned with Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and others in the party’s progressive wing. The party’s left backed his 2018 gubernatorial primary against center-left favorite and eventual Governor Gretchen Whitmer. 

In the Senate primary earlier this year, the party’s center-left largely backed Stevens and hinted that El-Sayed could not win a general election. Progressives went all in for El-Sayed. They wanted an ally in the Senate. But they also wanted to prove that a fairly progressive candidate could win in a swing state like Michigan. Centrist Democrats constantly say progressive views and politicians should be ignored because the left doesn’t understand how to win elections and therefore keep Republicans out of power. 

Game changed. A candidate calling for Medicare for All and fighting billionaires while welcoming Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders to campaign for him in the general election has won Michigan, the quintessential swing state. And several other progressive candidates won in swing districts and states too. This is a big blow to centrist arguments about electability. And they know it—prominent center-left Democrats spent the weeks ahead of the election demanding that El-Sayed win by as much as more centrist candidates in Michigan and around the country or they would diminish his win. That discrediting will be less effective after Stevens spent the days right before the election actively trying to defeat El-Sayed. She proved progressives’ arguments that centrists’ electability claims are often a pretext to mask their deep ideological opposition to progressive politicians and causes. 

One direct result of the Michigan results is that I expect Ocasio-Cortez to run for president. El-Sayed and others who won in swing districts and states ran on the anti-billionaire, working class–centered approach that the New York congresswoman has helped pioneer. Those victories will help Ocasio-Cortez rebut arguments that she could not win a general election. And the party’s progressive wing will likely want to push its own candidates at a time when it appears as if the electorate is deeply skeptical of billionaires and Republicans and might consider more nontraditional candidates. 

“Democrats everywhere, including moderates in swing seats, are running ads centered around a pro-working class message, opposing billionaires, foreign wars, corruption, and corporations,” said Evan Brown, executive director of the Congressional Progressive Caucus’s PAC, in a memo released on the eve of the election. 

Even if Ocasio-Cortez doesn’t launch a presidential campaign in the next few months, El-Sayed’s victory opens up new possibilities. Or more accurately, he reminds us that these possibilities exist. No one expected Obama and Trump to be elected president a few years before they were. Despite the confident claims of pundits and center-left Democrats, politics is not an exact science. A left-wing man named Abdul becoming the senator from Michigan doesn’t just prove that progressives or Muslims can be elected but that timing and circumstance really matter. Perhaps the next president will be Ocasio-Cortez. Or perhaps it’s someone none of us are thinking about right now. 

This is not 2008. Abdul El-Sayed will not be running the country. But even more than Obama, El-Sayed overcame deep skepticism about his faith, policy positions, identity, and patriotism—including from many Democrats. The biggest story of November 2026 is Democrats winning across the country, including in red states like Nebraska. But another huge story is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed’s triumph in a country that twice elected Donald Trump.

items.title: Trump Presidency on Life Support after Blue Tsunami’s Reach Shocks GOP
items.content_text: In a stunning series of outcomes, Democrats won control of the House and Senate on Tuesday. They’re projected to take control of at least 244 House seats, per NBC, and as of now, they’ve flipped Senate seats in South Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, and Maine. That means they’ll control at least 54 seats. But what also makes these results stunning is how Democrats captured a lot of new territory in places they’ve long struggled to reach. They made huge inroads into the South, won a Senate seat in the Great Plains, and reached deep into the parts of the Midwest that we all thought Trump had turned permanently red. We talked to New Republic editor Michael Tomasky about all of it. We discuss how Trump brought his party to this disastrous moment, how these Democratic gains will alter our political geography, what this all portends for JD Vance, how a new Democratic Party may be coming into being, and how it will handle a severely diminished Trump next year. Listen to this episode here. A transcript is here.

items.title: Say Goodnight, New Democrats. It’s the Era of the New New Democrats.
items.content_text:
There are about a thousand takeaways from a historic election like this one, the chief one being the thorough, and thoroughly gratifying, repudiation of you-know-who. But I’m going to focus on the one that gets at the heart of a key question for Democrats about what kind of party they’re going to be, heading into 2028 and beyond. And the lesson is this: With Tuesday’s election results, particularly the Senate victories of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas, the 1990s centrist rules about how you win a Senate race in a purple or red state are dead.

The ’90s gave birth to the so-called “New Democrats,” the centrists who’d jettisoned the old liberalism and adopted a more corporate-friendly aspect. For decades, you had to be a New Democrat to be taken seriously. But this week, we entered a new era.

El-Sayed and Talarico were never supposed to win these races. Talarico took positions in the past—notably on transgender rights, an issue that is supposed to be poison for Democrats—that the ’90s conventional wisdom would say there’s no way he could overcome, especially in deep-red Texas. El-Sayed was vehemently opposed by establishment Democrats, some of them because of his views on Israel, but many (and, in my anecdotal experience, most) of them on the grounds that he was too far left and absolutely unelectable in a swing state like Michigan. I had a number of conversations with Washington Democrats earlier this year in which I heard it said that if he was nominated, the party was just giving that Senate seat away.

But both candidates ran as aggressive economic populists, attacking billionaires and vowing to fight on behalf of working-class people. El-Sayed was ceaselessly on-message: Money out of politics, money in your pockets, Medicare for All. And Talarico, while he did walk back some of his more progressive stands on cultural issues, never wavered on economics and delivered what for my money was the single most memorable riff of the campaign: “The only minority destroying America is the billionaires. We are focused on the wrong one percent. Trans people aren’t taking away our health care. Muslims aren’t defunding our schools. Immigrants aren’t cutting taxes for themselves and their rich friends. It’s the billionaires and their puppet politicians.”

People who talk like that aren’t supposed to win Senate seats. But they both won and won fairly handily. Those inclined to disagree with my thesis will jump in and point out how lucky the candidates were. Talarico faced a uniquely appalling opponent.
