items.content_text:
Iran Reportedly Hands Out Iodine Tablets As Trump Locks Crosshairs On Pickaxe Mountain

Summary:

  • Iodine Tablets Being Distributed  
  • Iranian Video Tells Citizens How To Survive Nuke
  • Trump Says US 'Locked And Loaded' For Renewed Strikes Against Iran

Iran Hands Out Iodine Tablets

The US midterms are over, and Democrats swept this week's elections. The question now is what the Trump administration will do about Iran's Pickaxe Mountain and Kharg Island.

This morning's diplomatic signals couldchange at a moment's notice. Meanwhile, The Times reportsthat the Iranian government is distributing iodine tablets to communities near nuclear facilities as Tehran fears an attack on Pickaxe Mountain may be imminent.

Here's how The Times described the preparations: 

However, the video appears to tell citizens how to survive a nuclear explosion at Pickaxe. The video, examined by The Times, asks viewers to imagine a nuclear explosion before listing the approximate distances to nearby cities: 17 miles from Natanz, 25 from Kashan, 117 from Isfahan and 223 from Tehran. It gives three instructions for survival: "Get inside, stay inside and listen for updates."

It also warns that an attack on an underground facility could throw large quantities of radioactive earth and rock into the atmosphere, allowing winds to carry contaminated dust for hundreds of miles. People near the site may have only ten to 15 minutes before the fallout arrives, it claims, while those in more distant cities could have several hours.

It is not just the video that is adding to the belief among Iranians that an attack is imminent. Iodine tablets are being distributed to communities near nuclear facilities as a precaution against possible radiation exposure, according to a health ministry official. "Yes, we are distributing iodine," the official told The Times. 

"During every war, we have tried to distribute it within a two-to-three-kilometre radius of nuclear facilities. Trump can no longer be trusted. He may go through with this crime."

If the Trump administration decides to escalate, a cyberattack or other less lethal means could disrupt operations at Iran's oil export hub on Kharg Island. Pickaxe Mountain poses a much bigger challenge. 

Pickaxe Mountain's nuclear facilities lie 80 to 100 meters underground, making them difficult to destroy even with the most powerful US conventional bunker-busting bombs. However, a B61-11 nuclear bunker buster could destroy the facility. 

Recall what Trump said last week: "There are 'one or two sites' left that need to be dealt with, including Pickaxe Mountain. We can do it in ten minutes. We have a plan for it, and we can execute it very quickly."

***

Trump Says US 'Locked And Loaded' For Renewed Strikes Against Iran

Authored by Tom Ozimek via The Epoch Times (emphasis ours),

U.S. President Donald Trump said that Iran cannot do anything regarding its nuclear program without approval from Washington and that he would soon decide whether to resume renewed military operations against Tehran.

Trump's remarks on Thursday came during an Oval Office exchange with reporters, who asked for comment on reports that Iranian negotiators are reviewing a new proposal put forward by regional mediators for a deal that would constrain Iran's nuclear program.

"It doesn't make any difference what they're looking at," Trump said. "They're not going to have a nuclear weapon; they know that. So do I."

Trump said that he would soon decide whether to resume major combat operations in Iran, clarifying that his preference would be for a negotiated solution rather than destruction of the Middle Eastern country.

"In Iran we are there for seven months, and we control everything that we've wanted to control, and now we'll make a decision: do we want to go further," he said.

"I think it'll take them 25 years to rebuild the country. I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I'll have to; you'll know soon enough."

For weeks, Trump has threatened to return to a full-scale bombardment of Iran after the midterm elections if Tehran remained unwilling to reach a negotiated settlement on terms acceptable to the United States, particularly regarding its nuclear program.

"We're locked and loaded," Trump told reporters Thursday. "If we have to do the rest of the Iran thing, we're very much locked and loaded."

Iran's top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, said earlier Thursday that Tehran had set seven conditions to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and enter negotiations with Washington.

"As long as they do not execute our seven conditions, we will neither open the Strait of Hormuz nor have negotiations," he said during a visit to Russia.

Tehran's demands include sanctions relief, the release of frozen Iranian assets, and paying war reparations.

Washington, meanwhile, insists that any initial talks address Iran's nuclear program.

On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance publicly questioned whether the Iran war was worth ​it and said it cost Republicans control ​of Congress in the midterm election.

Vance's remarks stirred debate about whether Trump remained willing to proceed with a potential resumption of major combat operations against Iran. The president's latest Oval Office remarks suggest that renewed military action remains under consideration.

Trump on Monday expressed optimism about a possible settlement with Iran as talks continued in Qatar, with Vance saying he and the president had discussed the matter and both "feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement."

"We're going to keep working at it," Vance said.

The U.S.–Iran conflict has spread regionally, with clashes between Iran-backed Houthis and a Saudi Arabia-led coalition in Yemen, Saudi Arabia, and parts of the Red Sea.

The Saudi-led coalition said Friday that its air defense systems intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis toward Najran, a major city in Saudi Arabia.

"Debris fell as a result of the interception, and damage assessment is underway," the coalition said in a Nov. 6 post on X.

Trump held a phone call with Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani to discuss the regional situation and efforts to de-escalate tensions, Qatar News Agency reported on Friday.

The two men discussed the latest international efforts, notably the initiatives led by the State of Qatar, to bridge the gaps between the concerned parties and support the negotiation process, to pave the way for reaching a comprehensive agreement that resolves the crisis and ensures security and stability in the region, according to the Qatar News Agency.

Al Thani highlighted the importance of continuing dialogue and embracing diplomacy as a means of resolving disputes, while calling for safeguarding freedom of navigation and energy supply security, the agency said.

Qatar has been mediating between Iran and the United States, with Qatari intermediaries shuttling proposals between Tehran and Washington.

items.title: 'Vigorous Oversight' Coming To Pentagon, Top House Armed Services Democrat Says
items.content_text:
'Vigorous Oversight' Coming To Pentagon, Top House Armed Services Democrat Says

Authored by Ryan Morgan via The Epoch Times,

WASHINGTON - Rep. Adam Smith (D-Wash.), the current ranking member of the House Armed Services Committee, has forecast intensifying oversight of the Pentagon when Democrats take control of the committee in January.

"My Democratic colleagues on the House Armed Services Committee and I are ready to hit the ground running in the 120th Congress and the top priority will be to conduct vigorous oversight of the Department of Defense and the Trump Administration," Smith said in a Nov. 4 statement.

"My Democratic colleagues on the House Armed Services Committee and I are ready to hit the ground running in the 120th Congress and the top priority will be to conduct vigorous oversight of the Department of Defense and the Trump Administration (and) reestablish an Oversight &... pic.twitter.com/rxl6dGL41h

— House Armed Services Democrats (@HASCDemocrats) November 4, 2026

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth faces an impeachment push in Congress. The blooming oversight agenda could lay the groundwork for efforts to remove Hegseth from office.

"The list of potential oversight topics is long, but the illegal war against Iran is top of mind for me and the American people," Smith said.

"So too are sweetheart deals and favoritism to certain entities and individuals. We must dive into any waste, fraud, and abuse by examining contracts and other financial support awarded to private companies."

Smith said U.S. military operations in Latin America and the Caribbean - which have included lethal strikes on alleged drug smuggling boats, and more recent operations against land-based targets - would also be a subject for further investigation.

Hegseth's push to reshape the military's culture and leadership appears to be another matter for coming scrutiny. Smith described these efforts as a "purging of the ranks based on loyalty and ideology."

President Donald Trump's push for a $1.5 trillion defense budget also appears in doubt. Smith said the United States must rescope its national security goals and ensure the military's budget does not come at the expense of other key domestic programs.

Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) - who has opposed the war with Iran and who lost his primary to a Trump-backed Republican challenger - introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September. Massie's impeachment articles charge Hegseth with directing military operations without sufficient congressional approval, and with allowing extrajudicial killings and military actions without sufficient measures to avoid civilian casualties.

Following sweeping Republican electoral defeats on Nov. 3 that cost them control of both houses of Congress, Massie announced he would reintroduce his impeachment articles when the House returns to session unless Hegseth resigns first.

Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell pushed back on threats from Congress to remove him.

"Secretary Hegseth will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists," he told The Epoch Times on Nov. 5. "The Department of War has followed the law and our Secretary will continue to stand and fight every single day to support and defend the Constitution, lead our troops, and protect America."

Parnell said Hegseth remains entirely committed to leading the department until Trump's term ends.

While Trump has rebuffed talk of removing Hegseth, the president has not dismissed the idea of Hegseth leaving the Pentagon to pursue Sen. Marsha Blackburn's (R-Tenn.) seat when she takes office as the Tennessee governor in January.

"I actually think he'd be very popular if he did that, but I haven't heard that at all," Trump told reporters on Nov. 4.

Jill McLaughlin contributed to this report.

items.title: Cult Leader Gets 200 Years For Starvation Deaths Of 191 People, Nearly All Of Them Children
items.content_text:
Cult Leader Gets 200 Years For Starvation Deaths Of 191 People, Nearly All Of Them Children

A Kenyan judge sentenced cult leader Paul Mackenzie to 200 years in prison on Friday over the Shakahola massacre, in which 191 people, 190 of them children, were starved to death.

Justice Diana Kavedza of the High Court in Mombasa imposed 100 years for the murders by starvation and a further 100 years for eight counts of murder by direct homicide involving child victims, The Star reported. Sentences within each set run concurrently, but the two sets run one after the other, which brings the total to 200 years.

Doomsday cult preacher, Paul Mackenzie, sentenced to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people in Shakahola. pic.twitter.com/sh1dZ4Rrab

— Kahawa Tungu (@KahawaTungu) November 6, 2026

Prosecutors had asked for the death penalty. The judge declined, saying it would "foreclose the possibility of disengagement and rehabilitation." According to Kenyans.co.ke, she also noted that a convict who stays alive might disclose where the missing children's remains are.

The court found Mackenzie, who led Good News International Ministries, bore primary responsibility as the overall leader of the Shakahola settlement. She said he ordered followers to fast to death, targeted children first and commanded violence against those who resisted or tried to escape. Witnesses testified that he told followers they would enter heaven through "punches and kicks."

The 28 co-accused were convicted with him on Oct. 19. They received sentences of 10 to 160 years, with most getting aggregate terms of 160 years, Kenyans.co.ke reported. The judge ordered all of them except Mackenzie assessed for a government deradicalization and reintegration program, and convicts who have served a third or half of their terms may apply for review.

 

Mackenzie was arrested in April 2023 after a rights group tipped off authorities. Kenyan officials have recovered more than 400 bodies from the Shakahola forest in the years since, and the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights put the toll at 429 in 2024, Africanews reported. This case covers 191 of those deaths. Prosecutors argued at trial that Mackenzie "initiated and directed" extreme fasting at his ranch under a "structured hierarchy of death" in which children would die first.

Mackenzie also faces separate charges over 52 more bodies found in a nearby village. His lawyer, Lawrence Obonyo, said after the October verdict that he intended to appeal.

items.title: Burger Bloodbath Intensifies As Yet Another Major Franchisee Goes Bust
items.content_text:
Burger Bloodbath Intensifies As Yet Another Major Franchisee Goes Bust

Another fast-food franchisee has filed for bankruptcy, becoming the latest casualty of mounting financial pressures squeezing restaurant operators across the United States.

Global Midsouth Holding Corp., a franchisee of Checkers and Rally's, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on October 28, just one day before a scheduled foreclosure auction involving one of its Tennessee restaurant properties, according to TheStreet.

The Memphis-based company reported $1.9 million in assets against $1.3 million in liabilities. Revenue fell from $860,000 in 2024 to $800,000 in 2025, underscoring the financial difficulties facing the business.

However, Global Midsouth isn't the only burger franchisee that went bust.

Meritage Hospitality Group, one of Wendy's largest franchisees, filed for bankruptcy in September after struggling with declining sales, rising beef prices, and mounting financial obligations.

The operator, which ran 314 Wendy's restaurants across 15 states when it filed, had already shuttered 60 underperforming locations. Another 60 restaurants could shut down by mid-November, according to court documents.

The bankruptcies come as the restaurant industry faces even bigger problems.

As we reported yesterday, San Diego-based Out West Restaurant Group, also known as Cerca Trova Restaurant Group, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection Monday in Delaware, putting 61 restaurants across five Western states into bankruptcy proceedings.

The company's debt has exploded from $269 million in 2020 to approximately $449 million in 2026, according to the Los Angeles Times.

"Guest traffic and earnings continued to decline, while food, labor, and other production costs continued to rise," CEO David Goronkin said.

California's rising minimum wages have been a major problem, with more than half the company's employees working in the Golden State. The COVID-19 pandemic also delivered another devastating blow, sending revenue plunging approximately 35%.

Outback parent company Bloomin' Brands said that it is preparing to swoop in. The restaurant giant has offered $26.3 million to acquire the struggling franchisee's assets, alongside up to $5.5 million in emergency financing. "This is an isolated situation involving the franchisee," a Bloomin' Brands spokesperson said. The 61 restaurants are expected to remain open during bankruptcy proceedings.

items.title: Playing A Dangerous Game
items.content_text:
Playing A Dangerous Game

Authored by Jeff Gardner via The Epoch Times,

Commentary

This October, during games 1 and 2 of the 2026 WNBA Finals, players from the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries walked off the court before the playing of the national anthem.

In an interview concerning the walkoff, Vice President JD Vance called it "disgraceful," saying, "Without love of country you are going to be a disordered human being."

Vice President Vance's comments echo those of Vice President Mike Pence, who, in 2017, walked out of the San Francisco 49ers vs. Indianapolis Colts NFL game when members of the 49ers players knelt during the national anthem, saying, "I don't think it's too much to ask NFL players to respect the Flag and our national anthem."

From 2017 forward, protests during the national anthem spread through the NFL, then to the NBA, and now to the WNBA.

In 2020, in the wake of Black Lives Matter-fueled George Floyd riots, the NFL commissioner responded to the demands of many African American players by green-lighting the singing of the hymn "Lift Every Voice and Sing," now commonly known as the black national anthem, during the Super Bowl. At every Super Bowl since 2021, "Lift Every Voice and Sing" has been performed.

As of October 2026, the WNBA commissioner has refused to comment on players walking out during the national anthem or the possibility of an additional anthem.

We should all cry "foul" when professional athletes take on the role of in-game political activists. In doing so, they are driving out of bounds the meaning of three images crucial to our national unity: our flag, the anthem, and the athlete.

The first two images, our nation's flag and anthem, are either symbols of justice and freedom or, if some on the political left are to be believed, of inequity and tyranny. The third, the athlete, is either an inspirational actor in a physical theater or a righteous social justice warrior.

Images, the physical items and mental pictures that anchor beliefs in our minds, are tricky things. They can carry almost any meaning we give them. What images cannot do, at least not very well, is carry more than one meaning at a time, especially among the same group of people.

Take the cross, for example. For the Romans, the cross symbolized the state's right to punish, humiliate, and kill those who challenged its authority.

For the early Christians, the cross became a symbol of an authority beyond that of any earthly power, a gateway to individual freedom and salvation. The cross, even an image of a cross, could not stand for the two contradictory meanings simultaneously. One of the meanings had to give way to the other.

This brings us back to the flag, the national anthem and, especially, our athletes. Throughout the history of the West, athletics has played the role of physical, rough-and-tumble theater. And theater in the West, whether it is on a stage, screen, or field, has been the venue through which we Westerners work out (play out, if you like) our issues and conflicts, all while avoiding real civil strife and bloodshed.

In the West, actors, either on the screen or on the field, take on certain roles and, with them, certain expectations from the audience.

In football, and increasingly in the "knock-her-down!" atmosphere of the WNBA, the image of the athlete has come to embody many of our national aspirations: a love of rough competition, self-restraint, a sense of fairness, the operation of justice and the notion that anyone, regardless of his or her station at birth, can, through hard work, sacrifice, and discipline, rise to great heights of achievement and wealth.

The NFL and the WNBA are keenly aware of their athletes' images and have a long list of "dos and don'ts" that govern players' behavior both on and off the field or court. Those players who will not conform to the rules are fined or removed from play entirely. Adopting "a dignified posture along the sidelines" during the playing of the national anthem is still listed among the "dos" for WNBA players.

The flag and the national anthem are symbols of the values that are acted out on the field of athletics: universal fairness and equality of opportunity, justice and the belief that through personal and collective sacrifice, we can achieve a more perfect (note, not "perfected") union.

America is a multiethnic society, and these creeds are the ties that bind us together as a nation. Nations that lose their common bonds, their national glue, come apart, and often violently.

In contrast to the common meanings of the flag, the national anthem, and our athletes, groups like Black Lives Matter and the NAACP, which pushed "Lift Every Voice and Sing" as the black national anthem, claim that the flag and anthem should be seen and heard as symbols of oppression against black Americans. If such claims were true, I would be the first to kneel, cut down every flagpole from sea to shining sea, burning their odiously fluttering rags in one giant heap.

But the claims are not true. I live not far from Ferguson, Missouri, where, in 2014, police officer Darren Wilson shot and killed Michael Brown, and Black Lives Matter became a national movement. As documented by the Obama Justice Department, "hands up, don't shoot!" never happened. Brown was shot because he tried to take Wilson's gun, not because he was black.

Black Lives Matter, as well documented, has repeatedly lied about race and our judicial system. America's legal system, especially the police, is not focused on the destruction of anyone. There are violent forces loose in black communities, but they are not grounded in "systemic racism" or oppressive law enforcement.

In the hands of the politically unscrupulous, facts play little to no part in the meaning infused into an image. Even though Brown did not put his hands up and cry "don't shoot," both the slogan and the gesture were appropriated as symbols of protest, and, in the words of Matt Pierce, staff writer for the Los Angelous Times, "transformed into a different kind of weapon."

Political and racial tension is running high in 2026, and today's athletes, be they in the NFL, the NBA, or the WNBA, are playing, or perhaps being played, in a dangerous game, both for them and for our nation. To reassign meaning to the flag, the national anthem, or themselves as athletes further opens a Pandora's box of national conflict and hostility that no player or commissioner can foresee or control.

Views expressed in this article are opinions of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of The Epoch Times.

items.title: Father Of Doomed Learjet's 20-Year-Old Co-Pilot Breaks Silence On Her Final Mayday
items.content_text:
Father Of Doomed Learjet's 20-Year-Old Co-Pilot Breaks Silence On Her Final Mayday

The co-pilot of the Learjet that crashed into a Greenacres, Florida, neighborhood on Sunday was 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras. Her father, Allan Filgueiras, confirmed her identity to NBC Miami. Her sister, Giulia, said the family is from Brazil, that Nathalia learned to fly from their father, who is also a pilot, and that flying was her greatest passion, NBC reported.

On Friday, Allan Filgueiras spoke publicly for the first time. He told reporters he has played the air traffic control recording of his daughter's last words again and again, looking for any clue to what brought the jet down - and that what he heard instead was his daughter fighting to keep control of the aircraft to the very end, NBC News reported.

"She made me so proud," he said. "She showed me what it is to be a hero." The family's attorney, Stuart Grossman, said the point of the news conference was to protect her reputation as well as her memory.

Filgueiras earned her pilot's license in 2023 when she was 17, while a senior at West Boca Raton Community High School. Her license rated her to fly the jet but not to be in command of the flight, according to the same report. Her mother, Camila Corteleti, told the New York Times that she had logged more than 1,300 flight hours and worked for Upper Jets, a Fort Lauderdale private charter company, the Times reported.

Grossman said her father began taking her flying when she was 12. "When we were flying together, I used to instruct her. And then, she became my instructor," Allan Filgueiras said. Grossman acknowledged that many people will be surprised a 20-year-old was co-piloting a private jet. "But wait until you see her hours, and what the government proves about her capabilities," he said.

Her stepfather, Thiago Corteleti, told the New York Post she texted her boyfriend about 10 minutes before the crash: "I've got turbulence, I've got ice," the Associated Press reported. In the last air traffic control transmissions, the crew reported ice buildup and severe turbulence, then said: "We're going to crash into the ground." The AP also reports the call ended with "We're out of time!"

The jet, a Learjet 60 flying from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas with nine people aboard, had been at 35,000 feet when the crew reported problems and declared an emergency as it lost altitude rapidly. NTSB member Tom Chapman said "We do have some indication that the aircraft was breaking up before impact," and that parts could be found "some distance away from the actual impact site."

As we noted earlier, investigators have since found most of the left elevator miles from the crater, and the final minutes were captured in chilling air traffic control audio. Investigators have not said who was at the controls; the captain, Jeff Gregory, was 55.

The NTSB, which Grossman said has sent 20 investigators to South Florida, said Thursday it had recovered parts of one of the jet's engines and was still excavating the crater. The family is not pointing fingers yet. "We're not making allegations against anybody at this time," Grossman said, adding that the family will wait for the government's findings and then have its own experts review them.

Thinking back to Sunday's radio call, Allan Filgueiras said he wishes he could have been on the plane beside her to help. "It feels like someone is tearing the heart right out of my chest," he said, adding that he will "find a way to make her proud."

items.title: Microsoft Pulls The Plug On Oracle AI Rental As Post-Election Data Center Fallout Spreads
items.content_text:
Microsoft Pulls The Plug On Oracle AI Rental As Post-Election Data Center Fallout Spreads

More bad news for Oracle.

About an hour after we checked in with Oracle's PR team on how that whole "force majeure is commonplace" thing was working out...

... we got our answer, just not from Oracle:

According to Bloomberg, Microsoft has spent recent months switching off the computing capacity it rented from Oracle after declining to renew the contract. The reason is about as unflattering as it gets for a company that has staked its balance sheet on AI infrastructure: the Oracle hardware ran on older-generation Nvidia chips and, over time, "no longer fit the company's specifications."

ORCL promptly slid 4%, which put it, in our words, below the $116 equity offering price it sold $10 billion in stock at just four days ago. Recall that the stock hit $248.15 on June 1. Investors who bought the "de-risked" story this week are already underwater on a deal that is barely four days old, and the stock has lost more than half its value in five months.

But the Microsoft headline is just the latest entry on a list that has grown every single day since Tuesday night, when voters handed governors' mansions in the states holding roughly 45% of planned US data center capacity to candidates who promised to pause them. Put the two together and Oracle has a problem at both ends of its pipeline: its old capacity is too old to rent, and its new capacity may be too blue to build.

Too Old To Rent

Some history first. The Oracle-Microsoft deal was announced in 2023 to power the AI version of Bing, and at the time, Bloomberg notes, the idea of Microsoft renting servers from a direct rival was taken as early proof of just how short the world was of compute. (The full size of the deal was never disclosed.)

Three years later, the same arrangement is proof of something else: GPUs age, and the biggest buyer of rented compute in the world is no longer willing to pay for the old ones.

Oracle, naturally, disagrees. A spokesperson told Bloomberg demand for its AI infrastructure "remains strong, including for earlier-generation" GPUs, and reminded everyone that in September it said it was renewing contracts for four-year-old GPUs at a 20% premium to the original price. That 20% premium has been a staple of the bull case: just this Wednesday, Wells Fargo's Jerry Revich, in "Texas Policy Reset Adds Timing Risk to 20-30% of the Data Center Power Pipeline" (available to pro subs), cited Oracle's 97.9% AI infrastructure utilization and "20% average renewal/resale premium" as evidence that "token economics remain attractive."

Well, one renewal just came in at a 100% discount.

Microsoft's retreat also fits a pattern we have been tracking for weeks. Microsoft committed more than $80 billion to rent capacity from neoclouds like CoreWeave, Nscale and Nebius, and per Bloomberg, key leaders there have grown frustrated over high costs and delays, tightened oversight of data center projects and debated whether to sign any new neocloud deals at all. In October, Microsoft walked from Nscale's UK deal; on Thursday came the report that it won't expand its Texas deal with Nscale either, along with the disclosure that it spent $5 billion less on Q3 capex than projected due to delays at third-party capacity, including IREN's.

Translation: Microsoft wants new chips, on time, in its own specifications, and it is increasingly unwilling to pay landlords who can't deliver all three. Which is a problem for every landlord whose collateral is a rack of chips that gets one generation older every year the power doesn't show up.

Too Blue To Build

And the power is now even less likely to show up on time.

Cleanview counts nine states where the governor or governor-elect has promised or already imposed a pause on new data centers. Together they hold 158.6 GW of planned capacity, or 41% of the entire US pipeline:

Now look at who is most exposed. Every single gigawatt of OpenAI's planned capacity sits in a state whose new governor backed a pause on the campaign trail, as does 45% of Microsoft's:

Why does that matter for Oracle? Because OpenAI is Oracle. The $300 billion compute contract that sent ORCL soaring in September 2025 is being built across Texas (Abilene, Shackelford County), New Mexico, Wisconsin and Michigan, which is why OpenAI shows up at 100% above. Two of those states, Texas and New Mexico, delivered the most hostile results of the night.

Take New Mexico, home of Project Jupiter, the 2.45 GW Oracle-OpenAI Stargate campus that regular readers know all too well. Back on Sept 24 Oracle sent a force majeure notice to the Blue Owl unit developing the site, then insisted the notice was "commonplace" and meant nothing. We had a different reading at the time:

The more important detail came that night, when the FT reported that Oracle remains on the contractual hook regardless: if Jupiter isn't ready, Oracle still owes a "carry cost" in lieu of rent for up to three years, enough to cover the interest on the debt in full plus a set equity return for Blue Owl's funds. As one person familiar with the contract put it, "The power delivery risk sits with Oracle, not the investors." Here is the structure we mapped out at the time. Note who sits at the bottom of every arrow:

And for the record, here is what we wrote in that same Sept 24 post, six weeks before the vote: the construction delays "will only get worse if Democrats win back the house at the midterm elections." They won back a lot more than the House, so we'll allow ourselves a modest victory lap.

Two weeks later, Oracle was trucking compressed natural gas to its data centers because the Jupiter pipeline was running late, and the $18 billion of construction loans behind the campus were already quoted at 89-91 cents on the dollar (per the FT).

On Tuesday, New Mexico elected Deb Haaland, and the morning after, she told reporters her plan for day one: "a moratorium for large-scale data centers with the legislature passing a set of guardrails." As for Jupiter's gas plants specifically, Cleanview notes Haaland has written that under her watch they would "not exist." The fuel-cell air permit is still pending, with a Nov 23 decision deadline. Hey guys, any updates?

Texas is no better. As we laid out in "What's Next For Data Centers After The Blue Tsunami", governor-elect Gina Hinojosa turns Abbott's audit-based freeze into one tied to legislation, which means at least through the May 31, 2027 session end. And the Goldman TMT desk noted this morning that part of today's bounce came from "benign comments from Texas governor-elect on datacenters." When "benign" is the bull catalyst, you know where the bar is.

Goldman: "Timing Rather Than Cancellations"... For Now

Goldman's research department spent Friday pushing back on the panic, and in fairness, it has the numbers. In his "End of Week Market Intelligence: dc downside?" (available to pro subs), Chris Hussey frames this week's debate as follows:

"At the core of market concerns this week is a debate around whether all of the compute power that has been ordered (semiconductors, servers, fiber optic cables) will have a place to be installed when it is delivered in the years ahead."

Goldman's answer is mostly yes, at least through 2027. Hardware analyst Mike Ng "US Data Center Capacity update: Framing risks to our data center forecasts", also available to pro subs) says capacity already under construction implies 22/24 GW-IT of net additions in 2027/28, matching his 20/24 GW forecasts, and calls the key risk "timing rather than cancellations." The catch is Texas, which accounts for 20% of 2027 and 27% of 2028 under-construction additions:

E&C analyst Adam Bubes went a step further and actually raised his US data center construction spending forecasts to $80 billion/$100 billion for 2026/27 (from $67 billion/$87 billion), introducing $125 billion for 2028. His reasoning: every project in Goldman's 2027 forecast has already broken ground. 2028 is another story, though: only about half of the 2028 projects on Goldman's watch list have broken ground, and beyond that it's almost all PowerPoint:

Note the light blue. That is the "announced" capacity, and it is exactly what a governor's moratorium hits first. Bubes concedes as much, arguing moratoria "would primarily impact projects that have not yet started" and would smooth the cycle into 2029/30 "rather than impacting the TAM."

Maybe. But today's Microsoft story shows why "timing" is not as harmless as it sounds. A project that slips two years gets delivered into a world where the chips ordered for it are two years older. For a hyperscaler, a delay is a timing issue. For whoever owns the GPUs, it's a depreciation issue. Microsoft just told Oracle which one it is.

And somebody is going to have to fund the wait. Goldman credit strategist Amanda Lynam estimates hyperscalers are financing 36% of this year's capex with credit (and 35% next year), while only 43% of the $687 billion of AI-related financing so far this year came from hyperscalers. Oracle has already done its share: as we noted on Monday, it blew through its entire four-year $20 billion "hard cap" in a single morning, five days after promising it. Which, as regular readers know, is why we have been calling AI a debt bubble since last October.

The Casualty List Gets Longer

The Oracle news landed at the end of a week that saw the Nasdaq suffer its worst day since March 2020 on Thursday (-6.4%), while Goldman's AI data center-levered basket fell 12% in a single session. The headlines since then haven't helped much:

  • ING was said to be selling a $500 million data center loan portfolio (Thursday);
  • Bloomberg reported this morning that the ECB is mulling a review of bank loans to data centers, following the Bank of England's own probe last year;
  • and Nomura's Ting Lu argued that China's AI buildout "may benefit significantly" from a blue wave that slows US data center construction. Somewhere in Hangzhou, a capex budget just got revised higher.

Here is the updated ZH Casualty List, with Oracle as the newest entry:

Who's Left Holding The Old Chips?

Jefferies' Julien Dumoulin-Smith summed up the sellside consensus on the election in one line "The Blue Morning After: State-by-State Election Scorecard"): "Demand moves right, not away." Goldman says the same thing with more charts.

Perhaps they're right about demand. But capacity that moves right ages, financing that moves right costs more, and a landlord that moves right keeps paying for the slip (just ask Oracle's lenders on Jupiter). Today's Microsoft story is the first clear sign of what happens at the other end: the tenant with the deepest pockets in AI is choosing newer chips over older contracts, and that probably makes Oracle's 20% renewal premium look a lot more like an exception.

Which leaves Oracle squeezed on both sides: the older chips it already owns are losing their best renter, while the new campuses meant to replace them sit in exactly the states that just voted for a pause. Goldman hosted Oracle management today, of all days; we'd love to know what was said in the room. Until then, we'll keep asking the obvious question:

Much more in the full Goldman "End of Week Market Intelligence: dc downside?", and "US Data Center Capacity update" both available to pro subs.

CAIR Shuts Down Florida Operations After DeSantis Administration's Terror Designation Takes Effect

Authored by AG News Staff via American Greatness,

The Council on American-Islamic Relations has suspended its operations in Florida after the state's designation of its Florida chapter as a domestic terrorist organization took effect.

The move came after U.S. District Judge Allen C. Winsor of the Northern District of Florida rejected CAIR's emergency request to block the designation.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, who won reelection Tuesday over Democrat Jose Javier Rodriguez, confirmed the news on social media Thursday, the day the designation took effect. He called the ruling a "great win by our Solicitor General's office and for the people of Florida."

This morning, a federal court upheld Florida's Domestic Terrorist Organization law and rejected CAIR's attempt to stop the designations.

Great win by our Solicitor General's office and for the people of Florida!

— Attorney General James Uthmeier (@AGJamesUthmeier) November 5, 2026

Gov. Ron DeSantis also celebrated, calling it a "good win" and adding, "Florida is holding CAIR accountable."

Florida is holding CAIR accountable. https://t.co/KAZJYFJQBk

— Ron DeSantis (@RonDeSantis) November 5, 2026

DeSantis and other members of the Florida Cabinet have long maintained that CAIR has ties to Hamas and the Muslim Brotherhood. Last year, DeSantis signed an executive order labeling CAIR and CAIR Florida as terrorist organizations, cutting them off from public contracts, funding and benefits from state and local agencies.

CAIR blamed the governor for the shutdown. "We have suspended our operations in Florida because of Governor DeSantis and other state officials' baseless and unconstitutional enforcement of the state's unprecedented new 'domestic terrorist organization' laws against us," the group said. It said the ACLU, the Southern Poverty Law Center and other partners are representing it in a federal lawsuit on First Amendment and due process grounds.

The ACLU vowed to fight on. "Today's ruling is deeply disappointing and we are appealing it," said Ashley Gorski, senior counsel with the ACLU National Security Project. "We cannot allow this dangerous and sweeping censorship regime to stand."

Founded in Washington in 1994 by Omar Ahmad and Nihad Awad, CAIR describes itself as working to enhance understanding of Islam, protect civil rights and empower American Muslims. It has chapters in more than 20 states.

items.title: Dreaming Of Your Own "Human Drone"? FAA Throws Wrench In Part 103 Flight Plan
items.content_text:
Dreaming Of Your Own "Human Drone"? FAA Throws Wrench In Part 103 Flight Plan

Planning to buy a single-seat electric multicopter and zip around Class G airspace under Part 103 ultralight rules? The Federal Aviation Administration may have just grounded those hopes and dreams. 

YouTuber Jimmy (Jimmys World) recently flew a Chinese YiVTOL S-Zero Plus "human drone" at a dealer demonstration in Tennessee. The video racked up millions of views, but eight days later, the YouTuber received a letter from the FAA telling him the eVTOL was illegal under Part 103.

Jimmy said the $100,000 eVTOL was marketed as a Part 103 ultralight, meaning a lightweight recreational vehicle subject to minimal requirements.

The FAA's letter raises questions about whether applying 1980s-era rules written for gas-powered ultralights to battery-powered personal VTOLs is outdated and could inhibit eVTOL growth in the US while China fully embraces the new form of flying transportation.

Jimmy outlined the FAA's hard line on allowing flights in this eVTOL:

Batteries count toward the 254-pound empty-weight limit. Unlike aviation fuel, which burns off and is excluded, batteries remain on the aircraft and weigh essentially the same whether depleted or charged. A 2012 FAA Office of the Chief Counsel letter to Rainbow Aviation explicitly rejected treating batteries as fuel. Including them prevents unlimited battery capacity that would defeat the original 1981 intent of limiting range and endurance for uncertified pilots. Jimmy estimates the packs weigh 50-60 pounds each; two packs alone consume a large portion of the 254-pound allowance before the airframe, motors, propellers and seat are counted. Larger variants with more batteries are effectively impossible under the rule.

Remote-control training mode makes it a drone, not an ultralight. Part 103 is for manned operation by a single occupant with direct pilot control. The dealer's setup, which uses a ground-station remote for takeoff and training and allows control to be handed over or reclaimed, turns it into an unmanned aircraft system. Drone rules, such as Part 107 or exemptions for heavier aircraft, are entirely different. Jimmy's summary: "You're now a drone. You're not an aircraft."

Part 103 already bans flight over congested areas or open-air assemblies of people. Even if the weight and control issues were resolved, practical utility would remain constrained. Legal places to fly these aircraft remain limited.

Traditional experimental aviation pathways for these lightweight eVTOLs could be allowed but there would be considerably more regulation and bureaucracy. 

As Jimmy put it, "FAA won't allow him to fly it yet until they get all the approvals and avionics and radios, and basically it's going to be a small helicopter, and that's kind of the category they're looking at."

items.content_text:
Why Were Iranian-Linked Ships Lingering Over The World's Undersea Internet Cables

Brent futures remain below $100 a barrel in early New York trading as diplomatic signals continue to emerge. Markets are betting that the Democratic sweep has raised the odds of a near-term peace deal, which was enough to wipe out Brent's $20-a-barrel war risk premium this week. 

But the US and Iran could still return to all-out fighting as US planners want to wipe out Pickaxe Mountain and disable Kharg Island. 

All this hopium overlooks the fact that the global energy and refining crisis is far from over. Even if the two sides reach a deal, it will take time to replenish depleted stockpiles worldwide.

Another geopolitical wake-up call comes from the Financial Times, which reported this morning that at least four Iran-linked ships lingered over undersea telecommunications cables in the Gulf of Oman in October.

The report cited maritime intelligence firm Windward, which identified three tankers under US sanctions and a small Iranian fishing vessel. 

One tanker, the Celestial Sea, spent more than four hours circling near the 2Africa cable on Oct. 14. The next day, it switched off its automated tracking system while between two cable routes. The fishing vessel lingered over the Europe India Gateway and Transworld cables in the latter part of the month. 

Windward told the FT that the vessels sailed "normally until they reached a specific cable corridor, and only then slowed, looped, turned back, loitered or went dark." The firm said the pattern "fits the profile of mapping the cable routes, or placing charges or mines on them while dark."

Last month, Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said, "Seven major undersea internet cables run through the Strait of Hormuz, carrying all commercial and internet data. We just want [the US] to realize that new targets and new weapons shall be unveiled. And ultimately, we shall sweep the remnants of US power out of the region."

items.title: After Weeks Of Riots, France's Thursday General Strike Forces Macron's PM To Blink
items.content_text:
After Weeks Of Riots, France's Thursday General Strike Forces Macron's PM To Blink

France's nationwide strike put 575,000 people in the streets on Thursday by the Interior Ministry's count, topping the 550,000 it counted on Oct. 17, when protests in several cities turned into riots and looting. France's major labor union, the CGT, claimed close to 1.6 million, France 24 reports. After the marches, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu called unions and employers to Matignon on Monday for talks on wages and the cost of living.

The CFDT, CGT, FO, UNSA and FSU called the strike over wages, pensions and the 2027 budget, and Sortiraparis reported that every other union federation had said it would take part, with the CFTC backing it.

Grève du 5 novembre: la CGT prévoit 244 lieux de rassemblement à travers la France pic.twitter.com/G8EohjyrBP

— BFM Première (@BFMPremiere) November 4, 2026

The Interior Ministry said the declared marches "generally went well" (translated) and reported 448 arrests, according to franceinfo, against 1,314 after the Oct. 24 protests. 

Riot police fired teargas at the end of the marches in Lyon and Bordeaux, while officers in Lyon also used water cannon as fires were set in the streets. 

Police were pelted with pétanque balls in Rennes and projectiles in Pau and Orléans, and in Toulouse, fireworks fired at a school started a blaze that burned its student services office. In eastern Paris, police used teargas to keep students from reaching the Hélène Boucher high school after stopping students from building barricades out of wheeled bins outside of schools in the early morning.

The unions called the strike after leaders met Lecornu on Oct. 21 and left "unanimously disappointed," according to Euronews. CGT leader Sophie Binet said Lecornu announced no measures and showed "no consideration of our demands," and that she wants strikes to take over from street protests so the movement can "generalise the strike." The CFTC's Cyril Chabanier was more upbeat, saying the government "opened the door" to talks on the minimum wage.

The strike follows weeks of unrest. According to the Interior Ministry, the Oct. 17 protests at about 550,000 people and the Oct. 24 protests at 410,000, the Rio Times reports, with unions claiming higher figures. The Oct. 24 protests brought 1,314 arrests and 53 injured police and gendarmes. In response, Paris imposed a curfew from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. around Place de la République and Les Halles, and Lyon renewed its own. Euronews says Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin put the number of people taken into police custody nationwide at 2,500, with 917 sent for immediate trial, and that the government blames "the ultra-left" for much of the violence. President Emmanuel Macron, speaking from Qatar, called for "firmness" against those responsible.

High school and university students have been protesting for weeks as well, demanding more funding for education, repairs to school buildings and the scrapping of the Parcoursup admissions platform - which the government says will be replaced for the 2028 admissions round.

Rail was the most exposed sector to the strike, since the four representative SNCF unions called the strike. About one in ten TGVs was expected to be canceled, and Intercités, TER, RER and Transilien services disrupted, with only one train in three running on RER D. SUD-Rail secretary Fabien Villedieu called it "a big strike over pay, jobs and working conditions." Paris metro, bus and tram services were forecast to run normally, though CGT-RATP's open-ended strike notice let staff walk out individually. Airport ground-staff unions also called a strike, but France's civil aviation authority had not asked airlines to cancel flights at Roissy or Orly. The Eiffel Tower closed for the day.

In schools, the Education Ministry estimated 17.54% of public primary teachers were on strike, while the FSU-SNUipp union said nearly 80 Paris schools were closed and up to 75% of teachers were out in parts of Seine-Saint-Denis. The government said 81 high schools were disrupted on Thursday, against 1,000 by the student unions' count, and that a third of higher education sites were affected, the Guardian reports.

Monday's talks at Matignon will hopefully be more productive than the Oct. 21 meeting, where, by the unions' account, Lecornu offered nothing. Labor Minister Jean-Pierre Farandou told TF1 that "the government wants to act fast on the Smic," France's minimum wage, with a boost he said "is exceptional in nature" (translated). Echos Plus reports the government is weighing a 0.6% increase, against the extra 100 euros a month net the CFDT wants.

That said, the 2027 budget the unions are striking over has already hit a wall. On Wednesday, the day before the walkout, the National Assembly unanimously rejected the revenue half of the bill, as we noted, which sinks the whole bill in the lower house and sends the government's original text to the Senate, LCP reports.

Whether Thursday becomes the start of something longer is still an open question. Binet, who had urged workers to extend the strike beyond one day, called it "a very serious time, with a very dangerous authoritarian drift from the government" (translated), according to the Guardian. The eight unions in the coalition said "the only thing that will stop the mobilization is an answer to our demands" (translated), and they meet again Monday, after the Matignon talks, to decide what comes next.

The Yellow Vests coordination, which called Thursday a "People's November 5," called for the strike to "continue and spread" with blockades and local actions across France on Friday, Sortiraparis reported. For Saturday, Paris police approved a union march from République to Nation on Thursday's route but banned the Yellow Vests' "Act IV" rally at Place de la Concorde, both called for 2 p.m., it reported Friday. The movement says it will turn out anyway and "disobey massively" (translated); joining a banned demonstration carries a 135-euro fine.

items.title: Minnesota Just Sent A Somali Daycare Owner To The Statehouse - Wait Till You See The Money
items.content_text:
Minnesota Just Sent A Somali Daycare Owner To The Statehouse - Wait Till You See The Money

Minnesota voters on Tuesday elected a Somali daycare owner whose center has collected $7.29 million from the state childcare subsidy program at the heart of last winter's viral fraud scandal.

Democratic-Farmer-Labor (DFL) candidate Abdi Daisane, a Somali American who came to the US more than 15 years ago, won House District 14A with about 52% of the vote, beating Republican Mike Conway, the St. Cloud City Council president, and flipping a Republican-held seat, MPR News reported. He becomes St. Cloud's first Somali American state lawmaker. Daisane lost the same race in 2024 to Republican Rep. Bernie Perryman, who ran for the state Senate this year instead.

Daisane gave part of his victory speech in Somali.

He spoke Somali for his victory speech https://t.co/6P67kFelZT pic.twitter.com/9xxZyj3Wnd

— End Wokeness (@EndWokeness) November 4, 2026

Daisane launched his second run for the seat on Christmas Eve 2025, the New York Post reported at the time. Two days later, YouTuber Nick Shirley posted his video tour of seemingly empty Somali-linked daycares - drawing more than 131 million views on X in five days, and FBI Director Kash Patel said the bureau had surged agents and resources to Minnesota as the Trump administration froze childcare funding to the state. Days before Tuesday's election, the Justice Department uncovered another $29 million in Minnesota benefits fraud.

Daisane hasn't been charged with anything, and we found no sign his center appeared in Shirley's videos.

The Money

Daisane is the CEO of Blooming Kids Child Care Center in St. Cloud. The center received $7.29 million in Child Care Assistance Program (CCAP) payments from 2018 through 2025, according to Department of Children, Youth, and Families data posted by the Minnesota House's Fraud Prevention and State Agency Oversight Committee. The payments more than tripled in three years, from $439,034 in 2021 to $1.54 million in 2024, and held at $1.52 million in 2025. DCYF, which runs CCAP, wouldn't provide payment information when Alpha News asked.

Blooming Kids also took in $598,251.62 in approved claims from the federally funded Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP) since late 2020, according to Minnesota Department of Education records Alpha News obtained through a data request. MDE hadn't confirmed the figure as of Alpha's report.

From 2020 into early 2022, the center's CACFP sponsor was Partners in Nutrition, Department of Education records reviewed by Alpha News show. In September, Partners in Nutrition agreed to hand over $18.5 million, everything it had, and permanently dissolve to settle Attorney General Keith Ellison's lawsuit alleging it knowingly and repeatedly billed the state for meals that were never served between October 2020 and February 2022, and facilitated widespread fraud at the sites it was supposed to be monitoring.

Ellison put PIN in the same breath as Feeding Our Future, the nonprofit at the center of Minnesota's pandemic food-aid fraud prosecutions, blaming "bad actors like PIN and Feeding Our Future" for eroding trust in government programs. "My office continues to actively investigate a number of individuals and entities affiliated with PIN for violations of the Minnesota False Claims Act," he said. Blooming Kids was not among the food sites named in the lawsuit. Alpha News asked whether the center, Daisane or anyone tied to it had been investigated in connection with Partners in Nutrition; Ellison's office didn't respond.

So Where Are The Kids?

Late last month, a worker at a nearby business told Alpha News, "I do not recall ever seeing children entering or leaving the facility," and said a white van tied to the center carried only an adult driver. The same source later reported seeing roughly 5 to 10 school-age children on the rear playground around 5:00 to 5:30 p.m. on some occasions. Fox News Digital visited on Thursday and found a mostly empty parking lot, windows covered in tinted, mirrored film and a paper sign on the front door directing visitors to another entrance.

The Violations

State regulators have cited Blooming Kids for at least 16 licensing violations in three reviews between October 2024 and October 2025, Alpha News found in state records. In the October 2024 review, regulators found children "were subjected to prohibited disciplinary actions." An April 2025 licensing investigation found staff "did not supervise the children at all times." The October 2025 review flagged infants not placed on their backs to sleep without the required documentation, unlabeled infant bottles and lapses in required CPR and first-aid training.

The state also fined the center $400 in November 2024 for two background-study violations, including letting an employee work for nearly seven months after the worker's background study expired. The order was addressed to Daisane as the center's authorized agent. The Department of Human Services' licensing database shows another review, on Oct. 8 of this year, that also found violations. Blooming Kids is licensed for up to 113 children, and its license remains active.

During his first run in 2024, after a 2023 review cited the center for equipment in disrepair and missing immunization and staff-qualification records, Daisane told St. Cloud Live, "I have always prioritized providing a safe and nurturing environment for all children," and said that when problems come up, "we learn from our mistakes and we do better next time."

The Wife

Daisane's wife told BBC Somali in 2023 that she crossed the US-Mexico border to join him, an interview that resurfaced online during the campaign. "I smuggled myself and jumped over the wall for my love," she said, according to Alpha News' translation.

🚨 UPDATE: Somali "daycare owner" Abdi Daisane (D) has just been elected to the state Minnesota House - and is wife has BRAGGED about ILLEGALLY INVADING our country

Daisane's St. Cloud "daycare," Blooming Kids, has been cited for 16 state violations since July 2024 ‼️

"I... pic.twitter.com/9WlG5znxqK

— Eric Daugherty (@EricLDaugh) November 4, 2026

Daisane's campaign didn't answer Alpha News' questions about her entry or the violations, and Daisane didn't respond to Alpha or Fox News about the center's funding.

After the results came in, ACT for America founder Brigitte Gabriel tagged DHS and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on a post about Daisane's win and his wife: "great opportunity to do something about this."

@DHSgov @SecMullinDHS - great opportunity to do something about this

— Brigitte Gabriel (@ACTBrigitte) November 5, 2026

"We are a lost state. We should cede it to Canada," posted Matt Brodsky, president of Red Ax Strategies.

— Matthew RJ Brodsky (@MattRJBrodsky) November 5, 2026

items.title: Trump Names Miller New Chief Of Staff As 'Most Powerful' Wiles Is Out
items.content_text:
Trump Names Miller New Chief Of Staff As 'Most Powerful' Wiles Is Out

President Donald Trump has tapped longtime loyalist Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, effective Monday, in a major shakeup following Republicans' devastating midterm election defeat.

"I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026. Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff - She has done a great job!" the president posted on Truth Social.

Miller, currently serving as deputy chief of staff, would replace Susie Wiles and take command of the White House's day-to-day operations at a critical moment for Trump's second term. The move would elevate one of the president's most trusted and influential advisers, a driving force behind his hardline immigration policies and America First agenda.

Wiles' departure would also mean the exit of one of the White House's most powerful behind-the-scenes power brokers. During an appearance on Joe Rogan's podcast this week, Calley Means, a former adviser to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., described Wiles as the "most powerful chief of staff in modern American history," alleging that she exercised extraordinary control over virtually every major policy decision inside the Trump administration.

Means told Rogan that the White House operates under an unusually centralized power structure, with Wiles' office effectively holding veto power over policy decisions.

"No policy decision gets done without her office giving it the okay," he told Rogan, describing the arrangement as "absolutely systematic."

Means further explained that Cabinet secretaries routinely strategize about how to win Wiles' favor.

If his account is accurate, her departure would represent far more than a routine personnel change, potentially dismantling one of the administration's most consequential centers of power.sssssssssssss

items.title: 从 Linux 到维基百科：志愿者如何构建互联网
items.content_text: Linux 和维基百科代表了一种被称为同侪生产（Peer Production）的模式——这一名字由法学教授 Yochai Benkler 提出。古典经济学认为，如果想要人们开展合作以及有效分配合作所产生的成果，那么最有效方式是通过私人营利性企业实现，即由这些企业在开放市场中销售商品或服务。企业雇用员工并支付报酬，而员工则通过合同承担义务，按照管理者分配的任务开展工作。员工劳动所创造的产品归公司所有，公司负责为产品定价、管理销售交易，支付员工薪酬以及分配经营过程中产生的利润。从理论上说，这些方法能解决几个关键问题：如何协调各方的利益动机、如何组织和安排工作任务，以及如何确保最终产出的成果能分配给有意愿且有能力支付费用的人。然而同侪生产为古典经济学传所依赖的行为模式提供了一种替代方案。在同侪生产中，无论是合同义务、经济激励，还是官僚式权威，都无法确保参与者一定会贡献自己的劳动，也无法保证这些劳动能有效组织。由此产生的成果属于公共资源（Public Commons），受到非排他性知识产权的保护。这意味着同侪生产所创造的资源无法直接在开放市场上进行定价。在理想形态中，同侪生产项目对自身工作的范围、领导者权威的合法性，以及值得投入精力的任务选择，都保持着完全的集体自主控制权。但在实践中，同侪生产往往只是以不同程度的形式得到运用，实施主体也包括一些并不完全符合上述所有定义标准的机构。

items.title: 特斯拉将停产 Cyber​​truck
items.content_text: 特斯拉 CEO 马斯克（Elon Musk）宣布将于 2027 年年中停产电动皮卡 Cyber​​truck。生产电动皮卡的工厂很可能转为生产电动出租车 Cybercabs。马斯克于 2019 年末宣布了外形奇特的 Cyber​​truck，预计售价低于 4 万美元，宣称它会和其主力电动汽车 Model 3 和 Model Y 一样随处可见。然而 Cyber​​truck 研发比特斯拉的其它车型更坎坷，为量产还修改了底盘结构，而 25 万年预售目标也根本无法实现。如今马斯克的粉丝将只剩下几个月的时间购买这款奇特的电动皮卡。

items.title: NASA 通过 AI 生成图像宣布 X-70 试验机
items.content_text: NASA 宣布了新试验机 X-70 Fractal，它展示了一幅生成图像——即并非实图，而是 AI 生成的。NASA 称，X-70 是载人飞行器，设计巡航速度为 0.75 马赫，最大飞行高度约 13700 米，航程 2778 公里。X-70 起飞重量为 4536 公斤，设计可容纳 900 公斤的机内外试验载荷。NASA 局长 Jared Isaacman 表示，这架试验机有望在两年内首飞。关于其具体设计细节和研发时间表目前知之甚少。NASA 公布的生成图像显示 X-70 与超音速侦察机 SR-71 非常相似。

items.title: 中国三季度 CO2 排放下降 3%
items.content_text: 根据 Carbon Brief 的分析，中国第三季度 7-9 月的 CO2 排放量同比下降 3.1%，为 2022 年以来最大降幅。今年至今中国碳排放量累计下降 0.5%。数据显示，中国第三季度石油消费量同比下降 4%，煤炭使用量同比下降 3%。第三季度 CO2 排放量下降的关键因素之一是燃煤发电量减少 3.3%。背后的原因是电力需求增长放缓，同时风能和太阳能未被利用的发电量也有所减少。太阳能、风能和核能的发电量同比增加了 110 TWh，超过了同期电力总需求增幅的两倍。

items.title: Silver Lake 和 PIF 磋商收购 Unity Software
items.content_text: 私募股权公司 Silver Lake 和沙特主权财富基金 PIF 在今年八月完成以 550 亿美元收购 EA 之后正在磋商收购游戏引擎提供商 Unity Software。Silver Lake 持有 8% 的 Unity 股权。在 Unity 发布最新财报前，收购财团论过约 250 亿美元的估值；财报发布后 Unity 市值升至约 215 亿美元。如果交易达成，Unity 将和 EA 一样私有化。Unity 的游戏引擎和开发者工具在游戏行业被广泛使用。Unity 于 2004 年在丹麦成立。自上市以来，公司业务已从游戏引擎扩大到广告技术和实时 3D 软件。

items.title: Salon 宣布终止出版
items.content_text: 有 31 年历史的 Salon 于 2026 年 11 月 5 日宣布从即日起停止出版。Salon 创办于 1995 年 11 月 5 日，当时的互联网与今天截然不同。一小群记者开始尝试创造一些与众不同的东西：他们希望创办一种具有鲜明风格、对世界充满好奇，并且坚信互联网能以全新的方式将新闻报道与读者连接起来的出版物。他们开创了一种全新的新闻报道形式，这种形式后来成为定义了一个全新的出版时代。

items.title: 摩托罗拉宣布第一款支持 GrapheneOS 的旗舰手机
items.content_text: 摩托罗拉宣布了第一款支持安全加固发行版 GrapheneOS 的旗舰手机 Signature 27，但售价高达 1600 美元。Signature 27 配备了高通目前最强大的移动芯片骁龙 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6，内存只有 12GB 没有 16GB 版本（目前内存供应紧张而且价格昂贵），存储空间为 512G​​B (UFS 4.1）；显示屏为 6.8英寸 Extreme AMOLED Duo，120Hz刷新率，12,000 尼特峰值亮度；电池 7000 mAh，90W 有线充电，15W (Qi) 无线充电，等等。

items.title: 微软画图应用曝出远程代码执行漏洞
items.content_text: 微软画图应用曝出了一个越界读取导致的远程代码执行漏洞，受影响版本从 11.0.0.0 到 11.2605.91.0 之前。画图应用被预装在每一台 Windows PC 上，最近一段时间微软为画图应用引入了越来越多的新功能，其中包括 AI 生成功能，它同时也给画图引入了新 bug。微软用户目前可能需要通过 Microsoft Store 官方应用商店下载修正后的版本，Windows Update 尚未推送新版本。

items.title: Kagi 开放搜索
items.content_text: 付费无广告搜索引擎 Kagi 宣布了最新更新，向所有人开放搜索，但免费用户搜索次数有限额。现在任何人无需注册账号可搜索 50 次，注册账号之后再增加 100 次。Kagi 还抨击了 Google 最近的一项决定：如果美国学校选择禁用 AI 那么它的搜索引擎也将会对学校关闭。Kagi 认为：教育不应沦为广告公司的人质，应当停止将企业利润置于教育学生这一核心使命之上。它呼吁美国学校可选择包括 Kagi 在内的其它搜索引擎。

items.title: 《尼尔：自动人形》释出更新游戏容量从 50GB 暴涨至 366GB
items.content_text: 2017 年发售的《尼尔：自动人形（Nier: Automata）》释出了最新更新，加入了对简繁体中文以及韩文的支持，但游戏的打包显然存在 bug，整个游戏文件的容量从 50GB 暴涨至 366GB。《尼尔：自动人形》共有八个 DLC，每增加一个 DLC，游戏的容量就会增加 40GB，也就是每个 DLC 都包含了主游戏文件。现在想要玩《尼尔》的中韩玩家最好先等待游戏开发商释出修正，除非你的 SSD 有几百 GB 的可用空间。

items.title: 印度金融机构遭黑客利用 AI 工具发动的网络攻击
items.content_text: 印度计算机应急响应小组（CERT-In）星期三发布安全通报，被称为“狡猾猎鹰”（Crafty Falcon）的黑客组织，已入侵非银行贷款机构、金融科技公司及加密货币交易所。攻击者利用公开可用的 AI 工具，实现高速自动化入侵。印度计算机应急响应小组形容这项威胁“仍在发生，且持续活跃”。该机构点名四款用于入侵的工具，分别是 ARTEX、PentAGI、Cairn 和 CyberStrikeAI。ARTEX 此前曾被用于攻击韩国银行。印度计算机应急响应小组没有说明这些攻击事件由谁发动，也未透露该组织的运作地点。该机构也没有称这些攻击由国家支持或主导，且其点名的攻击工具均可在网络上免费获取。

items.title: 同步导致电网呈现周期为一分钟的震荡
items.content_text: 今天的电网接入了数以百万计的数字控制设备，为了维持电力供需平衡，精准预测和实时控制必不可少。电力系统因此转变成为一种信息物理融合的基础设施（Cyber–Physical Infrastructure）。物理设备与数字控制系统之间形成了紧密的相互依存关系，在带来前所未有的效率与灵活性的同时也引入了新的系统性风险。根据发表在《Nature Energy》期刊上的一项研究，德国研究人员指出全球电力系统存在的一种由信息物理同步效应所引发的、周期为一分钟的相干振荡现象。除了故障和恶意攻击外，即使是良性的控制程序，当大量设备以协同一致的方式运行时，也可能产生系统层面的影响。在大规模信息物理能源系统中，非预期的同步行为可能引发反复出现且具有潜在放大效应的振荡现象。

items.title: 越南对足球直播盗版者判刑最高一年
items.content_text: 越南一家法院对 14 名参与盗版足球赛事直播网站 Bun Cha TV 的团队判处最高一年徒刑。4 名内容、编程和运营团队负责人被判处 12 个月徒刑，另外 5 人判处 10 个月监禁，2 人判处 8 个月监禁，3 名解说员被判处 10 个月缓刑。所有 14 名被告都承认了指控，配合了调查。Bun Cha TV 累计直播逾 15 万场体育赛事，通过博彩及赌博广告非法获利逾 200 亿越南盾（约 512 万人民币）。内容团队负责人获利逾 4.3 亿越南盾，解说员非法所得则在 3100 万到 4.8 亿越南盾不等。美国 MPAA 的代表称赞了这一判决。

items.title: 白宫网络监测到住宅代理活动
items.content_text: 安全公司 Layer3 Intel 报告，他们在分配给白宫的自治系统 AS2650 中监测到住宅代理服务的活动。住宅代理服务会将用户的网络地址租给其他人使用。Layer3 在 10 月 5 日-11 月 3 日期间观察到了 236 次住宅代理连接活动。住宅代理的源头被认为来自 Windows 11 设备安装的俄罗斯代理程序 Infatica。Layer3 Intel 指出，在30 天内有 26 天出现了源自白宫的代理出口节点流量，涉及 6 个 IP，大部分活动发生在傍晚，即下午 5 点至午夜之间。

items.title: Bazzite 45 释出
items.content_text: 基于 Fedora 的游戏发行版 Bazzite 释出了 v45。主要变化包括；基于 Fedora 45，更新 Open Gaming Collective(OGC)内核，支持罗技 TrueWheel 设备等等。过去几年 Linux 对游戏的支持有了显著改善，但对很多用户而言仍然需要自行配置。Bazzite 项目旨在让 Linux 桌面用户无需额外配置就能畅玩游戏，设计类似 Valve 的 SteamOS，但更适合通用桌面使用情景：SteamOS 主要支持 AMD GPU，Bazzite 包含了私有的 NVIDIA 驱动。

items.title: Google 和 OpenAI 的模型对特定口音有偏见
items.content_text: 研究人员调查了先进多模态模型如何评估面试、会议报告和英语口语能力测试中的语音，测试的模型包括了 Google 的 Gemini 2.5 Pro 和 Gemini 2.5 Flash，以及 OpenAI 的 GPT-Audio 1.5，开放权重模型 Qwen 3 Omni。这些模型对五种不同口音——美国、英国、中国、印度和尼日利亚——的英语语音进行了评分。AI 模型普遍将中国和尼日利亚口音的评分最低，印度口音居中，美国和英国口音的评分最高。即使内容完全相同，系统仍然认为美国和英国口音的表达方式和内容都更胜一筹。研究团队发现，明显的等级划分也体现在模型的解释中。研究人员说，模型反复声称中国和尼日利亚口音的英语使用者含糊不清或难以理解，但实际上它们非常擅长转录带有口音的语音，它们理解说话者，但它们只是基于口音，对说话者存在一种隐性的等级观念。

items.title: 富钾盐替换普通盐有助于每年预防数百万人死亡
items.content_text: 澳大利亚乔治全球健康研究院的研究人员评估了在 193 个国家将食盐供应转换为富钾盐的健康益处。他们发现，全球每年可预防近 300 万例死亡和 1000 万例心血管疾病和肾脏疾病新发病例。富钾盐是通过用氯化钾替代部分氯化钠（即普通食盐的主要成分）制成的。它在外观、味道和烹饪方式上都与普通食盐一样。2025 年世界卫生组织（WHO）认可使用富钾盐来降低血压和心血管疾病风险。全球范围内，30-79 岁成年人中有三分之一患有高血压，相当于约 14 亿人。心血管疾病（CVD）是全球死亡和残疾的主要原因，2023 年导致 1920 万人死亡，过去 30 年增加了近 50%。虽然潜在益处很大，但一个担忧是晚期肾病患者出现高钾血症（血钾水平过高）的风险。然而，研究发现，即使在晚期肾病患者中，益处也大于风险。

items.title: Swift 天文台从印尼上空重返大气层
items.content_text: NASA Neil Gehrels Swift 天文台于 11 月 4 日 7:39 a.m. EST 从印尼苏门答腊上空再入大气层，坐标为北纬 3.4 度、东经 98.6 度。天文台的大部分组件在重返大气层过程中烧毁，可能有部分组件幸存下来。Swift 天文台重 1.5 吨，于 2004 年发射升空，旨在研究高能伽马射线暴的起源。过去 22 年受大气阻力的影响 Swift 天文台的轨道高度在缓慢下降，过去两年的太阳活动加速了其坠落。今年 7 月 NASA 曾尝试了一次拯救任务，但任务失败。

items.title: 任天堂最大 ROM 芯片供应商准备退出
items.content_text: 任天堂 Switch 游戏机实体游戏卡带使用的 ROM 芯片供应也受到了 AI 热的影响。任天堂最大 ROM 芯片供应商旺宏电子在其第三季度财报中宣布它准备终止 ROM 芯片生产，脱离游戏行业。旺宏电子表示，ROM 芯片的产量在过去一年中缩减了 39%，目前仅占其业务总量的 5%。ROM 芯片正逐渐被利润更高、需求更旺盛的其它存储芯片所取代。这意味着任天堂未来只能依靠其它 ROM 芯片供应商如罗姆（Rohm）和蓝碧半导体（Lapis Semiconductor），意味着游戏卡带生产成本可能会进一步上升。任天堂已经承诺未来会继续提供实体游戏卡带，不会效仿索尼只提供游戏的数字版本。

items.title: 新型牙刷通过产生电对抗牙菌斑病原体
items.content_text: 一款新型牙刷可通过刷毛移动产生电能，进而可对抗产生牙菌斑的病原体。在为期 3 个月、涉及 115 名志愿者的试验中，牙刷在减少口腔中导致龋齿和牙周炎的细菌方面的效果优于常规的机械刷牙法。牙刷是人类对抗牙菌斑的最强战士，它每晚都能物理性地清除牙齿上的细菌生物膜。然而细菌总会卷土重来，因此每天早晨都会重新开始这场战斗。北京大学口腔医学院的研究人员研发出一种牙刷，其压电单丝刷毛在刷牙过程中弯曲时会产生电荷。这一过程会产生活性氧，进而能破坏牙齿上的生物膜。在实验室中，该装置能有效杀灭口腔病原体，如牙龈卟啉单胞菌（Porphyromonas gingivalis，可引发牙周炎）。研究人员还在真实口腔环境中评估了这种牙刷的实用性。他们将这种牙刷分发给总计 115 名志愿者，这些人都接受了相同的刷牙指导。根据对样本的基因测序和宏基因组测序结果，志愿者口腔中有几种口腔病原体的相对丰度有所下降。总体而言，与传统尼龙刷毛牙刷相比，这种牙刷能更好地控制牙菌斑、减轻牙龈炎症和出血。

They showed up everywhere, spawning a genre of social media post that featured pictures of Cybertrucks in the wild with captions that were variations on "look at this asshole." They even showed up in Fortnite in which, like its real-world counterpart, the car was a buggy mess. More distressingly, the vehicle was involved in numerous fatal crashes in which victims' families allege that the truck's design resulted in their loved ones being locked inside as they burned alive.

items.title: Trump Runs Away as Reporter Reminds Him He’s a Big, Giant Loser
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump scurried away from reporters Friday who asked about his new loser status.

Trump had an awkward interaction with reporters outside the White House after they asked him to explain his decision to replace chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller.

“I wanted to make a change,” Trump said. The president had previously dismissed reporting that he was planning to oust his “ice maiden”—but that was before Republicans suffered staggering losses in the midterm elections this week.

“We gotta make moves, sometimes in life you gotta make moves,” Trump said.

“We’ve beaten Iran. We are doing very well with Iran, we are talking to Iran, we have been. We haven’t lost a soldier in seven months, or six months,” Trump said.

In July, just four months ago, Trump attended a funeral for four U.S. service members who were killed in Iranian attacks in the Middle East, amid reports accusing the Trump administration of hiding casualty numbers. As of October, 23 soldiers had died as a result of Trump’s disastrous military campaign.

Trump quickly departed from the press gaggle, as one reporter shouted after him, “How does it feel to lose?” The president continued to flee and did not respond.

items.title: Trump Plans to Accuse Nonprofits of Having Terrorist Ties
items.content_text:
When in doubt, call them a terrorist. The White House is tapping into its standby strategy in its latest attempt to cripple nonprofits.

Donald Trump is weighing an executive order that would brand some nonprofits as having terrorist ties, The Wall Street Journal reported Friday. In doing so, the executive order would nix the organizations’ nonprofit status and fundamentally unravel their operations.

Sources familiar with the matter told the Journal that the executive order has been in the works for months and is not yet finished. It remains to be seen if Trump signs the effort or scraps it altogether.

It was not immediately clear which groups could be targeted, though the dangerous label could offer a much more immediate route for the administration to penalize its perceived political opponents than by pursuing potential legal violations through the IRS.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent hinted that such an effort was underway while speaking before the Ministerial on the Resurgence of Political Terrorism in mid-July.

“We are examining where tax-exempt status has been exploited, which charitable entities have become financial conduits for foreign-influence activity, and how those entrusted with stewardship of these organizations have instead enabled violence,” Bessent said at the time. “Where the evidence leads, we will not hesitate to follow.”

Nine organizations have already been identified as having terrorist ties, though those designations came from federal agencies such as the Treasury Department, as opposed to from the White House, according to the Journal.

But there have been numerous other occasions in which Trump and his allies have baselessly resorted to the “T-word” to advance their agenda. Earlier this year, officials across the Trump administration branded Minneapolis residents Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti as terrorists in order to brush their deaths at the hands of federal agents under the rug. And even in the most recent election cycle, Republicans resorted to slandering Representative Ilhan Omar and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed as terrorists in futile attempts to discredit their authority and undermine their influence.

items.title: Democratic “Moderation” Isn’t What Produced the Wave
items.content_text:
You can watch this episode of Right Now With Perry Bacon above or by following this show on YouTube or Substack. You can read a transcript here.

The midterms were not a story of Democratic moderation, political scientists Adam Bonica and Jake Grumbach argue. Instead, they say that Democrats won everywhere due to strong turnout among left-leaning voters, weaker turnout among conservatives, and some voters flipping to Democrats because of anger at President Trump. Increased Black turnout in the South and Latino voters in the Southwest swinging back against Republicans were particularly huge factors, according to the two scholars. The two emphasized that Democrats across the country won by employing an anticorruption message. Looking forward, Bonica, who teaches at Stanford University, says Democrats can take actions to address corruption and billionaire power within the House of Representatives and other institutions they will control, without needing Trump’s signature. Grumbach, who teaches at the University of California, Berkeley, says the results are the latest indication that all kinds of candidates can win elections. Therefore, in upcoming primaries, Democratic voters should focus on policies and candidates they like, rather than polls and perceptions of electability.

items.title: Transcript: Democratic “Moderation” Isn’t What Produced the Wave
items.content_text:
This is a lightly edited transcript of the November 5 edition of Right Now With Perry Bacon. You can watch the video here or by following this show on YouTube or Substack.

Perry Bacon: Good afternoon. This is Right Now on The New Republic. I’m the host, Perry Bacon, joined by two regular guests at this point, two of my favorite political scientists. Adam Bonica is at Stanford, Jake Grumbach is University of California, Berkeley, and this is our second podcast where we’re going to break down the election results and talk through them some. So Adam, Jake, thanks for joining me.

Jake Grumbach: Thanks for having me.

Bacon: So let me start with, when I talked to you all about doing this, I wasn’t thinking about discussing Mississippi. And really didn’t think about South Carolina either, to be candid about it. So I definitely had in my head 52 Senate seats, 230. That was what all the data experts were saying. And I think NBC had over 250 estimated.

So let’s talk about that first in terms of your general impressions. I’ll start with Adam and then go to Jake. Your general impressions of what we saw on Tuesday.

Adam Bonica: I had expected 250 seats. And that was way above. And even that, the size of the wave—no one predicted it would be this large. No one predicted Mississippi would be in play.

And one thing I thought was probably pretty clear is that it was unlikely that we would see a situation where we would just have a few races that were really close. It was probably going to be in the Senate either a big win or a pretty devastating defeat. It was much more bimodal than we’ve seen in the past.

But the other thing is this majority is going to rival the size of the majority Democrats came into office with after 2008. The year in which they were able to get a lot done. And it is surprising. I think we’re all still processing it.

Grumbach: Yeah, I agree with Adam. I’m sorry, I’m a little choppy right now. I’m having some computer difficulty, so I’m a little choppy right now, but I hope you can hear me.

I was surprised at this wave election. The one thing I’ve learned from Adam over the years is that in the modern polarized era, parties rise and fall together in wave elections. And this was a blue wave election, that across the country you saw massive blue shifts, and the wave was big enough that it carried even parts of the Deep South. It looks increasingly like it’s going to include Mississippi. Of course, Texas was a massive sweep by the Democrats.

But for me, I think one of the most underemphasized pieces of this has been Black organizing in the South. I served as an expert witness for the NAACP Legal Defense Fund, pre-Callais, in a Voting Rights Act case in Mississippi. And as a Northerner, I’m a Californian through and through, my impression of Mississippi being there was that it was unlikely to shift blue anytime soon, despite the efforts of Black people in Mississippi and the occasional caucusing coalition with white liberals as well.

So I think this was a real national wave election, and that’s the main takeaway, is that the Democratic Party fielded pretty good candidates across the board, across the country, that were compelling in their areas, and that the Republican Party under Donald Trump is incredibly unpopular.

Bacon: So I want to do a little bit about geography now. You talked about the South a little bit, but is that the big geography story? Or is there anything else about geography we should think about?

Bonica: I think the geography story has been one long in the making. So when all is said and done, I think the story of this election, one of the stories in terms of demographic shifts, is going to be, A, a turnout story, where we’re going to see that Democrats finally matched or exceeded Republican turnout rates. And two, that the youth vote was incredibly important.

And this has been a trend, right? When young people turn out and show up for Democrats, they tend to win in wave elections. That’s been the pattern since 2008, really.

And if you looked at Mississippi, if you looked at Texas, you saw these generational curves that were overwhelming. And a lot of the backsliding, I think we saw, the Democratic backsliding that Jake has written about, the gerrymandering, the pushing democratic institutions away from electoral democracy to preserve these majorities, had a lot to do with the fact that there was this generational pressure building in Texas, even in Mississippi. Mississippi has a big curve, too. The younger people in Mississippi were pretty Democratic.

And we saw it happen first in Georgia, but Texas and Mississippi, they’re not as unpredictable as one would think. I think it happened sooner than I would have expected. But the geography story, again, I think is really more a geography story about how young and old people in a lot of these states have very different sort of partisanship and preferences.

Bacon: Jake, I asked while you were away about if there’s a geography story of the election. I think the one story we’re talking about is the South. But is there any other geography story? And also, if you want to talk about the South more. Because I think that’s the takeaway, was Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas. Talk about that story. What do you think is driving that?

Grumbach: First, apologies for my technical difficulties. This seems to happen every other Perry Bacon show session I go on. Won’t happen again, I’m investing in better hardware.

So I do think Adam’s right about a geography story, but overall I’ve really learned from Adam that national waves carry the day, and this was true of much higher turnout among Black voters and young voters than previous midterm elections outside of potentially 2018.

Adam talks a lot about differential turnout. So swing voters do matter here. A number of people did switch from voting Trump 2024 to in 2026 voting the Democratic slate in their areas. But really across the country it’s that Republicans were more likely to stay home, people who lean Trump or wouldn’t ever vote for a Democrat but are now a little bit disappointed or embarrassed by the MAGA sort of performance.
